Moore, H. G., & Galloway, J. L. (1992). We Were Soldiers Once... and Young: Ia Drang, the Battle that Changed the War in Vietnam. Random House.

Nadal, R. (2016). The Battle I'll Never Forget: Battle of Ia Drang. AARP.

U.S. Department of the Army. (2022). Mission Command in the Ia Drang Valley. NCO Journal.

docs.title: Case Study — Battle of Leuctra (371 BC): The Shattering of Spartan Supremacy
docs.text:
"The Theban left wing, fifty shields deep, struck the Spartan line at its strongest point, and the strongest point gave way." — Front Line Stories

This case study examines the Battle of Leuctra, fought in 371 BC between a Theban-led Boeotian force and a Spartan-led Peloponnesian alliance. The battle is one of the most tactically innovative engagements in military history and demonstrates several enduring principles of land warfare.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
For over two centuries, Sparta had been the dominant military power in Greece. The Spartan hoplite, the Spartiatae, was considered the finest heavy infantry in the Greek world. No Spartan army had lost a pitched land battle in living memory.

Thebes, the chief city of Boeotia, had long existed in Sparta's shadow. But by 371 BC, under the leadership of Epaminondas and Pelopidas, Thebes had developed a new approach to warfare that would shatter Spartan supremacy in a single afternoon.

docs.title: Spartan Alliance
docs.text:
The Spartan-led alliance numbered approximately 10,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry. The elite Spartiate hoplites formed the right wing — the position of honour in Greek warfare. King Cleombrotus commanded the Spartan forces personally.

The Spartan cavalry was of poor quality. Wealthier Spartans sent horses and hired substitutes to ride them, producing undertrained riders on unfamiliar mounts.

docs.title: Theban-Boeotian Force
docs.text:
The Theban-Boeotian force numbered approximately 6,000 to 7,000 infantry and 1,500 cavalry. The Theban cavalry was well-trained and fighting on home ground.

Epaminondas commanded the Theban forces. He had spent years developing new tactical concepts that broke from the conventional Greek approach to warfare.

docs.title: Conventional Greek Battle
docs.text:
Greek hoplite warfare was essentially a pushing contest between two rectangular formations. Each formation deployed in a line, typically eight to twelve ranks deep. The right wing was the position of honour, where the best troops were placed. The tendency was for the stronger right wing to push back the weaker enemy left, then wheel inward to roll up the enemy line.

This symmetrical approach had produced many battles but few decisive results. The stronger right wing usually prevailed, but the enemy could withdraw in good order.

docs.title: Epaminondas's Innovation
docs.text: Epaminondas rejected the symmetrical approach. His innovation had three elements:

docs.title: 1. Concentration on the Decisive Wing
docs.text:
Epaminondas stacked the Theban left wing to an unprecedented depth of fifty ranks. This was twice the depth of any previous Greek formation. The elite Sacred Band, under Pelopidas, formed the cutting edge of this mass.

The concentration was deliberate. Epaminondas intended to strike the Spartan right wing — the strongest point of the enemy line — with overwhelming force.

docs.title: 2. The Refused Flank
docs.text:
Epaminondas refused the Theban right wing. He ordered the weaker Boeotian contingents on the right to hold back and avoid engagement. This oblique approach meant the Theban right would not clash with the Spartan left and collapse, as it likely would have done on conventional terms.

The refused flank is one of the most important tactical innovations in military history. It allows a commander to concentrate overwhelming force at a decisive point while minimising risk elsewhere.

docs.title: 3. Cavalry as a Disruptive Force
docs.text: The Theban cavalry attacked early in the engagement and drove off the Spartan cavalry. The fleeing Spartan cavalry disrupted the Spartan infantry formations before the main infantry clash. This disruption weakened the Spartan right wing at the critical moment.

docs.title: The Battle
docs.text:
The decisive engagement lasted approximately thirty minutes. The sequence was:

  1. Cavalry engagement: The Theban cavalry routed the Spartan cavalry, which fled back into the Spartan infantry lines, disrupting their formation.

  2. Infantry clash: The Theban left wing, fifty ranks deep, struck the Spartan right wing. The Spartan formation, disrupted by its own cavalry and overwhelmed by the depth of the Theban formation, buckled.

  3. Death of Cleombrotus: King Cleombrotus was killed in the fighting. The loss of the king and the elite Spartiates broke the Spartan will to fight.

  4. Rout: The Spartan right wing collapsed. The Spartan left wing, which had not been heavily engaged, withdrew in good order. But the battle was lost.

docs.title: Aftermath
docs.text:
The battle resulted in the death of approximately 400 Spartiate citizens — a catastrophic proportion of the remaining Spartiate military class. The political and strategic consequences rippled across the Greek world within months:

  • Spartan hegemony over the Peloponnesian League collapsed
  • Arcadia moved toward confederation
  • Epaminondas's subsequent campaigns freed the Messenian helots
  • Sparta's capacity to project military power was permanently curtailed

docs.title: 1. Concentration at the Decisive Point
docs.text:
Epaminondas did not attempt to defeat the entire Spartan army. He concentrated overwhelming force at a single point — the Spartan right wing — and destroyed it. The rest of the Spartan army, deprived of its command and its best troops, could not fight on.

This is the principle of concentration applied with precision. The decisive point is not always the weakest point. Sometimes it is the strongest point, because destroying the enemy's greatest strength shatters their will to resist.

docs.title: 2. The Refused Flank
docs.text:
The refused flank allows a commander to mass force at the decisive point without risking defeat elsewhere. It is an economy of force measure that accepts risk in one area to achieve overwhelming advantage in another.

The refused flank has been used by commanders throughout history. Napoleon used it at Austerlitz. The Germans used it in the Schlieffen Plan. It remains a valid approach in modern operations.

docs.title: 3. Combined Arms
docs.text: Epaminondas integrated cavalry and infantry to produce an effect greater than either arm could achieve alone. The cavalry disrupted the Spartan formation before the infantry struck. This is the essence of combined arms.

docs.title: 4. Moral Factors Decide
docs.text:
The death of Cleombrotus and the loss of 400 Spartiates broke the Spartan will to fight. The physical destruction of the right wing was decisive not because of the numbers killed, but because of what it represented: the Spartan king and the finest warriors in Greece, destroyed by a Theban innovation.

This reflects the enduring truth that land warfare is fundamentally a clash of wills. Physical destruction matters because of its moral effect.

docs.title: 5. Tactical Innovation Prevails
docs.text:
Epaminondas broke the conventional wisdom of Greek warfare. The conventional wisdom said: deploy symmetrically, put your best troops on the right, push. Epaminondas said: concentrate overwhelmingly on the decisive wing, refuse the other wing, use cavalry to disrupt.

The conventional approach had produced stalemate. The innovative approach produced decision. This is a recurring theme in military history: those who innovate tactically defeat those who follow convention.

docs.title: The Malayan Emergency (1948–1960)
docs.text: "The Malayan Emergency has been scrutinised for 'lessons' about how to win counterinsurgencies from the Vietnam War to twenty-first century Afghanistan." — Cambridge University Press, The Malayan Emergency (Karl Hack)

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
The Malayan Emergency lasted from June 1948 until 31 July 1960. It pitted British-led forces against the Malayan Communist Party (MCP) and its armed wing, the Malayan National Liberation Army (MNLA), in a protracted insurgency during the final phase of British colonial rule. The Emergency ended with the defeat of the MCP as a large-scale military force and the independence of Malaya in 1957.

The conflict was rooted in the MCP's origins as an anti-Japanese resistance movement during the Second World War. After 1945, the party adopted a united-front strategy, using political and union activity. By early 1948, facing deportations, tightening union regulations, and a global communist turn away from united-front tactics, the MCP decided to prepare for armed conflict. The British pre-empted this by declaring a state of Emergency in June 1948.

docs.title: The Insurgent Force
docs.text:
The MNLA was more than ninety per cent Chinese, with small minorities of Malays and Indians. This ethnic composition created a fundamental political weakness: the majority Malay population looked to the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) to protect its interests, and Malay fears of becoming a minority in an independent Malaya made the MCP's bid for broad-based support structurally difficult.

At its peak, the MNLA numbered approximately 8,000 full-time insurgents—a small force operating in a country the size of England without Wales, with a population of 5–6 million. The security forces eventually grew to 40,000 British and Commonwealth troops, nearly 67,000 police including Special Constables, and more than 250,000 Home Guard—a ratio of roughly fifty security personnel per insurgent.

docs.title: Campaign Phases
docs.text: Hack's periodisation, based on Director of Operations records, identifies four distinct phases:

docs.title: Phase 1: Counter-Terror (June 1948–October 1949)
docs.text: The campaign was directed by the police with army support. With limited intelligence, the army often "rode to the sound of guns." Whole villages were burned, thousands detained or deported to China. This counter-terror had double-edged results: it increased Chinese alienation and MNLA numbers, but also broke up larger guerrilla groups and prevented the loss of whole districts.

docs.title: Phase 2: Escalation (October 1949–August 1951)
docs.text: The MNLA reorganised after Phase 1. Its mass organisation, the Min Yuen, was restructured to operate among rural squatters despite army patrols. From late 1949, the MNLA launched widespread small-scale attacks and sabotage intended to disrupt Malaya's rubber exports. Violence reached its peak in 1951.

docs.title: Phase 3: The Briggs Plan and Population Control (August 1951–July 1954)
docs.text:
The Briggs Plan—formalised in 1950 and implemented through 1951–1952—sought to bring the dispersed Chinese rural population under government control. Villagers were resettled into "new villages" surrounded by barbed wire, with perimeter lighting and Home Guard protection.

Short's assessment, based on access to Malayan Government confidential papers, challenges the view that resettlement was effective from the start. He notes that "there was very little resettlement that was 'completed' in 1951. Barbed wire was lacking, perimeter lighting was lacking, and, with their absence, one cannot pretend that any sort of security had been given." Coates similarly concludes that "it was not until Briggs left Malaya that [the home guard] became really effective."

Hack's periodisation places the turning point in 1950–52, when population control and security approaches were to the fore, while "winning hearts and minds, dynamic leadership, and efficient learning were in their early stages." The back of the revolt was broken during this phase, not during the later "optimisation" period traditionally emphasised.

docs.title: Phase 4: Optimisation (1952–1960)
docs.text: General Sir Gerald Templer arrived in February 1952 as High Commissioner and Director of Operations with full civil and military authority. The MNLA lost over half its strength. Security force and civilian casualties declined to less than one-seventh of the 1951 peak. Templer's tenure is associated with the intensification of "hearts and minds" initiatives, political concessions, and the integration of Chinese residents into Malayan political life—leading eventually to Malayan independence in 1957.

docs.title: The Population Control Debate
docs.text:
The Briggs Plan remains the most contested element of the Emergency. The "new orthodoxy" in counterinsurgency studies credits population control as the decisive factor. Short, Coates, and others challenge this, arguing that the physical structures of resettlement were initially inadequate, that security personnel were insufficiently trained, and that the plan's effectiveness emerged only after extensive remediation.

The debate matters because it shapes how subsequent conflicts—Vietnam, Afghanistan—have interpreted Malayan "lessons." If population control was decisive, then coercion is validated as a counterinsurgency tool. If coercion was initially ineffective and the turning point required subsequent political accommodation, then the lesson is more complex: security and legitimacy must develop in tandem, not sequentially.

docs.title: The Malaysian Perspective
docs.text:
Malaysian historical scholarship, based on archives in Kuala Lumpur and field research in new villages, provides a corrective to accounts that rely primarily on British National Archives. Opper and Tan Teng Phee's research, drawing on original MCP documents and new village testimonies, questions whether the Briggs Plan's population control mechanisms were as effective as the British official record suggests.

The Malaysian perspective also emphasises that the Emergency was a decolonisation conflict as much as a counterinsurgency. The MCP's defeat did not resolve the political questions that had driven the insurgency; it deferred them. The 1969 racial riots and the subsequent New Economic Policy revealed that the ethnic tensions underlying the Emergency persisted beyond military victory.

docs.title: Lessons and Limitations
docs.text:
The Malayan Emergency offers several enduring lessons, all qualified by context:

  1. Population control is necessary but not sufficient. Controlling the civilian population denies insurgents access to resources and intelligence. But control without political legitimacy produces temporary suppression, not lasting resolution.

  2. Counterinsurgency requires phase differentiation. The techniques appropriate to a counter-terror phase are not the techniques appropriate to an optimisation phase. The failure to distinguish phases led to misapplication of Malayan "lessons" in Vietnam, where American commanders attempted to skip the population-control phase and proceed directly to hearts-and-minds programmes.

  3. Learning organisations win. The British forces in Malaya adapted continuously—from the indiscriminate counter-terror of 1948 to the sophisticated population-control and political-accommodation strategies of 1952–54. The MNLA, by contrast, became progressively more doctrinaire and less adaptive.

  4. Small forces can defeat smaller insurgent forces. The ratio of security personnel to insurgents was exceptionally high. This ratio is rarely available to contemporary counterinsurgency operations, which makes direct replication difficult.

  5. Colonial context is not transferable. The Emergency was a war of decolonisation fought by a colonial power against a nationalist movement with limited external support. This context is fundamentally different from contemporary insurgencies in which insurgents enjoy regional sanctuary, external funding, and ideological global networks.

docs.text:

  2. Clutterbuck, R. (1966). The Long, Long War: Counterinsurgency in Malaya and Vietnam. Praeger.

docs.title: Peace Support Operations in Sub-Saharan Africa — The Austere Environment
docs.text:
"Virtually anywhere the brigade operates will be an austere environment, with little or no viable infrastructure and food supply." — LSE, Building an Effective African Standby Force

Sub-Saharan Africa is the primary theatre for peace support operations (PSOs) worldwide. The United Nations deploys seven of its twelve peace operations in Africa. The African Union and regional economic communities (RECs) have conducted over a dozen peace operations since 2003. These operations share a common characteristic: they are conducted in austere environments with minimal infrastructure, limited logistics, and complex political dynamics.

This page examines the nature of peace support operations in Sub-Saharan Africa, their challenges, and the lessons they offer for military practitioners.

docs.title: The Nature of the Operating Environment
The Tyranny of Distance
docs.text: Sub-Saharan Africa is vast. The Democratic Republic of the Congo alone is the size of Western Europe, with fewer than 500 kilometres of paved roads. Deploying forces across such distances requires strategic airlift that most African militaries do not possess. The UN depends on donor nations for airlift support, but this cannot always be guaranteed.

docs.title: The Austere Environment
docs.text: Most PSOs in Africa operate in environments with: - Minimal infrastructure: Few paved roads, limited airfields, unreliable power grids - Limited food and water supply: Forces must be self-sustaining - High disease burden: Malaria, Ebola, cholera, and other endemic diseases - Extreme weather: Monsoon rains, desert heat, tropical humidity - Complex political dynamics: Multiple armed groups, weak state institutions, competing national interests

docs.title: The Human Security Challenge
docs.text: Civilians are the primary victims of conflict in Africa. PSOs are mandated to protect civilians, but this is a complex task. Armed groups hide among the population. State security forces are often the perpetrators of abuse. Humanitarian access is restricted by insecurity, geography, and bureaucratic obstacles.

docs.title: The African Peace and Security Architecture
The African Union
docs.text: The African Union (AU) established the African Peace and Security Architecture (APSA) in 2002. APSA comprises: - The Peace and Security Council (PSC): The decision-making body for conflict prevention, management, and resolution - The African Standby Force (ASF): A multinational standby force for rapid deployment - The Continental Early Warning System (CEWS): For conflict prevention - The Panel of the Wise: For preventive diplomacy

docs.title: Regional Economic Communities
docs.text:
The AU's security architecture is built on regional pillars: - ECOWAS: Economic Community of West African States - ECCAS: Economic Community of Central African States - SADC: Southern African Development Community - IGAD: Intergovernmental Authority on Development - EAC: East African Community

Each REC has its own security mechanisms and standby forces. The relationship between the AU and RECs is governed by the principle of subsidiarity — regional organisations take the lead, with the AU providing coordination and support.

docs.title: The Dependency Trap
docs.text:
Most African troop-contributing countries (TCCs) cannot deploy and sustain their contingents independently. They depend on external partners for: - Strategic airlift: Transporting forces to the theatre - Equipment: Vehicles, communications, medical facilities - Sustainment: Food, water, fuel, ammunition - Training: Pre-deployment training and mission-specific skills

This dependency creates vulnerabilities. When external partners withdraw support, missions struggle to sustain themselves.

docs.title: The Mobile Rear
docs.text: The UN has developed the concept of a "mobile rear" — a logistics structure that enables sustained operations in austere environments. The UN Regional Service Centre in Entebbe, Uganda, serves as a hub for administrative, logistical, and technological support to UN missions in Africa.

docs.title: Lessons from MONUSCO
docs.text: The UN Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO) is the largest and most expensive UN peacekeeping mission. With over 16,000 personnel and an annual budget of USD 1.1 billion, it offers critical lessons:

docs.title: 1. Robust Mandates Work — But Have Costs
docs.text: MONUSCO's Force Intervention Brigade (FIB) was the first UN peacekeeping unit mandated to conduct offensive operations against armed groups. The FIB has been more effective at protecting civilians than traditional peacekeepers. But robust mandates compromise neutrality and can make the mission a party to the conflict.

docs.title: 2. Technology Is Essential
docs.text: MONUSCO pioneered the use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in UN peacekeeping. UAVs provide real-time intelligence, monitor armed group movements, and enhance situational awareness. But technology alone is insufficient — it must be integrated with ground operations and community engagement.

docs.title: 3. Community Trust Is Operational Infrastructure
docs.text: In eastern DRC, community trust is not a "soft" variable — it is operational infrastructure. Peacekeepers need trust to move, gather early warning, and support civilian protection. Humanitarian actors need trust to deliver aid. Health workers need trust to conduct surveillance and vaccination.

docs.title: 4. Withdrawal Requires Planning
docs.text: MONUSCO's drawdown has raised concerns about the mission's capacity to protect civilians. Withdrawal must be phased, responsible, and planned. The transfer of responsibilities to national authorities requires time and capacity-building.

docs.title: The Security-Development Nexus
docs.text:
Peace support operations in Africa cannot be separated from development. The World Bank estimates that a civil war costs the average developing country roughly 30 years of GDP growth. Countries in protracted crises fall over 20 percentage points behind in poverty reduction.

The AU's Post-Conflict Reconstruction and Development (PCRD) policy recognises this link. The revised 2024 policy framework integrates eight pillars: security, humanitarian assistance, governance, socio-economic recovery, human rights and justice, gender, youth, and environmental security.

docs.title: Platoon Commander's Landward Operations — Manoeuvre and Combined Arms at the Tactical Level
docs.text:
"The platoon leader must have a relatively complete knowledge of the terrain, and he must know as much as possible about the enemy." — FM 3-21.8, Infantry Platoon and Squad

The platoon commander operates at the tactical level where intent is translated into action. The platoon commander receives the company commander's intent and must achieve it through the coordinated action of multiple sections. This requires mastery of manoeuvre and combined arms at a higher level than the section commander.

This page discusses the landward domain at the platoon and company level, relevant to lieutenants and captains.

docs.title: The Manoeuvrist Approach
docs.text:
The manoeuvrist approach is an indirect approach that applies strength against enemy vulnerabilities. It blends lethal and non-lethal actions to shape the enemy's understanding, undermine their will, and break their cohesion.

The manoeuvrist approach is suited to a small, professional force. It avoids attritional warfare — the grinding destruction of enemy forces through superior firepower. Instead, it seeks to dislocate and disintegrate the enemy through speed, surprise, and the concentration of force at the decisive point.

docs.title: Shaping the Enemy's Understanding
docs.text: The manoeuvrist approach seeks to shape what the enemy perceives. Deception, feints, and indirect approaches confuse the enemy about the location and timing of the main effort. The enemy is induced to make mistakes — to commit reserves to the wrong location, to expose flanks, or to hesitate at the critical moment.

docs.title: Breaking Cohesion
docs.text: The manoeuvrist approach seeks to break the enemy's cohesion — the ability of the enemy force to act as a unified whole. Cohesion is broken by creating multiple dilemmas simultaneously. The enemy is forced to choose between responding to one threat or another. Whichever choice the enemy makes, they become vulnerable to the other threat.

docs.title: Combined Arms at the Platoon Level
docs.text: Combined arms is the synchronised and simultaneous application of tactical forces and capabilities to create an effect greater than if each element was used separately. At the platoon level, combined arms means the integration of infantry, armour, artillery, engineers, and aviation.

docs.title: Infantry
docs.text: Infantry is the primary arm of land warfare. Infantry can operate in any terrain. Infantry can close with the enemy and destroy or capture them at close range. Infantry can hold ground against counterattack.

docs.title: Armour
docs.text: Armour provides mobile protected firepower. Tanks and infantry fighting vehicles can destroy enemy armour, suppress enemy positions, and break through enemy defences. Armour is most effective in open terrain where its mobility and firepower can be fully exploited.

docs.title: Artillery
docs.text: Artillery provides indirect fire support. Mortars and field guns can suppress the enemy, destroy enemy positions, and provide smoke and illumination. Artillery is the primary means of shaping the battlefield before the assault.

docs.title: Engineers
docs.text: Engineers provide mobility and counter-mobility. Engineers breach obstacles, clear minefields, and construct defences. Engineers enable the force to move through denied terrain and prevent the enemy from moving through key terrain.

docs.title: Aviation
docs.text: Aviation provides reconnaissance, fire support, and mobility. Attack helicopters can destroy enemy armour and suppress enemy positions. Transport helicopters can insert troops into denied terrain. Unmanned aerial systems provide real-time intelligence.

docs.title: The Platoon Attack
docs.text: The platoon attack is a combined arms operation. The platoon commander coordinates the actions of sections, supporting weapons, and adjacent units to achieve the objective.

docs.title: The Plan
docs.text:
The platoon commander develops a plan that includes:

  • Mission analysis: What is the mission? What are the key factors? What are the enemy's likely courses of action?

  • Scheme of manoeuvre: How will the platoon achieve the objective? What is the main effort? What is the supporting effort?

  • Fire support plan: How will supporting weapons support the attack? What are the targets? When will fires be lifted?

  • Coordinating instructions: What are the control measures? What are the rules of engagement? What is the timeline?

docs.title: The Preparation
docs.text:
The platoon commander prepares the platoon for the attack. Preparation includes:

  • Reconnaissance: The platoon commander conducts a reconnaissance of the objective and the routes to the objective.

  • Briefing: The platoon commander briefs section commanders on the plan. Every section commander must understand the mission, the scheme of manoeuvre, and the fire support plan.

  • Rehearsal: The platoon rehearses the attack. Rehearsals identify problems and build confidence.

docs.title: The Execution
docs.text: The platoon commander controls the attack through fire and movement. The platoon commander designates the main effort and coordinates supporting fires. The platoon commander adjusts the plan as the situation changes.

docs.title: Consolidation
docs.text: The platoon consolidates on the objective. Consolidation includes reorganising the platoon, redistributing ammunition, and preparing for counterattack. Consolidation is often neglected but is critical to holding ground.

docs.title: The Platoon Defence
docs.text: The platoon defence is a combined arms operation. The platoon commander positions sections to maximise firepower while minimising exposure. The platoon commander coordinates supporting weapons to destroy the enemy before they reach the platoon's positions.

docs.title: The Plan
docs.text:
The platoon commander develops a defensive plan that includes:

  • Security: Early warning of the enemy's approach. Observation posts and patrols.

  • Main battle area: The positions where the platoon will fight. Primary, alternate, and supplementary positions.

  • Fire support plan: The integration of direct and indirect fires. Target reference points. Final protective fires.

  • Reserve: A section held back to counterattack or reinforce.

docs.title: The Preparation
docs.text:
The platoon commander prepares the defence. Preparation includes:

  • Position construction: Fighting positions, trenches, and obstacles.

  • Fire planning: Clearing fields of fire. Assigning sectors of fire.

  • Rehearsal: Rehearsal of the defence, including the counterattack.

docs.title: The Execution
docs.text: The platoon commander controls the defence. The platoon commander calls for indirect fire. The platoon commander commits the reserve at the decisive moment.

docs.title: The Platoon Commander's Landward Problem
docs.text:
The platoon commander faces a complex landward problem. The platoon commander must simultaneously manoeuvre sections, coordinate supporting weapons, and maintain situational awareness. The platoon commander must be able to shift from offence to defence quickly and to adapt to the changing situation.

The platoon commander who masters combined arms and the manoeuvrist approach is the platoon commander who wins.

docs.title: Section Commander's Landward Operations — Reading Ground, Fighting, and Holding
docs.text:
"The section is the smallest military unit capable of independent tactical action." — ATP 3-21.8, Infantry Platoon and Squad

The section commander operates at the lowest level of military command. Decisions are immediate. The consequences are direct. The section commander must read the ground, fight the battle, and hold the ground — all simultaneously.

This page discusses the landward domain at the tactical level most relevant to junior leaders: the lance corporal and corporal commanding a fire team or section.

docs.title: Reading the Ground
docs.text: Terrain is the physical framework within which every engagement occurs. The section commander must read terrain quickly and accurately.

docs.title: Key Terrain Features
docs.text:
Terrain is analysed using the military mnemonic OCOKA:

  • Observation: Where can you see the enemy? Where can the enemy see you? Good observation enables effective fire and early warning. Poor observation creates surprise.

  • Cover and concealment: Cover protects from fire. Concealment hides from observation. The section commander must identify both and use them to protect the section.

  • Obstacles: Natural or artificial features that impede movement. Rivers, walls, minefields, wire. Obstacles can protect flanks or block routes of advance.

  • Key terrain: Any feature whose seizure, retention, or control provides a marked advantage to either side. A hilltop. A bridge. A road junction. Key terrain is the spatial focus of the battle.

  • Avenues of attack: Routes along which a force can move to reach its objective. The section commander must identify covered and concealed avenues that allow the section to close with the enemy.

docs.title: Ground and Movement
docs.text:
The section commander must calculate not merely the distance to an objective, but the time required to traverse that distance in the specific terrain. A kilometre of open ground takes minutes. A kilometre of dense vegetation takes longer. A kilometre under fire takes longest of all.

Ground also determines the formation the section adopts. Open terrain may allow a wide skirmish line. Jungle requires a single file. Urban terrain requires bounding overwatch between buildings.

docs.title: Fighting the Battle
docs.text: The section commander fights the battle through fire and movement. Fire suppresses the enemy. Movement closes the distance. The combination of fire and movement is the fundamental tactic of land warfare.

docs.title: Fire and Movement
docs.text: Fire and movement requires one element to suppress the enemy while another element moves. The section commander designates which fire team suppresses and which moves. The timing is critical. If the suppressing fire lifts too early, the moving team is exposed. If it lifts too late, the moving team cannot advance.

docs.title: Fire Control
docs.text: The section commander controls fire through fire orders. Fire orders include the target indication, the rate of fire, and the duration of fire. The section commander must ensure that all members of the section understand the fire orders and can deliver accurate fire on the target.

docs.title: Close Combat
docs.text:
The section commander must be prepared to close with the enemy. Close combat is the defining characteristic of land warfare. The section that closes with the enemy and destroys or captures them achieves the objective.

Close combat requires aggression, training, and unit cohesion. The section commander must inspire the section to fight at close quarters and overcome the natural resistance to killing.

docs.title: Holding the Ground
docs.text: Seizing ground is only half the battle. The section must hold the ground against counterattack. Holding requires preparation, organisation, and the will to defend.

docs.title: Hasty Defence
docs.text: When the section seizes an objective, it immediately organises a hasty defence. The section commander designates primary and alternate positions. Fields of fire are cleared. Ammunition is redistributed. The section prepares for the inevitable counterattack.

docs.title: Positions
docs.text: The section commander positions the section to maximise firepower while minimising exposure. Positions must provide cover from fire and observation. They must also provide fields of fire that cover the likely avenues of enemy approach.

docs.title: Sectors of Fire
docs.text: The section commander assigns sectors of fire to each fire team. Sectors of fire ensure that all approaches are covered. They also prevent fratricide by ensuring that each fire team knows where friendly forces are located.

docs.title: The Section Commander's Landward Problem
docs.text:
The section commander faces a unique problem in the landward domain. The section commander must simultaneously read the ground, fight the battle, and hold the ground. These tasks are interdependent. Reading the ground enables effective fighting. Fighting enables holding the ground. Holding the ground provides the platform for the next advance.

The section commander who masters this cycle is the section commander who wins.

docs.text:

docs.title: Maritime Domain — Nature and Military Relevance
docs.text:
"The United States is the most powerful nation on earth, dependent upon transoceanic links commercial and military to allies, friends, and interests." — Naval Doctrine Publication 1

The maritime domain is the vast expanse of water that covers approximately 71 percent of the Earth's surface. It includes the oceans, seas, estuaries, coastal waters, and the airspace above them. It is the medium through which 90 percent of global trade flows and the arena in which naval forces have contested for centuries.

This page examines the nature of the maritime domain, its enduring characteristics, and its centrality to military operations.

docs.title: The Nature of the Maritime Domain
A Global Commons
docs.text:
The maritime domain is the ultimate global commons. Unlike land territory, which is subject to national sovereignty, much of the ocean is international water. Ships of all nations traverse these waters in peace and war. This freedom of navigation is the foundation of global commerce and naval power projection.

The law of the sea, codified in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), establishes the legal framework for maritime operations. Coastal states exercise sovereignty over their territorial seas (up to 12 nautical miles) and jurisdiction over their exclusive economic zones (up to 200 nautical miles). Beyond these limits lie the high seas, open to all.

docs.title: A Three-Dimensional Battlespace
docs.text:
The maritime domain is unique in its three-dimensional character. Operations occur simultaneously in three dimensions:

  • Up: Air warfare and air defence above the fleet
  • Out: Surface warfare across the sea
  • Down: Undersea warfare beneath the surface

Each dimension presents distinct challenges. Aircraft operate at high speed but limited endurance. Surface ships provide persistent presence but are vulnerable to air and submarine attack. Submarines offer stealth and endurance but limited sensors and weapons.

docs.title: The Scouting Problem
docs.text:
The defining characteristic of naval combat is the vastness of the ocean and the difficulty of finding the enemy. Wayne Hughes, the dean of naval tacticians, wrote that "the battle will be decided by scouting effectiveness and weapon range" (Hughes, Fleet Tactics and Naval Operations, 2018).

In the age of sail, scouting was limited to the horizon. In the modern era, sensors extend far beyond the horizon, but so do weapons. The modern naval duel is a race between scouting and weapons. The force that finds the enemy first and strikes first generally wins.

docs.title: The Navy's Foremost Function: Sea Control
docs.text:
Sea control is the Navy's primary objective. Without sea control, no other naval function is possible. Sea control enables the movement of military and commercial shipping. It enables the projection of power ashore. It enables the blockade of an enemy's coast.

Sea control is geographic and time-based. No navy can control all the sea all the time. Sea control is established "for just long enough, over just enough area, to achieve a desired outcome" (JDP 0-10). It is a spectrum of activity, from local sea control in a confined waterway to oceanic command of the sea.

Sea denial is the opposite of sea control. Sea denial prevents an enemy from using the sea. It is achieved through submarines, mines, land-based anti-ship missiles, and asymmetric tactics.

docs.title: Enduring Characteristics of the Maritime Domain
1. The Primacy of Attrition
docs.text: Naval combat is fundamentally a process of attrition. Attrition comes from the successful delivery of firepower. The force that delivers more effective firepower over time prevails. This is true whether the combatants are galleys exchanging cannon broadsides or destroyers launching anti-ship missiles.

docs.title: 2. Scouting Determines Victory
docs.text: Scouting — locating the enemy sufficiently to deliver effective firepower — is the crucial process of naval tactics. The force that scouts more effectively gains the initiative and strikes first. Hughes wrote that "the choice of tactics will also be governed by scouting effectiveness and weapons range."

docs.title: 3. Command and Control Transforms Potential into Reality
docs.text: Command and control (C2) transforms scouting and firepower potential into the reality of delivered force. The force with better C2 — better situational awareness, better decision-making, better coordination — will prevail. In the age of network-centric warfare, C2 is both a strength and a vulnerability.

docs.title: 4. Maneuver Positions Forces to Scout and Shoot
docs.text: Maneuver is the activity by which C2 positions forces to scout and shoot. The force that maneuvers more effectively gains the advantage. Maneuver in the modern era is not merely geographic positioning. It is the integration of capabilities across domains — the orchestration of sensing, shooting, and countersensor/shooting capabilities across the entire fleet.

docs.title: 5. The Side That Attacks Effectively First Generally Wins
docs.text: Hughes's basic precept is that naval combat is a duel, and the side that attacks effectively first generally wins. This is the temporal equivalent of the land warfare principle of seizing the initiative. The force that acts inside the enemy's decision cycle gains a cumulative advantage.

docs.title: 6. Maritime Forces Are Self-Sustaining
docs.text: Maritime forces can deploy independently and provide a persistent, self-sustaining forward presence. Ships carry their own logistics — fuel, food, ammunition, and spare parts. This self-sustaining quality gives maritime forces unique strategic flexibility.

docs.title: 7. Maritime Power Enables Joint Operations
docs.text: Maritime power enables joint operations. Sea control enables the movement of land forces by sea. Aircraft carriers provide airpower independent of land bases. Amphibious forces project power from sea to land. The maritime domain is the enabling medium for joint campaigns.

docs.title: Naval Warfare Areas
docs.text: Naval forces fight in multiple warfare areas simultaneously:

docs.title: Surface Warfare
docs.text: Surface warfare is the massing of fires to take or sink enemy ships. It has evolved from cannon broadsides to a combined-arms effort involving aircraft, ships, submarines, and shore-based systems.

docs.title: Undersea Warfare
docs.text: Undersea warfare encompasses actions to establish and maintain control of the undersea portion of the maritime domain. It includes antisubmarine warfare, mine warfare, and submarine operations. Undersea warfare remains the most intricate and complex tactical problem.

docs.title: Air and Missile Defence
docs.text: Air and missile defence protects the fleet from aircraft, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles. It includes active and passive measures — fighters, surface-to-air missiles, electronic warfare, and decoys.

docs.title: Strike Warfare
docs.text: Strike warfare is the use of naval forces to deliver lethal and nonlethal fires to create desired effects against targets on land. It includes aircraft strikes, cruise missile strikes, and naval gunfire support.

docs.title: Amphibious Warfare
docs.text: Amphibious warfare is the projection of naval forces into, and their employment within or from, a foreign country and adjacent waters. It includes amphibious assaults, raids, and withdrawals.

docs.title: Mine Warfare
docs.text: Mine warfare includes the laying of mines to deny sea areas to the enemy and the clearing of mines to enable friendly operations. Mines are the most cost-effective sea denial weapon.

docs.title: Information Warfare
docs.text: Information warfare encompasses operations to exploit, deceive, degrade, or destroy enemy information and information systems. It includes electronic warfare, cyber operations, psychological operations, and deception.

docs.title: The Maritime Domain and Multi-Domain Operations
docs.text:
Modern maritime operations are inherently multi-domain. Maritime forces operate in the air, on the sea surface, under the sea, in space, and in cyberspace. They enable operations on land. They depend on space-based communications and positioning. They are vulnerable to cyber attack.

The future of maritime operations lies in distributed lethality — the integration of capabilities across widely distributed platforms. This requires tight integration of sensing, shooting, and C2 across the fleet, loosening the ties of geography and organisational boundaries.

docs.title: Implications for Military Operations
docs.text:
The maritime domain has direct implications at every level of war:

  • Strategic: Maritime power enables global power projection. Control of the seas enables the movement of military and commercial shipping. Denial of the seas can strangle an enemy's economy.

  • Operational: Maritime campaigns are designed to achieve sea control and project power ashore. The arrangement of naval forces to support joint campaigns is the essence of operational art at sea.

  • Tactical: Naval engagements are fought at specific locations and times. The coordination of surface, air, and undersea forces to destroy enemy naval forces is the essence of naval tactics.

docs.title: Case Study — Falklands War (1982): Maritime Power in a Littoral Campaign
docs.text:
"The British victory would have to be judged anyway as a fairly close run thing... We fought our way along a knife-edge." — Admiral Sir John Woodward, Task Force Commander

This case study examines the 1982 Falkland Islands campaign, the largest maritime campaign since the Second World War. It demonstrates the application of maritime power to achieve political objectives in a littoral environment.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: On 2 April 1982, Argentine forces invaded and occupied the Falkland Islands (Islas Malvinas), a British overseas territory 275 nautical miles from Argentina and 6,700 nautical miles from Britain. The British government resolved to retake the islands by force. The campaign lasted 74 days.

docs.title: British Challenges
docs.text:
Britain faced a severe logistical challenge. The nearest British base was Ascension Island, 3,500 nautical miles from the Falklands. The task force would have to operate 8,000 miles from home with no local infrastructure.

Britain had only two small aircraft carriers (HMS Hermes and HMS Invincible), 33 Sea Harrier V/STOL fighters, and a limited number of escorts. There was no airborne early warning (AEW) capability. The Royal Navy had been cut back in recent years and was not designed for this type of operation.

docs.title: Argentine Advantages
docs.text: Argentina enjoyed significant geographic advantage. The Falklands were within range of Argentine land-based aircraft. Argentina possessed a fleet of 17 combatant ships, three submarines, and approximately 130 operational fixed-wing attack aircraft, including Dassault Super Etendards armed with Exocet anti-ship missiles.

docs.title: Deployment (April 1982)
docs.text: The British task force sailed from Britain on 5 April. Rear Admiral John Woodward's carrier battle group departed Ascension Island on 18 April, arriving in the Total Exclusion Zone around the Falklands on 1 May.

docs.title: Sea Control (May 1982)
docs.text:
The first priority was sea control. On 2 May, the nuclear submarine HMS Conqueror sank the Argentine cruiser ARA General Belgrano with two torpedo hits. The Argentine Navy, fearful of further submarine attacks, withdrew its surface fleet to port for the remainder of the war.

This single action eliminated the Argentine surface navy from the campaign. It was a decisive application of undersea warfare.

docs.title: Air Superiority (May 1982)
docs.text:
The Sea Harriers flew combat air patrols over the task force and strike missions against Argentine positions. They proved highly effective, shooting down 20 Argentine aircraft without loss in air-to-air combat.

However, the British lacked AEW. Argentine aircraft could approach at low level and attack before being detected. The task force suffered losses. HMS Sheffield was sunk by an Exocet missile on 4 May. HMS Coventry was sunk by bombs on 25 May. Three other ships were damaged.

docs.title: The Amphibious Landing
docs.text:
On 21 May, the amphibious task force landed 3 Commando Brigade at San Carlos Water on East Falkland. The landing was unopposed, but Argentine aircraft attacked the ships in the anchorage.

The British established a beachhead at San Carlos and began the advance toward Port Stanley. The land campaign lasted three weeks. Port Stanley fell on 14 June, and the Argentine garrison surrendered.

docs.title: 1. Sea Control Is Essential
docs.text: British success depended on establishing sea control. Without sea control, the amphibious landing would have been impossible. The sinking of the Belgrano was the decisive action that secured sea control.

docs.title: 2. Submarines Are Decisive
docs.text: The single submarine HMS Conqueror eliminated an entire navy. The undersea domain is the most asymmetric domain. A small submarine force can achieve disproportionate effects.

docs.title: 3. AEW Is Essential
docs.text: The lack of AEW was the most significant British deficiency. Argentine aircraft could approach at low level and attack before being detected. AEW would have extended the detection range and increased the effectiveness of the Sea Harriers.

docs.title: 4. The Sea Harrier Was Decisive
docs.text: The Sea Harrier proved that a small number of highly capable aircraft can achieve air superiority. The Sea Harrier shot down 20 Argentine aircraft without loss. It demonstrated the value of V/STOL aircraft in maritime operations.

docs.title: 5. Integrated Defence Is Required
docs.text: The San Carlos anchorage was defended by an integrated system: Sea Harriers patrolled the airspace, surface ships provided missile defence, and ground forces provided close-in defence. This integrated defence defeated the Argentine air attacks.

docs.title: 6. Logistics Determine the Campaign
docs.text: The campaign was a logistical feat. The task force operated 8,000 miles from home. Merchant ships were requisitioned to carry supplies and troops. The campaign demonstrated the importance of logistics in maritime operations.

docs.title: 7. The Littoral Is the Future
docs.text: The Falklands campaign was a littoral campaign. The maritime, land, and air domains were closely integrated. The littoral is the most complex operational environment. Future campaigns will be fought in the littorals.

docs.text:

docs.title: Battle of Midway (1942) — Intelligence and Decision
docs.text:
"I want you to be specific... After all, this is the job I have given you — to be the admiral commanding the Japanese forces, and tell me what is going on." — Admiral Chester W. Nimitz to Commander Edwin T. Layton, 27 May 1942

On 4 June 1942, six months after Pearl Harbor, the United States Navy engaged the Imperial Japanese Navy at Midway Atoll. The battle is widely regarded as the turning point of the Pacific War. It was won not primarily by courage or firepower, but by intelligence, decision-making, and the effective use of limited resources.

This case study examines the battle through the first-hand accounts of Admiral Chester Nimitz (Commander-in-Chief, Pacific Fleet), Commander Edwin T. Layton (Fleet Intelligence Officer), and the official after-action reports.

docs.title: Codebreaking
docs.text:
By May 1942, the U.S. Navy's codebreaking team at Pearl Harbor — led by Lieutenant Commander Joseph Rochefort and intelligence officer Edwin T. Layton — had decrypted sufficient Japanese messages to advise Nimitz of the Japanese plan to attack Midway. The critical breakthrough came from a ruse: Midley sent a plaintext message (which the Japanese intercepted) reporting problems with its fresh water plant. When Japanese intelligence referenced "AF" having water problems, the Americans confirmed that "AF" was Midway.

Layton's account, published in And I Was There (1985), described the moment:

"I want you to be specific," Nimitz said, fixing me with his cool blue eyes. "After all, this is the job I have given you — to be the admiral commanding the Japanese forces, and tell me what is going on."

Layton told Nimitz that the carriers would probably attack on the morning of 4 June, from the northwest on a bearing of 325 degrees, sighted at about 175 miles from Midway at around 0700 hours.

docs.title: The Disagreement
docs.text:
There was a critical rift between Layton's team (HYPO) and Washington (OP-20-G). Washington believed that the Japanese would commit five carriers to the Midway operation, including Zuikaku. HYPO assessed four carriers, excluding Zuikaku. Nimitz's formal "Estimate of the Situation" on 26 May explicitly noted the disagreement.

Nimitz chose to trust his local intelligence team. This decision was vindicated by events: the Japanese committed four carriers (Akagi, Kaga, Hiryu, Soryu) — exactly as HYPO predicted.

docs.title: Point Luck
docs.text:
Nimitz positioned his three carriers (Enterprise, Hornet, and the damaged Yorkwood) at "Point Luck," 200 nautical miles northeast of Midway — outside Japanese scouting range but within striking distance. This positioning was deliberate: it gave the American carriers time and standoff room to make an informed go-no-go decision before committing to battle.

Nimitz's plan was to use Midway-based aircraft and submarines to whittle down the Japanese carrier force before committing his own carriers. His operation order stated:

"It is essential that enemy carrier decks be damaged to immobilize enemy planes" and, if possible, that "enemy carriers be sunk before they get within striking range of Midway."

docs.title: The Morning of 4 June
docs.text:
At 0430, PBY scouts launched from Midway. At 0534, they sighted enemy carriers. At 0603, a more detailed report arrived: "2 carriers and battleships bearing 320 degrees, distance 180, course 135, speed 25 knots."

Rear Admiral Frank Jack Fletcher, commanding the carrier force, ordered Rear Admiral Raymond Spruance (TF 16) to proceed southwest and attack. Fletcher would follow as soon as his planes were recovered.

docs.title: The Afternoon
docs.text:
The decisive strikes came in the late afternoon. Dive bombers from Enterprise and Yorktown caught three Japanese carriers (Akagi, Kaga, and Soryu) while their flight decks were loaded with armed and fueled aircraft. All three were fatally hit. The fourth carrier, Hiryu, was sunk later that evening.

The Japanese lost all four carriers, plus 248 aircraft and 3,057 men. The Americans lost Yorktown, 145 aircraft, and 307 men.

docs.title: 1. Intelligence Wins Battles
docs.text: The victory at Midway was made possible by codebreaking, traffic analysis, and the willingness of a commander (Nimitz) to trust his intelligence team over Washington.

docs.title: 2. Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
docs.text: Nimitz made his plans with incomplete information. He did not know the exact number of Japanese carriers, the exact timing, or the exact bearing. He planned for the most likely scenario and positioned his forces to adapt as the situation developed.

docs.title: 3. Technology and Doctrine
docs.text: The American victory depended on the integration of codebreaking, scouting, and strike aircraft. But technology alone was not decisive — it was the way Nimitz and his commanders used technology that mattered.

docs.title: 4. The Japanese Failure
docs.text: The Japanese assumed the Americans would not be at Midway in force. Their scouting was inadequate. Their carriers were caught with loaded flight decks. The Japanese failure was a failure of imagination and assumption, not of courage.

docs.title: References
docs.text:

Layton, E. T. (1985). As quoted in Steeljaw Scribe, Midway 70 Years Later: Forces in Motion.

Symonds, C. L. (2011). The Battle of Midway. Oxford University Press.

docs.title: South China Sea — A Southeast Asian Perspective
docs.text: "ASEAN has never officially recognized the 2016 South China Sea Arbitral Award... yet ASEAN has repeatedly affirmed UNCLOS as the comprehensive legal framework governing all activities at sea." — The Diplomat, 10 Years After the South China Sea Arbitration

docs.title: The Dispute in Context
docs.text:
The South China Sea dispute involves China's expansive "nine-dash line" claim against the maritime entitlements of Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Vietnam. The dispute is simultaneously a legal contest, a strategic competition, and an economic contest over fisheries, hydrocarbon resources, and sea lines of communication.

From a Southeast Asian perspective, the dispute is not abstract. It shapes coastal state sovereignty, affects the livelihoods of fishing communities, determines access to energy resources, and structures the region's relationship with China—its largest economic partner and its most assertive strategic competitor.

docs.title: The 2016 Arbitral Award
docs.text:
On 12 July 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague issued its award in the case brought by the Philippines against China under Annex VII of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). The tribunal: - Ruled that China's "nine-dash line" has no legal basis under UNCLOS. - Clarified the maritime status of features in the Spratly Islands. - Found that China had violated the Philippines' sovereign rights within its exclusive economic zone.

The award is final and binding. China rejected it. The United States, while not a party, supported the ruling's legal conclusions. The Philippines, under President Duterte, initially downplayed the award while pursuing closer economic ties with China. Under President Marcos Jr., Manila elevated the award into the central pillar of its South China Sea strategy.

docs.title: ASEAN's Dilemma
docs.text:
ASEAN's response to the award illustrates the organisation's structural constraints. At the 49th ASEAN Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Vientiane, just two weeks after the ruling, member states could not reach consensus to include any direct reference to the ruling in the joint communiqué. According to Philippine officials, every proposed reference was vetoed by a member state without explanation or counter-proposal.

This pattern persisted. Nearly a decade later, ASEAN has never issued a collective statement formally recognising or directly invoking the 2016 award. CSIS AMTI's Arbitration Support Tracker documents that, aside from the Philippines, none of the ASEAN countries have formally endorsed the tribunal's decision. Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Vietnam, and Myanmar have taken a more cautious approach by only positively acknowledging the ruling.

ASEAN's consensus-based decision-making enables opponents of the award to block supportive language while supporters avoid public confrontation. This structural reality means that ASEAN's collective position remains one of studied ambiguity.

docs.title: The Philippine Perspective
docs.text:
For the Philippines, the award is not merely a legal victory; it is a strategic instrument. Philippine strategy has evolved through three phases:

  1. Litigation phase (2013–2016). The Aquino administration initiated the arbitration case. The legal strategy was designed to clarify rights without immediately confronting China militarily.

  2. Accommodation phase (2016–2022). The Duterte administration de-emphasised the award, prioritising economic relations with China. The Philippines did not abandon its legal claims, but it did not operationalise them.

  3. Implementation phase (2022–present). The Marcos Jr. administration has sought to operationalise the award through law, practice, and diplomacy. The Philippine approach now combines:

  4. Transparency strategy. Documenting and publicising Chinese coercive activities at sea to build international normative pressure.
  5. Legal consolidation. Aligning domestic legislation, maritime zone definitions, and fisheries regulation with the award's findings.
  6. Diplomatic embedding. Incorporating the award into bilateral and multilateral engagements with the United States, Japan, Australia, and ASEAN.
  7. Coalition-building. Anchoring the award within a wider network of UNCLOS-committed states.

Philippine analysts note that the award is not self-executing. Without domestic legal consolidation and disciplined state practice at sea, its strategic potential remains underdeveloped.

docs.title: The Legal Framework: UNCLOS as Common Ground
docs.text:
UNCLOS provides the legal framework within which all Southeast Asian claimants operate. The ASEAN Leaders' Declaration on Maritime Cooperation, adopted in May 2026, referred to UNCLOS no fewer than 18 times—reaffirming the convention as the comprehensive legal framework governing all maritime activities.

This repeated invocation of UNCLOS is significant. It represents ASEAN's preferred mechanism for managing the dispute: not by directly confronting China's claims, but by affirming a rules-based framework that all claimants have accepted. The Code of Conduct (COC) negotiations between ASEAN and China, ongoing since 2013, are the institutional expression of this approach.

However, the COC process faces significant obstacles. China opposes linking the COC to the 2016 award. ASEAN members are divided on the legal status and binding force of a future COC. The 2026 deadline for concluding an "effective and substantive" COC is approaching with little evidence of imminent agreement.

docs.title: Grey-Zone Tactics and the Strategic Environment
docs.text:
China's approach to the South China Sea has evolved since 2016. The award did not alter Chinese behaviour on the ground. Instead, China expanded its use of grey-zone tactics: coast guard patrols, maritime militia presence, island reinforcement, and diplomatic coercion against Southeast Asian claimants.

CSIS AMTI documents continued Chinese activity at features such as Second Thomas Shoal, Scarborough Shoal, and Antelope Reef. Philippine vessels have been blocked, shadowed, and water-cannonned. These incidents are not merely localised harassment; they represent a sustained effort to change the facts on the water while the legal dispute remains unresolved.

The strategic environment has also shifted in ways that affect Southeast Asian calculations. Under the second Trump administration, US leadership has become less predictable. Southeast Asian states, including the Philippines, have raised concerns about US reliability. China-Southeast Asia economic integration has deepened, with China remaining the region's largest trading partner. These factors create pressure on claimant states to avoid confrontation with Beijing.

docs.title: The Southeast Asian Strategic Dilemma
docs.text:
Southeast Asian claimants face a fundamental dilemma. The legal framework—UNCLOS and the 2016 award—favours their claims. The strategic reality—Chinese power, economic integration, and US unpredictability—favours accommodation or silence.

This dilemma manifests differently across the region: - Vietnam has adopted the most assertive legal stance within ASEAN, officially welcoming the award and using its findings to defend its own maritime rights. - Malaysia and Indonesia have taken cautious positions, positively acknowledging the ruling without openly supporting it. Indonesia's recent recognition of an overlapping claim with China and proposal for joint development in the North Natuna Sea reflects a shift toward accommodation. - Brunei remains silent, avoiding direct confrontation. - The Philippines has moved from accommodation toward operationalisation, but remains constrained by material asymmetries.

docs.title: The Normative Significance of the Award
docs.text:
Despite limited immediate impact on Chinese behaviour, the 2016 award has reshaped the normative terrain of the South China Sea dispute. It has: - Clarified that historic rights claims cannot override UNCLOS. - Established that artificial islands do not generate maritime entitlements. - Created an authoritative legal baseline against which all state actions are measured.

Every Chinese coercive act at sea is now measured against the award's findings. Beijing can dominate the water on a given day, but it struggles to dominate the normative narrative. The award has denied China the comfort of ambiguity.

docs.title: Lessons for Maritime Strategy
docs.text:
1. Legal victory requires operational follow-through. The Philippine experience demonstrates that an arbitral award is a strategic instrument, not a strategic outcome. Implementation requires legal consolidation, disciplined state practice, diplomatic embedding, and coalition-building—applied continuously over years.

  2. ASEAN consensus constrains collective action. ASEAN's consensus mechanism enables members to avoid confrontation with China, but it also prevents the organisation from acting collectively to uphold international law. The result is a regional order managed through avoidance rather than resolution.

  3. Grey-zone tactics exploit legal ambiguity. China's strategy depends on operating below the threshold of armed conflict while changing facts on the ground. Legal clarity—provided by UNCLOS and the award—is a necessary but insufficient counter. Physical presence and enforcement capacity must accompany legal argument.

  4. Economic dependence shapes strategic choice. Deepening China-Southeast Asia economic ties create pressure on claimant states to avoid confrontation. This structural factor will persist regardless of legal rulings or diplomatic statements.

  5. Small and middle states need multi-layered strategy. International law is not self-enforcing. Small states must combine legal, diplomatic, military, and economic instruments to sustain their claims. The Philippines' evolving approach—law, practice, diplomacy, alliances—represents a model of this multi-layered strategy.

docs.title: Fleet Commander's Maritime Operations — The Joint Force Maritime Component
docs.text:
"The numbered fleet commander integrates fleet and joint capabilities into tactical operations, employing naval power in a holistic manner across platforms and domains." — NWP 3, Fleet Warfare

The fleet commander operates at the operational level of maritime warfare. The commander leads a numbered fleet or joint force maritime component. The fleet commander integrates surface, subsurface, air, amphibious, and information capabilities to achieve sea control and project power ashore.

This page discusses the maritime domain at the fleet level, relevant to flag officers and senior staff.

docs.title: The Fleet Commander's Maritime Problem
docs.text: The fleet commander operates across the full spectrum of competition — from peacetime engagement to major combat operations. The commander must integrate capabilities across domains and services to achieve maritime superiority.

docs.title: Sea Control as the Primary Objective
docs.text:
Sea control is the Navy's foremost objective. Without sea control, no other naval function is possible. The fleet commander establishes sea control through the integration of surface, subsurface, and air forces.

Sea control is geographic and time-based. The fleet commander cannot control all the sea all the time. The commander must prioritise areas and times based on the joint force commander's objectives.

docs.title: Power Projection
docs.text: The fleet commander projects power ashore through carrier air wings, cruise missiles, amphibious forces, and naval gunfire. Power projection requires sea control in the objective area. It also requires air superiority and suppression of enemy air defences.

docs.title: Planning
docs.text:
The fleet commander develops operational plans that integrate naval forces with other components. Planning includes:

  • Campaign design: The arrangement of naval operations to achieve strategic objectives.
  • Force allocation: The assignment of forces to tasks based on capability and availability.
  • Logistics planning: The sustainment of forces across vast distances.
  • Risk assessment: The identification and mitigation of operational risks.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text: The fleet commander prepares the fleet for operations. Preparation includes training, exercises, and pre-positioning of forces. The fleet commander must ensure that the fleet is ready to transition from peacetime to combat operations quickly.

docs.title: Execution
docs.text: The fleet commander executes the campaign through mission-type orders. The fleet commander provides intent and guidance but trusts subordinate commanders to execute. This requires mutual trust and shared understanding.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: The fleet commander assesses the progress of the campaign and adjusts as needed. Assessment includes battle damage assessment, intelligence updates, and logistics status.

docs.title: Maritime Interception Operations
docs.text: The fleet commander conducts maritime interception operations to enforce sanctions, blockades, and exclusion zones. This requires the ability to visit, search, and divert vessels at sea.

docs.title: Amphibious Operations
docs.text: The fleet commander supports amphibious operations by providing sea control, air superiority, fire support, and logistics. The fleet commander coordinates the movement of amphibious shipping and protects it from enemy attack.

docs.title: Strike Operations
docs.text: The fleet commander conducts strike operations against land targets using carrier aircraft and cruise missiles. Strike operations require suppression of enemy air defences and precision targeting.

docs.title: Maritime Security Operations
docs.text: The fleet commander conducts maritime security operations to protect shipping, ports, and critical infrastructure. This includes counter-piracy, counter-terrorism, and counter-smuggling operations.

docs.title: The Fleet Commander and Multi-Domain Operations
docs.text:
The fleet commander integrates capabilities across all domains. Space provides communications and positioning. Cyberspace provides information and electromagnetic effects. Land-based aircraft provide airpower. Land forces provide security for naval bases.

The fleet commander must be able to operate in a contested electromagnetic environment. This requires emission control, electronic warfare, and the ability to fight without network support.

docs.title: The Fleet Commander's Landward Problem
docs.text:
The fleet commander faces a complex maritime problem. The commander must simultaneously establish sea control, project power ashore, and support joint operations. The commander must integrate capabilities across domains and services. The commander must operate across vast distances with limited forces.

The fleet commander who masters operational art and multi-domain integration is the fleet commander who wins.

docs.text:

docs.title: Gulf of Guinea — Maritime Security and the Blue Economy
docs.text:
"Almost 40 per cent of the fish caught in West African waters is taken illegally." — Chatham House, Maritime Security in the Gulf of Guinea (2013)

The Gulf of Guinea — the coastal zone stretching from Senegal to Angola — is one of the world's most significant maritime regions. It is an economic lifeline for coastal and landlocked West African states, a source of global energy production, and a hub of international trade. It is also the world's most dangerous maritime domain.

This page examines the nature of maritime insecurity in the Gulf of Guinea, its causes, consequences, and the regional architecture developed to address it.

docs.title: Piracy and Armed Robbery at Sea
docs.text:
The Gulf of Guinea is the global epicentre of maritime piracy. In 2020, more than 95 percent of global piracy incidents occurred in this region. Unlike Somali piracy, which focused on kidnap for ransom, Gulf of Guinea piracy primarily targets cargo theft. Crew kidnapping occurs but is secondary to the theft of fuel, equipment, and valuables.

Pirate attacks in the Gulf of Guinea are characterised by high levels of violence. Of the 58 incidents reported to the International Maritime Bureau in 2012, 37 involved the use of firearms. Pirates are often well-organised, well-armed, and well-funded.

docs.title: Illegal, Unreported, and Unregulated Fishing
docs.text:
IUU fishing is the most economically damaging maritime crime in the Gulf of Guinea. West African governments collectively lose up to USD 1.5 billion annually to IUU fishing. Foreign industrial trawlers — often Chinese, European, or Russian — operate illegally in West African waters, depleting fish stocks that sustain coastal communities.

IUU fishing is not merely an environmental issue. It is a security issue. The depletion of fish stocks undermines food security, destroys livelihoods, and drives young men toward piracy and other forms of maritime crime. The link between IUU fishing and piracy is a vicious cycle: IUU fishing destroys legitimate livelihoods, creating recruits for pirate networks.

docs.title: Oil Theft and Petro-Piracy
docs.text: Nigeria loses approximately 7 percent of its oil output to theft and piracy. Criminal networks siphon crude oil from pipelines and offshore platforms, selling it on the black market. This deprives the government of revenue, causes severe environmental damage, and funds further criminal activity.

docs.title: Trafficking
docs.text: The Gulf of Guinea is a major transit hub for narcotics from Latin America destined for Europe. It is also a corridor for human trafficking and weapons smuggling. Maritime crime in the Gulf of Guinea is interconnected — the same networks that traffic drugs also traffic weapons and people.

docs.title: The Yaoundé Architecture
docs.text:
In 2013, heads of state and government of West and Central African states met in Yaoundé, Cameroon, to address maritime insecurity. The Yaoundé Code of Conduct established a regional maritime security architecture comprising:

  • Inter-Regional Coordination Centre (CICC): Based in Yaoundé, coordinating ECOWAS and ECCAS maritime security efforts.
  • Multinational Maritime Coordination Centres (MMCCs): Regional centres in zones across the Gulf of Guinea.
  • National maritime security committees: Coordinating national responses.

The Yaoundé architecture has achieved significant results. Piracy incidents declined by roughly 90 percent from their peak in 2020 to 2024. However, challenges remain: IUU fishing continues, trafficking persists, and the prosecution of suspected pirates remains extremely limited.

docs.title: Direct Costs
docs.text: Piracy imposes significant direct costs on maritime stakeholders. Shipping companies incur additional expenses of up to USD 50,000 per voyage due to extended routes, armed escorts, and security infrastructure. Insurance premiums increase. Port efficiency declines.

docs.title: Indirect Costs
docs.text: Indirect costs include disrupted supply chains, loss of investor confidence, and reduced competitiveness of regional ports. Crude oil theft and piracy in Nigerian waters alone cost the country over USD 1.5 billion annually.

docs.title: The Criminal Economy
docs.text: Piracy generates income for coastal communities where legitimate opportunities are scarce. A single successful hijacking can net hundreds of thousands of dollars — far exceeding average annual incomes in Nigeria or Cameroon. This creates a perverse incentive structure that sustains pirate networks.

docs.title: The Blue Economy Approach
docs.text:
The blue economy concept reframes maritime security as an economic development issue. Rather than focusing solely on naval patrols, the blue economy approach addresses the root causes of maritime crime: poverty, unemployment, and resource depletion.

Key elements include: - Sustainable fisheries management - Alternative livelihood programmes for former pirates - Port infrastructure development - Maritime domain awareness - Regional cooperation

docs.title: Lessons for Maritime Operations in Africa
1. Maritime Security Is a Development Issue
docs.text: Maritime insecurity in the Gulf of Guinea is driven by poverty, unemployment, and resource depletion. Naval patrols alone cannot solve the problem. Sustainable maritime security requires economic development.

docs.title: 2. Regional Architecture Works — But Requires Capacity
docs.text: The Yaoundé architecture has reduced piracy significantly. But implementation remains uneven. Regional coordination is hampered by language barriers, equipment incompatibilities, and national rivalries.

docs.title: 3. Prosecution Is a Critical Gap
docs.text: Only three piracy cases have been tried in court in the past decade — in Togo, Nigeria, and Denmark — despite 115 piracy incidents reported in 2020 alone. Without prosecution, there is no deterrence.

docs.title: 4. Land-Sea Integration Is Essential
docs.text: Maritime crime in the Gulf of Guinea is organised from land. Pirate networks operate from coastal communities. Effective responses must address both the maritime and terrestrial dimensions of the problem.

docs.title: 5. International Partnerships Matter
docs.text: The Gulf of Guinea is a global concern. International navies — including those of the EU, US, China, India, and Brazil — conduct joint exercises and capacity-building programmes. But these must be coordinated with regional frameworks to avoid duplication and ensure local ownership.
