docs.title: Case Study — Operation Desert Storm: The Left Hook
docs.text:
"The greatest military victory in a generation, achieved through mastery of space and time." — Williamson Murray and Kevin Woods, The Iran-Iraq War

This case study examines the 1991 Gulf War's ground campaign, focusing on the operational-level mastery of space and time that enabled coalition forces to defeat the Iraqi army in 100 hours.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
On 2 August 1990, Iraq invaded Kuwait. The United States led a coalition of 35 nations to liberate Kuwait. The campaign had two phases:

  1. Desert Storm (17 January – 28 February 1991): A 38-day air campaign that destroyed Iraqi air defenses, command and control, and logistics.

  2. Desert Sabre (24 – 28 February 1991): A four-day ground campaign that liberated Kuwait and destroyed the Iraqi Republican Guard.

This case study focuses on the ground campaign and the operational maneuver known as the "Left Hook."

docs.title: The Operational Problem
docs.text:
The coalition faced a significant space-time problem. The Iraqi army occupied Kuwait and southern Iraq. The coalition could attack directly into Kuwait — a frontal assault against prepared defenses. Or it could maneuver around the Iraqi flank — a wide envelopment through the western desert.

The frontal assault was spatially direct but temporally costly. The Iraqis had months to prepare defenses: minefields, wire, fire trenches, and pre-registered artillery. A frontal assault would be slow and costly.

The envelopment was spatially complex but temporally advantageous. The western desert was largely undefended. A rapid maneuver through the desert could outflank the Iraqi army and cut its lines of retreat. But the maneuver required moving hundreds of thousands of troops and vehicles across hundreds of kilometers of desert in a matter of days.

docs.title: The Left Hook
docs.text: General Norman Schwarzkopf, the coalition commander, chose the envelopment. The plan had two elements:

docs.title: 1. The Direct Attack
docs.text: The U.S. Marine Corps and Arab coalition forces attacked directly into Kuwait. This attack fixed the Iraqi army in place. The Iraqis reinforced their defenses in Kuwait, weakening their western flank.

docs.title: 2. The Left Hook
docs.text:
The U.S. VII Corps and XVIII Airborne Corps executed a wide envelopment through the western desert. The corps moved west of Kuwait, then turned east to attack the Iraqi Republican Guard from the rear.

The Left Hook covered approximately 300 kilometers of desert. The corps moved at speeds of 40 to 80 kilometers per hour. The maneuver was completed in less than 48 hours.

docs.title: Spatial Factors
docs.text:
The Left Hook exploited a critical spatial gap in the Iraqi defense. The Iraqis had concentrated their forces in Kuwait and along the Saudi-Kuwait border. The western desert was undefended. The coalition exploited this gap by moving through terrain the Iraqians considered impassable.

The maneuver required precise navigation across featureless desert. The coalition used GPS (then in its early operational stages) and inertial navigation systems to maintain orientation. Without GPS, the Left Hook would have been impossible.

docs.title: Temporal Factors
docs.text:
The Left Hook was a race against time. The coalition had to complete the maneuver before the Iraqis detected the envelopment and redeployed their forces. The coalition used deception to mask the maneuver. The Marines' attack into Kuwait convinced the Iraqis that the main effort was frontal.

The corps moved continuously for 48 hours. Troops slept in vehicles. Maintenance was performed on the move. The tempo was relentless. The corps that arrived at the objective on time was the corps that won.

docs.title: Synchronisation
docs.text:
The Left Hook required precise synchronisation between the direct attack and the envelopment. The Marines had to fix the Iraqi army in place before the VII Corps and XVIII Airborne Corps completed the envelopment. If the Marines attacked too early, the Iraqis would have time to redeploy. If the Marines attacked too late, the envelopment would be exposed.

The synchronisation was achieved through a detailed timeline. The Marines attacked on 24 February at 0400. The VII Corps completed the envelopment on 25 February. The XVIII Airborne Corps cut the lines of retreat on 26 February. The Republican Guard was destroyed by 28 February.

docs.title: The Result
docs.text:
The ground campaign lasted 100 hours. The coalition destroyed 38 Iraqi divisions. Iraqi casualties exceeded 50,000. Coalition casualties were fewer than 500.

The Left Hook demonstrated the decisive advantage of operational-level space-time mastery. The coalition moved faster than the Iraqis could react. The coalition exploited spatial gaps the Iraqis did not know existed. The coalition synchronised its actions with precision the Iraqis could not match.

docs.title: 1. Tempo Is Decisive
docs.text: The coalition's tempo was overwhelming. The Iraqis could not comprehend the speed of the maneuver. By the time they understood what was happening, it was too late.

docs.title: 2. Space Must Be Exploited
docs.text: The western desert was a spatial gap. The coalition exploited it. The Iraqis assumed the desert was impassable. They were wrong.

docs.title: 3. Synchronisation Requires a Timeline
docs.text: The Left Hook succeeded because of a detailed timeline. Every element knew when to act. The timeline was the temporal framework for the operation.

docs.title: 4. Deception Masks Intent
docs.text: The Marines' attack into Kuwait convinced the Iraqis that the main effort was frontal. The Left Hook was masked until it was too late.

docs.title: 5. Technology Enables Maneuver
docs.text: GPS enabled navigation across featureless desert. Without GPS, the Left Hook would have been impossible. Technology compressed the space-time domain.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Keaney, T. A., & Cohen, E. A. (1993). Gulf War Air Power Survey. U.S. Government Printing Office.

Murray, W., & Woods, K. M. (2014). The Iran-Iraq War: A Military and Strategic History. Cambridge University Press.

U.S. Department of Defense. (1992). Conduct of the Persian Gulf War: Final Report to Congress. Washington, DC.

Scales, R. H. (1993). Certain Victory: The U.S. Army in the Gulf War. U.S. Army Command and General Staff College Press.

docs.title: Tempo in African Peace Ops: MONUSCO
docs.text: "Time is the most constrained resource in war. Unlike ammunition or fuel, time cannot be stockpiled. Once lost, it cannot be recovered." — Space-Time Domain, Strategos Telos

docs.title: The Space-Time Problem in MONUSCO
docs.text:
The United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO) operated in one of Africa's most spatially vast and temporally complex conflict environments. Eastern DRC covers terrain the size of Western Europe. Armed groups—M23, ADF, FDLR, CODECO—moved across porous borders with impunity. Civilians were displaced in days. The mission's mandate required it to protect civilians, support stabilisation, and assist security sector reform across this expanse.

The space-time problem was structural: MONUSCO could not be everywhere at once. Its tempo was dictated by logistics, politics, and the initiative of the enemy.

docs.title: The Mandate and Its Temporal Constraints
docs.text:
MONUSCO's mandate, renewed annually by the UN Security Council, imposed a rhythm that conflicted with operational tempo. Mandrup notes that the mission was simultaneously expected to stabilise vast territory, support political processes, and respond to emergency civilian protection tasks—without the forces or political authority to do all three at once.

The Force Intervention Brigade (FIB), established in 2013, represented a deliberate tempo shift. Mandated to conduct offensive operations, the FIB defeated M23 in 2013 within days of engagement. This demonstrated that tempo advantage—concentrated combat power applied rapidly—could achieve decisive results when political authority permitted.

However, the FIB's tempo could not be sustained. Subsequent M23 resurgences in 2022 exposed the gap between kinetic tempo and political patience. Vrey's framework for tempo in the African battlespace identifies this as the central tension: African security operations are conducted under intense temporal pressure from civilians and political principals, while the operational environment resists speed through terrain, logistics, and institutional friction.

docs.title: Friction and the Loss of Tempo
docs.text:
Clausewitz's concept of friction manifested in MONUSCO through multiple layers:

  1. Logistical friction. Supply lines across Central Africa were long, fragile, and vulnerable to ambush. The MONUSCO Military Logistics Base at Entebbe depended on air and river corridors that could be disrupted.
  2. Political friction. The UN Security Council's incremental approach to mandate adaptation meant that force posture often lagged behind events on the ground. When M23 advanced in 2022, the mission's rules of engagement and force structure required weeks to adjust.
  3. Institutional friction. Coordination between MONUSCO, the East African Community Regional Force (EACRF), and the Southern African Development Community Mission in the DRC (SAMIDRC) introduced additional temporal delays. Mandrup documents how competition between regional actors for influence in the DRC slowed operational synchronisation.
  4. Emission and information friction. The electromagnetic environment in eastern DRC was contested. Insurgent radio networks, cell-phone-based command systems, and information operations created a dense electromagnetic battlespace that degraded both MONUSCO and adversary tempo.

docs.title: The EACRF and SAMIDRC Transitions
docs.text:
When MONUSCO began its withdrawal from South Kivu in December 2023, the transition to regional forces introduced new tempo challenges. EACRF's mandate was short and its exit rapid. SAMIDRC—led by South Africa—assumed a more offensive posture, but Mandrup notes that the South African National Defence Force (SANDF) faced significant resource constraints that affected deployment speed and operational sustainability.

The tempo of regional force deployment was slower than the tempo of insurgent adaptation. M23 exploited the security vacuum during transition periods. This pattern—withdrawal, gap, re-entry—repeated across eastern DRC from 2013 through 2024, demonstrating that tempo transitions are themselves a critical vulnerability in peace operations.

docs.title: Tempo and Civilian Protection
docs.text:
The central MONUSCO task—protecting civilians—was the most temporally sensitive. Civilians displaced by violence required immediate response. MONUSCO's forward operating bases, quick reaction forces, and community alert networks were designed to compress the response-to-threat timeline. However, Vrey's analysis of African peace operations shows that civilian protection tempo is frequently frustrated by:

  • Distance. MONUSCO bases were often tens or hundreds of kilometres from the populations at risk.
  • Terrain. Poor road networks in North Kivu and Ituri slowed ground movement.
  • Rules of engagement. Escalation procedures required headquarters approval that could not keep pace with unfolding atrocities.
  • Information lag. Reports of attacks reached MONUSCO through community networks that depended on cellular coverage and civilian courage.

The result was a persistent tempo gap between threat and response—a gap that insurgent groups learned to exploit.

docs.title: Lessons from MONUSCO for African Peace Ops
docs.text:
1. Tempo is a mandate function. Peace operations require mandates that allow rapid response without incremental political approval for each engagement. The FIB demonstrated what is possible when authority matches operational tempo.
  2. Regional transitions are tempo events. Withdrawal or handover periods are predictable windows of vulnerability. Planning for these transitions must include tempo-sustaining measures—overlapping deployment, reserve forces, and emergency bridging capacities.
  3. EMCON discipline affects protection tempo. In an environment where insurgents use commercial communications, the electromagnetic domain directly shapes the speed of threat detection and response. EW and signals intelligence must be embedded in civilian protection task forces.
  4. African solutions must account for African friction. Vrey argues that African peace operations face friction patterns distinct from UN or NATO contexts: logistics across vast territory, political pressures from multiple regional actors, and the persistence of asymmetric threats that exploit tempo gaps. Strategies imported from other contexts fail if they do not address these specific constraints.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Vrey, F. (2020). "Tempo and the African Battlespace: Time Compression in African Peace Operations." Military Strategy Magazine.
  2. Mandrup, T. (2023–2024). Various analyses on MONUSCO, SAMIDRC, and DRC security governance. Stellenbosch University, Security Institute of Governance and Leadership in Africa. Articles published in The Conversation Africa and Africa Defense Forum.
  3. United Nations. (2023–2024). MONUSCO Mandate Renewals and Drawdown Plans. UN Security Council Resolutions and Secretary-General Reports.
  4. African Union. (2013). Peace and Security Council Communiqué on the Force Intervention Brigade. AU PSC.
  5. Africa Center for Strategic Studies. (2023). "Understanding the Democratic Republic of the Congo's Security Transition."

docs.title: Chinese Anti-Access/Area Denial — The Space-Time Dimension
docs.text: "China's A2/AD capabilities are, to date, the most robust within the First Island Chain, although the PLA is increasingly able to project power into the Philippine Sea." — 2022 China Military Power Report, US Department of Defense

docs.title: The Concept
docs.text:
Anti-Access/Area Denial (A2/AD) is a strategy designed to restrict an adversary's access to a operational area and limit their freedom of movement within it. China's A2/AD capabilities are built on a network of land, sea, air, space, and cyber systems that create layered defensive and offensive bubbles extending into the Western Pacific.[^1]

Key components include: - Long-range precision strike: Ballistic and cruise missiles (DF-21D, DF-26, DF-17) targeting air bases, ports, and aircraft carriers - Integrated Air Defense System (IADS): Robust radar networks, SAM systems, and fighter aircraft - Surface and undersea operations: Modern naval vessels and submarines with anti-ship cruise missiles - Space and counterspace: ASAT weapons, jammers, and directed energy systems - Cyber and electronic warfare: Disrupting C4ISR and logistics networks

docs.title: The Space-Time Dimension
docs.text:
Space and time are central to China's A2/AD strategy:

Temporal manipulation: By threatening early destruction of adversary forces, China seeks to compress the timeline for intervention — making it impossible for the US to generate combat power fast enough to prevent fait accompli. As RAND notes, the US military must traverse 4,000+ miles to reach the fight, while China is less than 100 miles from Taiwan and has "interior lines" for rapid force employment.[^1]

Space as an enabler: Nearly all A2/AD capabilities depend on space-based assets for C4ISR, SATNAV (BeiDou), and SATCOM. China's ASAT missiles (capable of targeting all orbits), co-orbital systems (Shijian-21 with robotic arms), and reversible counterspace systems (lasers, jammers) are designed to deny the US its space-based advantages.[^2]

The First Island Chain: China's A2/AD umbrella extends from Japan through Guam to New Guinea. Within this zone, US surface vessels, aircraft, and bases are highly vulnerable to Chinese missile and drone attacks. CSIS wargames indicate the US could exhaust its inventory of long-range missiles within the first week of a Taiwan conflict.[^3]

docs.title: The Escalation Problem
docs.text:
RAND's analysis of a potential US-China conflict over Taiwan highlights the nuclear dimension. China now possesses a second-strike nuclear capability, making any conflict fundamentally different from post-Cold War operations against non-nuclear states.[^4]

Six types of conventional strikes could provoke Chinese nuclear first use: 1. Attacks on critical infrastructure generating mass civilian casualties 2. Attacks on civilian nuclear infrastructure 3. Medium/high-intensity attacks on major cities 4. Any attack turning the strategic situation against the CCP regime 5. Attacks on nuclear forces or C2 elements 6. Decapitation attacks on CCP leadership[^4]

This creates a paradox: the more successful conventional strikes are militarily, the higher the risk of nuclear escalation. Long-range strike against Chinese mainland targets — while militarily effective — is inherently escalatory.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text:
1. A2/AD is a system-of-systems: It cannot be defeated by any single capability. Countering it requires a new operational concept — CSIS suggests "Hellscape" (massive drone swarms to delay invasion) while RAND advocates for "Blue A2/AD" (using denial to prevent aggression rather than defeating it outright).
  2. Space is contested: Future operations must assume space-based C4ISR will be degraded. Hardened GNSS, alternative navigation, and resilient communications are essential.
  3. Time is a weapon: China seeks to win quickly before the US can mobilize. The US must pre-position forces, stockpile munitions, and develop rapid deployment capabilities.
  4. Escalation management is paramount: In a nuclear-armed adversary context, military effectiveness must be balanced against the risk of catastrophic escalation.
  5. Munition stockpiles matter: The US could exhaust LRASMs, JASSMs, and Tomahawks within days. A protracted conflict requires massive increases in production.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text: [^1]: USCC Testimony. "Countering China's Military Strategy in the Indo-Pacific Region." Caitlin Lee, RAND, 2024. [^2]: US Department of Defense. 2022 China Military Power Report (CMPR). 2022. [^3]: CSIS. "Is the United States Prepared for a War with China?" CSIS Analysis, 2015. [^4]: RAND. Denial Without Disaster—Keeping a U.S.-China Conflict over Taiwan Under the Nuclear Threshold. RRA2312-1, 2023.

docs.title: Platoon Commander's Space-Time — Synchronising Intent Across the Battlespace
docs.text:
"The platoon leader must have a relatively complete knowledge of the terrain, and he must know as much as possible about the enemy." — FM 3-21.8, Infantry Platoon and Squad

The platoon commander operates at the tactical level where intent is translated into action. The platoon commander receives the company commander's intent and must achieve it through the coordinated action of multiple sections. This requires mastery of space and time at a higher level than the section commander.

This page discusses the space-time domain at the platoon and company level, relevant to lieutenants and captains.

docs.title: The Platoon Commander's Spatial Problem
docs.text: The platoon commander must visualise the battlespace in three dimensions. Where are the enemy? Where are my sections? Where is the terrain that affects the plan? Where are the boundaries between adjacent units?

docs.title: Key Spatial Tasks
docs.text:
The platoon commander performs several spatial tasks simultaneously:

  • Terrain analysis: Identifying key terrain, observation and fields of fire, cover and concealment, obstacles, and avenues of approach. The platoon commander uses OCOKA and METT-TC (Mission, Enemy, Terrain, Troops, Time, Civil Considerations) to analyse the ground.

  • Section positioning: Placing sections in positions that maximise their combat power while maintaining mutual support. The platoon commander must ensure that sections can support each other with fire and that no section is isolated.

  • Route selection: Choosing routes that balance speed with security. The fastest route may be the most dangerous. The safest route may be too slow. The platoon commander must select the route that achieves the intent in the time available.

  • Boundary management: Operating within the company's area of operations while coordinating with adjacent platoons. The platoon commander must be aware of boundaries to prevent fratricide and ensure seamless coordination.

docs.title: The Platoon Commander's Temporal Problem
docs.text: Time at the platoon level is measured in minutes and hours. The platoon commander must synchronise multiple actions in time.

docs.title: Key Temporal Tasks
docs.text:
• Timeline management: The platoon commander works backwards from the time of the attack or defence. When must sections be in position? When must supporting fires begin? When must the objective be seized? The platoon commander builds a timeline that accounts for movement, preparation, and execution.

  • Synchronisation: The platoon commander synchronises the actions of sections, supporting weapons, and adjacent units. Synchronisation ensures that all elements act at the right time to produce maximum combined effect. A section that arrives too early may be destroyed in isolation. A section that arrives too late may miss the window of opportunity.

  • Tempo control: The platoon commander controls the tempo of the platoon's operations. Tempo is not constant. It accelerates during the assault and slows during consolidation. The platoon commander must be able to change tempo quickly in response to the situation.

docs.title: The OODA Loop at the Platoon Level
docs.text: Boyd's OODA loop applies at the platoon level, but the cycle is more complex than at the section level. The platoon commander must process information from multiple sources: sections, the company commander, adjacent platoons, and supporting units.

docs.title: Observe
docs.text: The platoon commander observes through multiple channels: reports from section commanders, radio traffic, personal observation, and information from higher headquarters. The challenge is to filter relevant information from noise.

docs.title: Orient
docs.text: The platoon commander orients by matching new information with the existing understanding of the situation. Is the enemy as expected? Is the terrain as expected? Are sections where they should be? The orientation process is continuous and must be updated rapidly as new information arrives.

docs.title: Decide
docs.text: The platoon commander decides on a course of action. At the platoon level, decisions are more complex than at the section level. The platoon commander must consider the impact on multiple sections, supporting weapons, and the company plan. Decisions must be communicated clearly and quickly.

docs.title: Act
docs.text: The platoon commander acts by issuing orders to section commanders. The orders must be clear, concise, and timely. The platoon commander must ensure that sections understand not only what to do, but why — the intent behind the order.

docs.title: Synchronisation and the Platoon Sergeant
docs.text:
The platoon commander does not manage space and time alone. The platoon sergeant is the platoon commander's principal assistant for synchronisation. The platoon sergeant manages logistics, coordinates supporting weapons, and ensures that sections are in position on time.

The platoon commander and platoon sergeant form a two-person command team. The platoon commander focuses on the enemy and the mission. The platoon sergeant focuses on the troops and the timeline. Together, they ensure that the platoon operates as a cohesive unit in space and time.

docs.title: Space-Time and the Platoon Attack
docs.text:
The platoon attack is a space-time problem. The platoon commander must:

  1. Plan: Analyse the terrain, the enemy, and the time available. Develop a scheme of manoeuvre that places the platoon on the objective at the right time.

  2. Prepare: Move the platoon to the line of departure. Coordinate supporting fires. Brief section commanders. Ensure all sections understand the plan and the intent.

  3. Execute: Control the platoon's movement to the objective. Adjust the plan as the situation changes. Commit the assault at the right time and place.

  4. Consolidate: Secure the objective. Reorganise the platoon. Prepare for counterattack. The consolidation phase is often neglected but is critical to holding ground.

Each phase has spatial and temporal dimensions. The platoon commander must manage both simultaneously.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Boyd, J. R. (1986). Patterns of Conflict. Unpublished briefing.

Clausewitz, C. von. (1832). On War. Translated by M. Howard and P. Paret. Princeton University Press, 1976.

Osinga, F. P. B. (2005). Science, Strategy and War: The Strategic Theory of John Boyd. Routledge.

U.S. Department of the Army. (2016). FM 6-0: Commander and Staff Organization and Operations. Washington, DC.

U.S. Department of the Army. (2019). ATP 3-21.8: Infantry Platoon and Squad. Washington, DC.

U.S. Department of the Army. (2019). FM 3-21-10: The Infantry Rifle Company. Washington, DC.

docs.title: Section Commander's Space-Time — Reading Ground, Time, and Intent
docs.text:
"Get there firstest with the mostest." — Confederate General Nathan Bedford Forrest

The section commander operates at the lowest level of military command. Decisions are immediate. The consequences are direct. There is no time for detailed analysis. The section commander must read the ground, understand time pressure, and act on intent.

This page discusses the space-time domain at the tactical level most relevant to junior leaders: the lance corporal and corporal commanding a fire team or section.

docs.title: Reading the Ground
docs.text: Terrain is the physical framework within which every engagement occurs. The section commander must read terrain quickly and accurately.

docs.title: Key Terrain Features
docs.text:
Terrain is analysed using the military mnemonic OCOKA:

  • Observation: Where can you see the enemy? Where can the enemy see you? Good observation enables effective fire and early warning. Poor observation creates surprise.

  • Cover and concealment: Cover protects from fire. Concealment hides from observation. The section commander must identify both and use them to protect the section.

  • Obstacles: Natural or artificial features that impede movement. Rivers, walls, minefields, wire. Obstacles can protect flanks or block routes of advance.

  • Key terrain: Any feature whose seizure, retention, or control provides a marked advantage to either side. A hilltop. A bridge. A road junction. Key terrain is the spatial focus of the battle.

  • Avenues of attack: Routes along which a force can move to reach its objective. The section commander must identify covered and concealed avenues that allow the section to close with the enemy.

docs.title: Ground and Movement
docs.text:
The section commander must calculate not merely the distance to an objective, but the time required to traverse that distance in the specific terrain. A kilometre of open ground takes minutes. A kilometre of dense vegetation takes longer. A kilometre under fire takes longest of all.

Ground also determines the formation the section adopts. Open terrain may allow a wide skirmish line. Jungle requires a single file. Urban terrain requires bounding overwatch between buildings.

docs.title: Understanding Time
docs.text: Time at the section level is measured in seconds and minutes. The section commander must understand three temporal factors:

docs.title: 1. Time Available
docs.text: How long before the section must be at the objective? How long before the enemy will arrive? How long before the supporting artillery lifts? The section commander works backwards from these deadlines to determine what is possible.

docs.title: 2. Time to Move
docs.text: The section commander must estimate movement time based on terrain, load, and conditions. A fit section moves at approximately four kilometres per hour on roads. This drops to two kilometres per hour cross-country and one kilometre per hour in dense vegetation. Under fire, movement is slower still.

docs.title: 3. Time to React
docs.text:
The most critical temporal factor. When contact occurs, the section commander must recognise the threat and issue orders within seconds. The faster the section reacts, the more likely it is to survive and win.

Boyd's OODA loop applies at the section level. The section that observes the enemy first, orients correctly, decides quickly, and acts decisively gains the initiative. The section that hesitates loses.

docs.title: Acting on Intent
docs.text:
The section commander receives orders from the platoon commander. These orders include the commander's intent — the purpose of the operation and the desired end state. The section commander must understand intent well enough to act when the plan changes.

Intent at the section level is simple. "Seize that hilltop." "Defend this position." "Provide covering fire for the platoon advance." The section commander must be able to achieve the intent even when communication fails or the situation changes.

This requires mission command at the lowest level. The platoon commander states the intent. The section commander decides how to achieve it. If the planned route is blocked, the section commander selects an alternative. If the enemy appears from an unexpected direction, the section commander reacts without waiting for orders.

docs.title: The Section Commander's Decision Cycle
docs.text:
The section commander's decision cycle is compressed. There is no time for detailed analysis. The cycle is:

  1. Observe: Detect the enemy. Identify terrain features. Note changes in the situation.

  2. Orient: Match what you see with what you know. Is this the expected enemy? Is this terrain as expected? Does this change the plan?

  3. Decide: Choose a course of action. The section commander has limited options: advance, defend, delay, or withdraw. The decision must be quick.

  4. Act: Issue fire orders. Direct movement. Control the section. The action must be immediate.

This cycle repeats continuously throughout the engagement. The section commander who cycles faster than the enemy section gains the advantage.

docs.title: Space-Time and the Junior Leader
docs.text:
The lance corporal does not plan campaigns. But the lance corporal must understand space and time at the most fundamental level. Where am I? Where is the enemy? Where is my objective? How long will it take to get there? How long do I have? What happens if I am late?

These questions are the foundation of tactical decision-making. The section commander who can answer them quickly and accurately is the section commander who wins.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Strategos Telos is a curated knowledge base for military theory, wargaming, scenario design, and strategic analysis. It exists to serve the SANDF and broader defence community with rigorously sourced, properly attributed content.

docs.title: Content Diversity Principle
docs.text:
For every one "Western" thing on this site — be it a concept, page, article, example, or case study — there must be two more:

  1. An African perspective — grounded in Sub-Saharan Africa specifically, with attention to the continent's diversity (not reducing Africa to a monolith).
  2. A perspective from Asia, South America, or another "developing" part of the world — ensuring the site reflects the majority of the world's population and military experience.

This 2:1 ratio is a guiding principle. It applies to: - Case studies (e.g., one Western battle → one African battle → one Asian/South American battle) - Examples and scenarios - Historical narratives - Theoretical frameworks (e.g., one Western theorist → one African theorist → one Asian theorist) - Training manual procedures (adaptable to different resource environments)

Within Africa: Sub-Saharan Africa is the primary focus. North African perspectives are included where relevant but do not substitute for Sub-Saharan representation.

Why: Military knowledge has been overwhelmingly written from a Western perspective. This site corrects that imbalance. A military officer from Ghana, Vietnam, or Bolivia should see their experience reflected here — not as an afterthought, but as a core part of the catalogue.

Implementation: When proposing or writing a content piece, the author must identify the "two non-Western counterparts" that will accompany it. If they do not yet exist, they are flagged as pending.

  1. All substantive claims must cite their source. No unattributed assertions.
  2. NO SANDF DOCTRINE. No internal SANDF doctrine, no documents marked RESTRICTED, no confidential or classified material of any kind.
  3. Publicly available = fair game. Information available on the internet may be used. Foreign military doctrine is permitted.
  4. Human-approved exceptions only. If Tobias explicitly provides a document for wiki content, it is pre-approved — this does not create a precedent for future SANDF-internal documents.
  5. Attribution preserved. Source documents are cited by title, reference number, and author where applicable.
  6. Draft → Review → Deploy. No content reaches the live site without review.

docs.title: The Security-Development Nexus in Sub-Saharan Africa
docs.text:
"The scourge of conflicts in Africa constitutes a major impediment to the socio-economic development of the continent." — Constitutive Act of the African Union

The relationship between security and development in Sub-Saharan Africa is not linear — it is a complex, dynamic system in which each dimension shapes and is shaped by the other. This page examines the security-development nexus through an African lens, drawing on the African Union's frameworks and academic research.

docs.title: The Traditional View
docs.text: The traditional view treats security and development as separate domains. Security is about military force and state stability. Development is about economic growth and poverty reduction. In this view, security is a precondition for development — you cannot develop without peace.

docs.title: The African Union's View
docs.text: The African Union's Constitutive Act recognises the interdependence of peace and security with development. Article 3 states that the AU shall "promote peace, security, and stability on the continent" and "promote sustainable development at the economic, social and civic levels." These are not separate objectives — they are mutually reinforcing.

docs.title: The Human Security Approach
docs.text:
The UNDP's concept of human security broadens the definition of security beyond state security to include: - Freedom from want: Economic security, food security, health security - Freedom from fear: Personal security, community security, political security - Freedom to live in dignity: Human rights, rule of law, participation

In the African context, human security is particularly relevant. Most Africans face threats not from foreign invasion but from poverty, disease, environmental degradation, and internal conflict. The African Union's African Human Security Index integrates these dimensions.

docs.title: The Causality Debate
docs.text:
Does development drive security, or does security drive development? Recent research using panel data from 33 African countries (2004–2019) reveals a nuanced picture:

  • In lower-income and lower-middle-income countries: Economic development drives national security. Growth reduces conflict vulnerability.
  • In upper-middle-income countries: National security drives economic development. Stability enables investment and growth.

This finding has important policy implications. In the poorest countries, development interventions are security interventions. In more developed countries, security enables further development.

docs.title: The Cost of Conflict
docs.text: The World Bank estimates that a civil war costs the average developing country roughly 30 years of GDP growth. Countries in protracted crises fall over 20 percentage points behind in poverty reduction. Between 1990 and 2005, conflict-related GDP losses across Africa totalled approximately USD 284 billion.

docs.title: The Peace Dividend
docs.text: Conversely, peace enables development. Stabilised post-conflict zones attract increased investment and aid. Governments can shift spending from military operations to health, education, and infrastructure. The African Development Bank estimates that African countries lose up to 2 percent of GDP annually to conflict.

docs.title: Post-Conflict Reconstruction and Development (PCRD)
docs.text:
The AU's PCRD policy, first adopted in 2006 and comprehensively revised in 2024, provides a practical framework for operationalising the security-development nexus. The revised policy is structured around eight interlinked pillars:

  1. Security: DDRRR, security sector reform, small arms control
  2. Humanitarian Assistance: Emergency relief, protection of civilians
  3. Governance: Constitutional reform, elections, rule of law
  4. Socio-Economic Recovery: Infrastructure, livelihoods, economic recovery
  5. Human Rights and Justice: Transitional justice, reconciliation
  6. Gender: Women's participation, gender-based violence prevention
  7. Youth: Youth employment, education, participation
  8. Environmental Security: Climate adaptation, natural resource management

docs.title: The African Peace and Security Architecture (APSA)
docs.text: APSA integrates conflict prevention, peacebuilding, and development. The Continental Early Warning System (CEWS) monitors both conflict and development indicators. The Panel of the Wise engages in preventive diplomacy. The African Standby Force provides rapid response capability.

docs.title: The African Governance Architecture (AGA)
docs.text: AGA complements APSA by addressing governance — the institutional foundation for both security and development. The African Peer Review Mechanism (APRM) assesses governance performance. The African Charter on Democracy, Elections, and Governance sets standards.

docs.title: The Implementation Gap
docs.text: Despite comprehensive policy frameworks, implementation remains weak. The gap between policy and practice is driven by: - Institutional fragmentation: Peace and security policymakers and development policymakers operate in separate silos - Divergent working methods: Military and development actors have different cultures, timelines, and metrics - Donor dependency: African institutions rely on external funding, which shapes priorities - Limited capacity: Most African states lack the institutional capacity to implement complex, multi-dimensional programmes

docs.title: The Climate-Security Link
docs.text: Climate change is a threat multiplier in Africa. The Lake Chad Basin illustrates the interaction: environmental degradation, resource scarcity, and livelihood collapse create conditions for state fragility, human insecurity, and violent extremism. The revised PCRD policy's environmental sustainability pillar addresses this link.

docs.title: The Digital Dimension
docs.text: Digital technologies create both opportunities and risks. Mobile money drives financial inclusion but creates cybersecurity risks. Social media enables political participation but facilitates disinformation. The security-development nexus must account for the digital dimension.

docs.title: 1. Security and Development Are Inseparable
docs.text: Military operations in Africa cannot be separated from development. Peacekeeping missions that ignore economic recovery and governance will not achieve sustainable peace.

docs.title: 2. Local Ownership Is Essential
docs.text: Externally imposed solutions fail. African-led approaches, grounded in African knowledge systems and institutional realities, are more effective and more sustainable.

docs.title: 3. Prevention Is Cheaper Than Response
docs.text: Conflict prevention costs a fraction of conflict response. Early warning, preventive diplomacy, and development interventions reduce the need for military operations.

docs.title: 4. The Anthropocene Changes Everything
docs.text: Climate change, resource depletion, and environmental degradation are reshaping the security landscape. Military practitioners must understand these dynamics and integrate them into planning.

docs.title: 5. Youth Are the Key
docs.text: Africa's youth population is both an opportunity and a risk. Youth unemployment drives conflict. Youth engagement in peacebuilding and development creates resilience. The security-development nexus must centre youth.

docs.title: After Action Review and Lessons Learned
docs.text: "An After Action Review (AAR) is a guided analysis of an organization's performance, conducted at appropriate times during and at the conclusion of a training event, with the objective of improving future performance." — US Army TC 7-0.1, After Action Reviews

docs.title: What Is an After Action Review?
docs.text:
An After Action Review (AAR) is a professional discussion of a training event that enables participants to discover for themselves what happened and develop a strategy for improving performance. It is not a critique — it does not judge success or failure. It is a structured conversation focused on learning.

Key characteristics: - Conducted during and after the exercise (not just at the end) - Led by a facilitator (controller, evaluator, or leader) - Focuses on training objectives and standards - Involves all participants - Emphasises self-discovery over instruction

docs.title: Step 1: Plan
docs.text: Planning for the AAR begins before the exercise. The AAR plan identifies: - What events and tasks will be observed - Who will observe them - When and where AARs will be conducted - What standards will be used for evaluation

docs.title: Step 2: Prepare
docs.text: Preparation begins before the exercise and continues during execution: - Brief observers and controllers on the AAR plan - Collect observations from working papers - Review the sequence of events and cause-effect relationships - Develop a discussion outline - Prepare thought-provoking questions

docs.title: Step 3: Conduct
docs.text:
Each AAR contains three major steps:

  1. Restatement of training standards — The facilitator briefly restates the specific standards
  2. Discussion of events — The facilitator guides a discussion of what happened and why
  3. Summary and recommendations — The facilitator summarises and identifies improvements

Conduct techniques: - Ask leading, open-ended questions focused on training standards - Have participants describe what happened in their own words - Relate tactical events to subsequent results - Explore alternative courses of action - Avoid detailed examination of events not related to major training standards

docs.title: Step 4: Follow Up
docs.text:
• Retrain immediately to address weak task proficiencies
  • Revise SOPs to reflect lessons learned
  • Share lessons with other units
  • Record AAR results for future reference

docs.title: Types of AARs
docs.text: Type When Conducted Scope Formal Company level and above; externally evaluated events Detailed planning, scheduled, facilitated Informal Crew, squad, or platoon level; on-the-spot Minimal planning, leader-facilitated Interim At logical breakpoints during the exercise Correct deficiencies before they compound Hot Wash Immediately after the exercise concludes Initial impressions while fresh

docs.title: The After Action Report
docs.text:
The After Action Report (AAR) is the formal written record of the exercise. It is produced concurrently with or immediately after the exercise.

AAR Format:

Section Content Executive Summary Significant lessons learned, readiness discussion, recommendations Exercise Objective Restated from the Commissioning Instruction General Discussion Significant events, lessons learned, support requirements Findings and Conclusions Associated with each lesson learned and deficiency Recommendations Specific recommendations for future training

Critical rule: Formal AARs should be submitted within 1–2 weeks of exercise completion.

docs.title: Lessons Learned Process
docs.text:
The lessons learned process extends beyond the AAR to ensure observations are captured, validated, and integrated into future training:

Phase Activity Discovery Collect observations from AARs, controller reports, working papers Validation Screen observations to determine if a best practice or issue exists Integration Resolve validated issues through changes to doctrine, training, SOPs Assessment Observe implemented solutions to determine if they met requirements

Critical principle: Lessons learned must be recorded, shared, and institutionalised — not merely identified.

docs.title: Conducting Effective AARs
docs.text:
The facilitator's role: - Guide the discussion, do not lecture - Ask open-ended, thought-provoking questions - Emphasise the positive while addressing weaknesses - Keep the discussion focused on training standards - Ensure all participants contribute

Common pitfalls: - Critiquing rather than facilitating - Lecturing participants on what went wrong - Focusing on individuals rather than processes - Allowing the discussion to drift from training objectives - Failing to identify actionable recommendations - Not following up with retraining

docs.title: Assessment and Evaluation During Military Exercises
docs.text: "Assessing nothing and trying to assess everything are evil twins — both are unproductive and both will hamper improvement." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 9

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Military exercises are planned and conducted to achieve specific goals and objectives. The success of the exercise is determined by the extent to which these goals and objectives are achieved. To determine whether a goal or objective has been achieved, some form of assessment or evaluation is required.

No exercise should be conducted without a credible and deliberate assessment and evaluation plan — otherwise participants will only go through the motions and the exercise becomes nothing more than a "show" or demonstration.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
Term Definition Assessment An informal, non-empirical, formative process used to continuously diagnose performance. Subjective in nature; focuses on identifying strengths, weaknesses, and potential growth areas. Feedback is informal and provided directly. Evaluation A formal summative process directed at a specific target audience conducting a specified action under set conditions. Performance is objectively measured against a predetermined standard (outcomes-oriented). Uses specialised data collection tools; results in qualified grades, scores, or certification.

These two processes are often used in tandem, with one supporting the other or even overlapping.

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text: No target group (force structure element, HQ, or individual) should be assessed or evaluated if the member or element has not been trained and certified as competent prior to the assessment or evaluation process. Assessing or evaluating untrained military personnel provides very little value, expends unnecessary resources, and wastes valuable time.

docs.title: Aim of Assessment and Evaluation
docs.text:
Assessment and evaluation should not be seen as a test or examination. Its higher purpose is to identify gaps and lessons that can be used to increase the effectiveness and performance of units, systems, and soldiers.

The aim is to provide the chain of command with objective information regarding:

  • The effectiveness of training (competency, proficiency)
  • The readiness level of military forces
  • The functionality and effectiveness of systems, doctrine, and TTPs
  • Identification of training gaps

docs.title: Assessment and Evaluation Agency
docs.text: Type Description Internal Assessment Conducted by members within the chain of command of the focus group being evaluated External Assessment Conducted by members or agencies outside the focus group's operational chain of command

docs.title: Focus Group
docs.text: Approach Description Collective All members of the group are assessed and evaluated Sample Group A smaller sample group represents a cross-section of the overall group Specified Focus Group A specific group within the larger focus group is identified for assessment

docs.title: Focus Area
docs.text:
Broad focus areas include: - Doctrine (Tactics, Techniques, Procedures, and Processes) - Systems - Capabilities - Products/Outcome (End State) - Performance

Each focus area can be broken down into levels: - Level 1: Technical - Level 2: Individual - Level 3: Crew/Section - Level 4: Sub-sub unit (Platoon) - Level 5: Sub-Unit (Company/Combat Team) - Level 6: Unit (Battalion/Regiment/Combat group) - Level 7: Brigade/Formation - Level 8: Division/Joint Task Force

docs.title: Assessment Tools
docs.text:
• Questionnaires and exams
  • Practical demonstrations
  • Assessment of products handed in
  • Observation

docs.title: Assessment Standard
docs.text: Type Description Comprehensive Assessment Standards Large number of standards covering the total spectrum of tasks, functions, and responsibilities Selective Assessment Standard Only key performance areas are identified for assessment

docs.title: Appointment of Assessors and Evaluators
docs.text: Assessors and evaluators must be: - Technically qualified to the level being assessed - Subject matter experts (SME) in the field they will assess - Of equivalent or higher rank than the training audience - Operationally experienced in the aspect being assessed - Honest, objective, able to work as part of a team - Good interpersonal and communication skills - Able to persevere under extreme and difficult conditions

docs.title: Grouping of Assessors and Evaluators
docs.text:
System Description Pool System Assessors grouped in a centralised pool and tasked on an ad-hoc basis. Centralised command and control. Resource-heavy. Embedded System Assessors attached to specific units or sub-units. Remain with the unit for the duration. Decentralised command and control.

"Double-hat" appointments: The practice of utilising a member in more than one role. Common but carries risks — should not be used to appoint members to act as controller/assessor/evaluator simultaneously during execution.

docs.title: Stage 2: Design and Development
docs.text:
• Phase 1: A&E assists with analysis and formulation of objectives in the Final Integrated Objective List (FIOL)
  • Phase 2: A&E verifies and identifies potential events and incidents to be evaluated
  • Phase 3: Injects are drafted and the Exercise Control Matrix is constructed. Expected outcomes are transformed into A&E criteria.

Assessment and Evaluation Concept must address: - Focus group, capability, or individuals to be assessed - Events and incidents to be assessed - Assessment and evaluation standard (competency & proficiency) - Performance indicators - Method of data collection - Assessment tools (grading) - Size of A&E structure and minimum criteria of members - Reporting line and routine - End users for findings and recommendations

docs.title: Stage 3: Planning
docs.text:
Assessment and Evaluation Plan is drawn up in detail during the Main Planning Conference and presented during the Final Planning Conference.

Statement of Assessment Objectives lists: - Objectives, incidents, or activities to be assessed - Focus group - Location of activity - Timing (start time, end time, total duration)

Assessment/Evaluation Sheet (mark sheet) must indicate: - Assessment standard (task, condition, required performance standard) - Grading system

docs.title: Data Collection Methods
docs.text:
• Performance mark sheets based on set standards
  • Observation reports
  • Statements, questionnaires, lessons learned sheets
  • Formative and summative evaluations
  • Portfolio of Evidence (physical products)
  • Hot wash-up debrief / After-action report
  • Buddy ratings
  • Voice recordings
  • Video recordings
  • Aerial photos and videos captured by UAVs
  • Playback recording when using constructive simulation (CAX)

docs.title: Grading
docs.text:
Grading is determined in terms of:

Measurement Description Measurement of Performance (MOP) Determines whether the task was completed within a defined standard or condition Measurement of Effectiveness (MOE) Measures how effectively the task was completed

docs.title: Grading Scales
docs.text:
Example 1: Numerical Scale (0-6) - 0: Event not evaluated - 1: Required to do task but did not - 2: Task partially completed / performance unsatisfactory - 3: Task completed with major shortcomings - 4: Task completed with minor shortcomings - 5: Satisfactory - 6: Highly competent

Example 2: Color Codes - Black: Not measured or not executed - Red: Below required standard - Amber: Meets minimum requirement but requires additional training - Green: Meets the requirement

docs.title: Stage 4: Delivery
docs.text: The bulk of performance data is collected during delivery. All members of the A&E cell must receive specialised training prior to the start of the exercise, including: - Orientation training - Specialised training (first aid, map reading, safety, equipment, report writing)

docs.title: Stage 5: Post-Exercise Activities and Reports
docs.text:
Analysis is the reviewing of evidence gathered to assess performance. Key components include data management and triangulation to validate findings.

Analysis can take place: - On-site: As the incident unfolds; reporting immediately after the activity - Off-site: For operational or strategic level events requiring more time

Findings may be published as: - Lessons Identified: Recommendations based on observations relating to the discrepancy between required and actual performance - Lessons Learned: A Lesson Identified that has been validated and integrated into doctrine and TTPs

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text:
• After Action Review and Lessons Learned — AAR and lesson learned process
  • Post-Exercise Activities — Post-exercise reporting
  • Exercise Design Templates and Checklists — A&E plan template
  • Detailed Planning Conferences — A&E planning during Stage 3

docs.title: Exercise Commissioning
docs.text: "The Commissioning Instruction is a critical document that will be required to initiate the planning and design process for an exercise." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 3

docs.title: What Is Exercise Commissioning?
docs.text:
Exercise commissioning is the formal process by which an exercise is authorised, resourced, and initiated. It transforms a training requirement into a mandated planning activity with clear authority, objectives, and resources.

The commissioning document — variously called a Commissioning Instruction, Exercise Directive, or Tasking Order depending on the echelon and nation — is the single most important document in the exercise lifecycle. Without it, planning cannot begin.

docs.title: The Commissioning Authority
docs.text:
Exercises are commissioned by the appropriate authority based on the type and scale of the exercise:

Exercise Type Typical Commissioning Authority Service-unique Chief of Service / Commander of Formation Joint (multi-service) Chief Joint Operations / Joint Force Commander Multinational Lead Nation / Joint Force Commander National-level National command authority / designated minister

The commissioning authority is often referred to as the Officer Scheduling the Exercise (OSE) or Convening Officer. This individual holds the authority to initiate the exercise, appoint the Exercise Director, and allocate resources.

docs.title: Exercise Specification Meeting
docs.text:
Before the Commissioning Instruction is issued, the OSE typically convenes an Exercise Specification Meeting (also called an Exercise Conference or EXSPEC Conference). This meeting brings together key stakeholders to define the broad requirements:

Attendees: - OSE / Convening Officer - Prospective Exercise Director - Senior exercise control representatives - Resource / budget representatives

Key outputs: - Exercise name and code name - Purpose and type of exercise - Aim and objectives (broad) - Primary Training Audience (PTA) - Participating and supporting forces - Time and duration - Location(s) and training area - Budget envelope and resource guidance - Key appointments - Planning schedule and milestones - Restrictions and constraints

docs.title: Commissioning Instruction Components
docs.text: The Commissioning Instruction is a formal document that mandates the exercise and authorises planning. While formats vary across nations and organisations, the following components are standard:

docs.title: 1. Exercise Identity
docs.text: Element Description Exercise name Unique code name for the exercise (e.g., Exercise STEADFAST, Exercise UPLIFT) Type of exercise Classification (CPX, FTX, CAX, etc.) Polarity One-sided, two-sided, or multi-sided Level Strategic, operational, or tactical

docs.title: 2. Purpose and Aim
docs.text:
Element Description Purpose Why the exercise is being conducted (training, evaluation, development, deterrence) Aim Broad, singular statement of intent Goal More specific, measurable, time-bound outcome

Example aim: "To train all forces designated to form part of Exercise STEADFAST in the planning, conduct, and support of joint task force-level operations in a complex multi-domain environment."

docs.title: 3. Exercise Objectives
docs.text:
Objectives are the specific, measurable outcomes the exercise must achieve. They serve as building blocks for the aim and guide all subsequent design and evaluation.

Critical distinction: - Exercise Objectives — What the exercise must achieve overall - Training Objectives — What the PTA must learn or demonstrate

Objectives must be: - Specific — Unambiguous and clear - Measurable — Capable of being assessed - Attainable — Achievable within the exercise parameters - Relevant — Aligned with the aim - Time-bound — Achievable within the exercise duration - Inspectable — Capable of being observed and evaluated (SMART-I)

docs.title: 4. Primary Training Audience (PTA)
docs.text: The Commissioning Instruction identifies the PTA — the main participants who will be formally assessed. It may also identify Secondary Training Audience (STA) and supporting elements.

docs.title: 5. Participating and Supporting Forces
docs.text: Element Description PTA Primary Training Audience (to be assessed) STA Secondary Training Audience (not assessed) OPFOR Opposing force (if applicable) Support elements Logistics, medical, signal, etc.

docs.title: 6. Time and Duration
docs.text:
• Start and end dates
  • Operational periods (if phased over months/years)
  • Key milestones (conferences, reconnaissance, execution)

docs.title: 7. Location(s)
docs.text:
• Primary training area(s)
  • Alternative or secondary locations
  • Requirements for specific terrain or infrastructure

docs.title: 8. Key Appointments
docs.text: Appointment Responsibility Exercise Director (EXDIR) Overall command of the exercise Deputy EXDIR Assists EXDIR (optional) Chief Exercise Control Controls exercise execution Force Commander (FC) Commands the PTA Chief Scenario Leads narrative and scenario development Other key posts As required by exercise type and scale

docs.title: 9. Resources and Budget
docs.text:
• Financial authority and budget envelope
  • Specific resource allocations (rations, ammunition, flying hours, vehicles)
  • Any special equipment or capabilities

docs.title: 10. Planning Guidelines and Restrictions
docs.text:
• Dates for planning conferences (CDC, IPC, MPC, FPC)
  • Planning timeline and milestones
  • Specific restrictions (safety, environmental, political)
  • Classification and security guidelines

docs.title: Exercise Directive vs. Commissioning Instruction
docs.text:
In joint and multinational contexts, the Exercise Directive serves the same purpose as the Commissioning Instruction but may be issued by a joint operations centre rather than a single service. The key difference is the issuing authority and the scope of the mandate:

Document Issuing Authority Scope Commissioning Instruction Single service or formation Service-unique or single-formation exercise Exercise Directive Joint operations centre Joint (multi-service) exercise Tasking Order Higher headquarters Any exercise formally tasked to a subordinate

docs.title: Issue and Distribution
docs.text:
The Commissioning Instruction must be issued as early as possible — ideally well in advance of the first planning conference. The timing depends on the size and complexity of the exercise:

Exercise Type Typical Lead Time Small tactical exercise 3–6 months Medium operational exercise 6–12 months Large joint/multinational exercise 12–24 months

Distribution is limited to key planners and is marked as "For EXCON Eyes Only" to prevent the PTA from gaining advance knowledge of the scenario.

docs.title: The Commissioning Instruction in Practice
docs.text:
The Commissioning Instruction is not a formality — it is the foundation of the entire exercise. A poorly written Commissioning Instruction leads to:

  • Ambiguous objectives
  • Misaligned design
  • Resource shortfalls
  • Re-work and delay
  • Exercise failure

Critical principle: The Commissioning Instruction must be drafted with care, issued with sufficient lead time, and contain as much detail as possible. Without it, the planning group lacks direction and the exercise deviates from the requirement.

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text:
• The Exercise Planning Process — How the Commissioning Instruction drives planning
  • Exercise Control Structures — How EXCON is established under the Commissioning Instruction
  • Typology of Military Exercises — Classifications referenced in the Instruction

docs.title: Exercise Concept Development
docs.text: "Exercise design is the intellectual core of the exercise planning process. It is the point at which training objectives are translated into operational reality." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 7

docs.title: What Is the Exercise Concept?
docs.text: The Exercise Concept is the blueprint for the exercise. It integrates the Main Events List (MEL) and Master Incident List (MIL) into a coherent operational narrative, with timelines, locations, safety considerations, and control arrangements. Once approved by the Exercise Director (EXDIR), the Exercise Concept becomes the framework for all detailed planning.

docs.title: The Three-Phase Design Process
docs.text:
Stage 2 — Design and Development — is itself a three-phase process:

STAGE 2: DESIGN AND DEVELOPMENT
├── Phase 1: Objective Analysis → Final Integrated Objective List (FIOL)
├── Phase 2: Design and Concept Development → MEL, MIL, Exercise Concept
└── Phase 3: Exercise Construction → Injects, ECM, ICS

docs.title: Phase 1: Objective Analysis
docs.text:
The purpose of Phase 1 is to produce the Final Integrated Objective List (FIOL) — a validated, prioritised, and SMART-I compliant set of training objectives that will guide all design decisions.

Key activities: 1. Objective Review and Reformulation — Review initial objectives; reformulate ambiguous or overlapping ones 2. SMART-I Compliance Test — Ensure each objective is Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant, Time-bound, and Inspectable 3. Grouping — Cluster objectives into thematic groupings reflecting operational functions 4. Integration — Resolve conflicts and overlaps between objectives 5. Prioritisation — Rank objectives by criticality

Output: The FIOL — the single most important document in exercise design. Every subsequent product is derived from it.

docs.title: Step 1: The Main Events List (MEL)
docs.text:
The MEL is the structural skeleton of the exercise. It translates the FIOL's thematic groupings into a sequence of operational events.

Construction method:

Step Activity 1.1 Identify Themes — Review FIOL and identify common operational themes 1.2 Sequence Themes — Order themes in realistic operational sequence 1.3 Decompose Themes into Events — Identify specific events that exercise associated objectives 1.4 Link Events to Objectives — Specify which FIOL objective(s) each event addresses

MEL Format:

Theme Event Objective(s) / Comments 1. ISR 1.1 Route reconnaissance Obj 2: Conduct tactical reconnaissance 1. ISR 1.2 Intelligence preparation Obj 3: Produce IPB 2. Planning 2.1 Staff estimate Obj 4: Conduct operational estimate

Quality criteria: - Addresses every objective in the FIOL at least once - Contains no events that cannot be traced to an objective - Is sequenced in a logically coherent operational flow - Is realistic given available time, space, and forces

docs.title: Step 2: The Master Incident List (MIL)
docs.text:
The MIL deconstructs each MEL event into the specific tactical incidents that will require a response from the PTA. If the MEL is the skeleton, the MIL is the nervous system.

Construction method:

Step Activity 2.1 Deconstruct Each Event — Ask: "What specific occurrences will challenge the PTA?" 2.2 Define Each Incident — Define occurrence + required PTA response 2.3 Number Incidents — Number to correspond with parent event (1.1.1, 1.1.2, etc.)

MIL Format:

Event Incident Occurrence Response 1.1 Route recc 1.1.1 Locals report insurgent infiltration route PTA conducts ambush 1.1 Route recc 1.1.2 IED discovered on primary route PTA conducts route clearance

Quality criteria: - Deconstructs every MEL event into at least one incident - Contains no incidents that cannot be traced to an event and objective - Provides incidents that collectively stress every objective in the FIOL - Is realistic given the operational context and PTA capabilities

docs.title: Step 3: Conceptualisation and Exercise Concept Construction
docs.text:
Conceptualisation is not a single act; it is an iterative process of review, sequencing, mapping, safety assessment, and scheduling.

The Conceptualisation Process:

Step Activity 3.1 Review Known Facts and Requirements — Type, aim, objectives, budget, locations, time, PTA, forces, control approach, exercise model, MEL/MIL 3.2 Construct the Activity List — Sequence all events and incidents in operational time 3.3 Map Placement — Plot all incidents on a training area map 3.4 Safety Assessment — Identify live-fire areas, civilian presence, evacuation routes 3.5 Scheduling — Allocate timings and plot on a Gantt chart or timeline

Activity List format:

Event / Incident Date Time Location Target Audience Expected Outcome Comments 1.1.1 D+1 0600–0700 Grid ABC123 Recce Platoon Ambush executed Coordinate with safety 1.1.2 D+1 0800–0900 Route BLUE Recce Platoon Route cleared IED script attached

docs.title: Site Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Once the concept is drafted, a physical site reconnaissance confirms that the training area can support the planned events.

Reconnaissance Team:

Role Purpose Chief Real-Life Support / Exercise Warrant Officer Accommodation, facilities, sustainment Chief Scenario Development Terrain suitability for planned incidents Chief Exercise Control Control positions, communications, observation Battlefield Preparation / Simulation Representative Live-fire areas, simulation infrastructure Signal Officer Communications footprint, cell coverage Medical Officer Medical facility access, evacuation routes

Focus areas: - Terrain: Size, geography, vegetation, hydrography, time/distance between locations - Infrastructure: Office space, mess, ablutions, accommodation, power, water, sewerage - Restrictions: Grave sites, heritage sites, environmental sensitivities, legislation - Safety: Live-fire areas, civilian presence, emergency services availability - Liaison: Military controlling authority, local government, security structures

Back brief: The reconnaissance team presents site suitability assessment, real-life support implications, and required adjustments to the EXDIR.

docs.title: Presenting the Exercise Concept
docs.text:
The Exercise Concept can be presented using any combination of: - Map overlays showing event locations and timelines - D-Day timeline showing the sequence of events - Lines of operations showing the operational flow - Visual mind maps or infographic showing thematic relationships - Activity List / descriptive work document

Presentation to the EXDIR must include: - Conceptual approach and broad themes - Description of each event and supporting incident - Sequence and timing of events - Location(s) on a training area map - Primary Training Audience and objectives to be achieved - Focus areas for evaluation - Strengths, weaknesses, risks, and implications

EXDIR decision: The EXDIR assesses the concept and either approves it or provides additional guidelines for adjustment.

docs.title: Detailed Planning Conferences
docs.text: "Planning for an exercise should be conducted with the same sense of urgency and focus on detail as when planning for a real-time operation." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 13

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Planning Stage — also referred to as Detailed Planning — is Stage 3 in the Exercise Design Process. During this stage, detailed planning takes place to ensure that the approved Exercise Concept developed during Stage 2 is developed into a comprehensive Exercise Plan that can be executed during Stage 4: Execution.

Exercise planning is a continuous process involving a wide range of complex activities that interact, often in indirect ways. For an exercise to achieve its objectives, these activities must be aligned and synchronised through a detailed Exercise Plan.

docs.title: Planning Conferences
docs.text: The exercise planning process consists of several integrated planning conferences, staff liaison, site visits, and back briefs. These activities occur over a set period and aim to bring together key role players, stakeholders, and participants.

docs.title: Initial Planning Conference (IPC)
docs.text:
The IPC takes place after the Concept Development Conference and is initiated by the Exercise Director (EXDIR) with all of EXCON in attendance.

Purpose: Introduce the main planning group to the Exercise Concept and training package. Exchange information to allow the exercise management team and planners to fully understand each other's requirements.

Key topics: - Introduction to the Exercise Concept based on exercise objectives - Exercise Plan focusing on planned main events - Training requirements (refresher, integrated, specialised) - Proposed EXCON structures - Exercise Support Package (Narrative, Scenario, MEL/MIL, Master Event Synchronisation List) - Technical requirements (ICT, Legal) - Public Information/Media and Visits - Real-Life Support - Evaluation and Assessment Plan

Deliverables: - Confirmation of Exercise Plan layout and content - Exercise Order/Directive - Draft exercise plan - OPFOR requirements defined - EXCON Appointments

docs.title: Main Planning Conference (MPC)
docs.text:
The main planning event for the exercise. Plans drafted independently by the work groups are reviewed and integrated into the Exercise Plan.

Objectives: - Finalise and issue the Exercise Order/Instruction - Finalise the EXCON structure - Finalise the Exercise Plan - Confirm objectives - Confirm international PTA/STA participants - Finalise Real-Life Support requirements - Confirm Security plan - Finalise the Evaluation Plan - Hand over the Military Problem to the Force Commander

docs.title: Final Planning Conference (FPC)
docs.text:
Convened to confirm that all planning goals have been achieved and to review and update the exercise plan should there have been any unforeseen incidents or changes.

Deliverables: - Signed Exercise Plan (EXPLAN) - Final objectives list - Exercise Narrative/Scenario - MEL-MIL (key events) - Exercise manning document (EXCON Structure with appointments) - Evaluation and Assessment plan - Training and Mentor plan - Real-Life Support plan - Transportation plan, Medical plan, Communications plan - Opening and closing ceremony, DV Day programme

docs.title: Work Groups
docs.text:
The task of detailed planning is delegated to specialised work groups. The exercise director appoints a work group leader for each group:

Work Group Responsibility Exercise Control Control structures, procedures, and management Scenario Narrative, scenario, MEL/MIL development MEL/MIL Main Events List and Master Incident List construction Training, Evaluation and Assessment Training plan and evaluation/assessment plan Technical Support IT, communications, simulation systems Public Information/Media and Visits Media simulation, DV day, public affairs Real-Life Support Logistics, personnel, facilities, administration

Work groups may be further divided into smaller sub-groups focusing on specific aspects or disciplines.

docs.title: Back Briefs
docs.text:
To guide and coordinate the planning process, the IPC includes daily and end-of-conference back briefs from the various work groups:

Meeting Purpose Morning Coordination Meeting Confirm activities and outputs required for the day; confirm corrections from previous day End of Day Back Brief Present completed products; update status on outstanding tasks Focused Feedback Exercise director requires focused feedback on key aspects with specific work groups

docs.title: Exercise Control Matrix — ECM
docs.text: "The ECM is the real-time management tool for exercise execution. It links every inject to a specific date, time, location, PTA element, and OPFOR element." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 7

docs.title: What Is the ECM?
docs.text:
The Exercise Control Matrix (ECM) is the primary document used by Exercise Control (EXCON) to direct, coordinate, and monitor exercise execution. It is the real-time management tool that links every inject to a specific date, time, location, PTA element, and OPFOR element.

The ECM is derived from the Activity List but is not the same document. The Activity List is a design product showing intended flow. The ECM is an execution product showing actual or planned control actions.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
The ECM serves several critical functions:

  • Lists injects, incidents, and events chronologically on a timeline
  • Indicates which PTA and OPFOR elements are involved in each incident
  • Monitors and measures progress during execution
  • Identifies overlapping or clashing incidents
  • Supports contingency planning

docs.title: ECM Format
docs.text:
Inject No. Event Incident Date Time Location PTA Element OPFOR Element Controller Status 1.1.1-I1 1.1 1.1.1 D+1 0600 Grid ABC123 Recce Pl Insurgent Pl Alpha Cell Planned 1.1.2-I1 1.1 1.1.2 D+1 0800 Route BLUE Recce Pl N/A Bravo Cell Planned 1.2.1-I1 1.2 1.2.1 D+1 0900 Grid DEF456 Intel Cell N/A Charlie Cell Planned

Status codes:

Code Meaning Planned Scheduled but not yet executed In Progress Currently executing Complete Executed and assessed Cancelled Intentionally not executed Modified Executed with changes from plan

docs.title: Relationship to Other Documents
docs.text:
Activity List (Design) → ECM (Execution) → ICS (Per-Inject Detail)

The ECM is derived from the Activity List but contains control detail — controller assignments, OPFOR elements, status tracking — that the Activity List does not require.

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text:
• Exercise Concept Development — How the ECM fits into the three-phase design process
  • Inject Design and Construction — How injects are managed in the ECM
