docs.title: Exercise Control Structures — EXCON
docs.text: "EXCON serves as the implementation structure through which the Exercise Director will plan, control, and execute the exercise." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 4

docs.title: What Is EXCON?
docs.text:
Exercise Control (EXCON) is the organisational structure responsible for planning, controlling, directing, and monitoring an exercise. It is the mechanism through which the Exercise Director (EXDIR) ensures the exercise achieves its objectives in a safe, realistic, and environmentally responsible manner.

EXCON is sometimes referred to as the "White Cell" or "Control Group" — the body that remains outside the player bubble and governs the exercise environment.

docs.title: The Command Group
docs.text:
The Command Group is the senior leadership of EXCON, responsible for overall direction and decision-making:

Appointment Responsibility Exercise Director (EXDIR) Overall command of the exercise; responsible for achieving objectives within budget Deputy Exercise Director Assists EXDIR; represents EXDIR in their absence Exercise Chief of Staff (COS) Coordinates and aligns all EXCON cell activities; manages administration Budget Manager Financial advice and support to EXDIR from day one Personal Staff Officer (PSO) Assists EXDIR Exercise Warrant Officer Discipline, welfare, and regimental aspects for EXCON staff

docs.title: Exercise Control Centre (ECC)
docs.text:
The Exercise Control Centre (ECC) is the physical and operational nodal point from which the EXDIR commands and controls all aspects of the exercise. It must be:

  • Established before the arrival of participants
  • Operational 24/7 for the duration of the exercise
  • Restricted — out of bounds to all training audience members
  • The last structure to demobilise after the exercise

ECC responsibilities: - 24/7 oversight of the exercise - Real-world incident response and consequence management - Movement control (MOVECON) for forces to and from the exercise - Message management (logging and dissemination) - Location tracking and display of all participating units - Daily SITREPs and update briefs to EXDIR - Coordination with the Safety Cell

docs.title: EXCON Cells
docs.text: EXCON is organised into functional cells, each responsible for a specific aspect of exercise control:

docs.title: Exercise Control Cell
docs.text:
Under the command of the Chief Exercise Control (Chief EXCON) or Senior Controller, this cell manages the flow of events and incidents:

Appointment Responsibility Chief Exercise Control Senior controller; third most senior post in EXCON after EXDIR and COS Event Managers Coordinate EXCON structures for specific events; appointed for larger exercises Controllers Introduce PTA to events and incidents; observe and report on performance Higher Control (HICON) Next higher HQ for the PTA; issues orders and directives Lower Control (LOCON) Virtual units under command of the FC; provides realistic feedback Flank Control (FLANKCON) Simulates flanking units and coalition forces Adjudicators Determine outcomes of battle engagements in two-sided exercises

docs.title: Scenario Development Cell
docs.text:
Under the command of Chief Scenario, this cell develops and manages all narrative and scenario products:

  • Narrative (General Idea)
  • Road to War / Crisis
  • Military Problem / Mission
  • Scenario (Special Idea and initial situation)
  • Vignettes / Situation Sketches
  • Main Events List (MEL)
  • Main Incident List (MIL)
  • Control Matrix / Master Events Synchronisation List (MESL)
  • Inject Control Sheets and Injects
  • INTREPs, INTSUMs, and supplements
  • Simulated media
  • Rules of Engagement / Rules of Contact
  • UN / AU Resolutions, MOUs, SOFAs
  • Country profiles and character profiles

docs.title: Training and Evaluation Cell
docs.text:
Responsible for two distinct functions:

  1. Training: Deliberate training plan to address identified gaps before the PTA is assessed
  2. Evaluation: Assessment and evaluation plan to measure PTA performance against objectives

Critical rule: These are two separate plans and must not be combined.

docs.title: Response Cell
docs.text:
The Response Cell provides real-time opposing forces and external role players. It is colour-coded by actor type:

Colour Actor Type White AU, UN, international agencies Grey NGOs, local government, police Blue Own forces Red Enemy / OPFOR Green Alliance partners / host country Brown Local population Black / Purple Criminal groups Orange Armed groups (no clear alliance) Yellow Media (including social media)

Critical rule: The Response Cell must not act independently or "rogue." All actions must be planned, controlled, and based on approved scenarios.

docs.title: Role Players (Enactors)
docs.text: EXCON members appointed to enact specific characters or institutions: - Rebel leaders, mayors, political leaders, NGO representatives - Protesting communities, striking employees, roadblock operators - Hostage-takers, suicide bombers, important EPWs

docs.title: Battlefield Preparation Team
docs.text: Responsible for physical preparation of the battlefield: - Target preparation (mock targets) - Site preparation (trenches, command posts, bunkers, patrol lanes, crash sites)

docs.title: Battlefield Simulation Team (BatSim)
docs.text: Responsible for battle effects simulation: - Battle noise simulation - Pyrotechnical effects - Wound simulation (Moulage kits)

docs.title: Real-Life Support Cell
docs.text: Responsible for all logistical support to EXCON, the PTA, and supporting elements: - Accommodation and facilities - Transport and movement - Catering and sustenance - Medical support - Supply and replenishment

docs.title: Controllers
docs.text:
Controllers form the backbone of EXCON. They are responsible for:

  • Managing and controlling inject and incident input at the tactical level
  • Observing and reporting on PTA performance
  • Coordinating planned activities with the Response Cell
  • Ensuring safety regulations are adhered to
  • Providing inputs for the After Action Report (AAR)

Controller types:

Type Function Higher Control (HICON) Issues orders and directives; provides "enemy" and environmental inputs Lower Control (LOCON) Commands virtual units under FC; provides realistic feedback Flank Control (FLANKCON) Simulates flanking units and coalition forces Observer-Controllers (OBCON) Embedded with units; observe and report Observer-Controller Trainers (OCT) Embedded with units; observe, report, and train

Critical rule: Controllers must not form part of the immediate chain of command of the unit to which they are attached.

docs.title: EXCON Size and Structure
docs.text:
The size and structure of EXCON depends on:

  • Type of exercise (CPX requires fewer controllers than FTX)
  • Size of the PTA
  • Geographical spread of events
  • Complexity of the scenario
  • Level of realism required

Critical principle: A custom-built EXCON structure is required for each exercise. Generic structures or over-inflated control structures waste resources and create safety challenges.

docs.title: Identification
docs.text: All EXCON staff and vehicles must be clearly identified: - Distinct armbands, coloured jackets, or hats - Marked vehicles - Freedom of movement — no PTA, STA, or OPFOR may interfere with EXCON movement

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text:
• Exercise Commissioning — How EXCON is mandated and resourced
  • The Exercise Planning Process — How EXCON is planned and managed

docs.text: [^1]: NATO AJP-3, Allied Joint Doctrine for the Conduct of Operations, Annex C. [^2]: US FM 25-4, Training Units and Developing Leaders: Exercise Control. [^3]: EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 4: Exercise Control Structures.

docs.title: Exercise Delivery and Execution
docs.text: "Execution is Stage 4 of the Exercise Design process — the pinnacle of the exercise's design process and the 'long pole' in achieving the objectives." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 14

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Delivery (also called Execution) is Stage 4 of the Exercise Design process. At this point, all planning has been completed, the Exercise Order and Exercise Plan have been issued, and all elements are in the training area ready to start.

As with real-time operations, the start of an exercise is linked to a specific H-hour on a predetermined D-day.

docs.title: Key Documents
docs.text: Document Description Distribution Exercise Order Issued at the end of the Main Planning Conference. Includes all Support Plans. Instruction for elements identified to participate. All role players: participants, EXCON, supporting elements Exercise Plan Prepared by EXCON. Sets out the sequence of events according to the approved Exercise Time Line. Detailed activity list of all events. EXCON Eyes Only — never shared with the training audience Exercise Control Matrix Management tool used by EXCON to plan, monitor, and control delivery. Links activities to injects, locations, and date-time groups. EXCON Schedule of Events List of planned events and activities outside the player bubble (opening/closing ceremony, DV Day, etc.) All participants

docs.title: Phase 1: Off-Site Planning, Preparation, and Movement
docs.text:
Starts after the Final Planning Conference and Exercise Order distribution.

  • Off-site planning: Each unit conducts planning and preparation at home station
  • Preparation: Preparatory/refresher training, collecting equipment, preparing vehicles/ships/aircraft
  • Movement: All elements move to the exercise area according to the Movement Plan

MOVECON: EXCON establishes a movement control cell to coordinate all movement, handle incidents, coordinate military police escorts, and manage personnel/equipment at ports of entry.

docs.title: Phase 2: On-Site Preparation, Planning, Training, and Set-Up
docs.text:
Activities before the exercise starts:

  • Reception and Accreditation: Clearing in of members, accreditation, allocation of messing/workspace
  • EXCON Training: Specialised training and orientation for EXCON staff
  • Refresher Training (PTA): Specific drills and actions for participants
  • Response Cell Training: OPFOR and role players train and rehearse
  • Battlefield Preparation: Creating enemy positions, setting up targets, preparing simulated scenes
  • All Participants Brief: Chief EXCON briefs all commanders on aim, objectives, concept, timeline, ROE, safety
  • Set-up of HQs: Establishing headquarters and command posts
  • Opening Ceremony: Official opening of the exercise
  • Final Rehearsal: COMEX (communications test) and MEDEX (medical exercise)

docs.title: Phase 3: Execution (STARTEX to ENDEX/FINEX)
docs.text: The exercise is initiated with the code word "STARTEX" on all command channels, followed by the first inject.

docs.title: Starting the Exercise
docs.text:
Method Description Cold Start / Slow Start PTA gradually introduced to the situation. Opening Scenario, Warning Order, INTSUMs, INREPs, Operational Directive. Hot Start PTA immediately exposed to a crisis requiring urgent action. No lead-up or unfolding of events.

Lessons learned from past exercises show that the best approach is often a combination of both methods.

docs.title: The Player Bubble
docs.text:
The execution of the exercise takes place in the "Player Bubble" — the world described in the Narrative and Scenario.

  • EXCON is responsible for activating incidents within the player bubble using injects
  • The A&E cell observes and measures the PTA response
  • EXCON isolates the PTA from real-world and external influences to allow focus on scheduled events

docs.title: The Role of EXCON During Execution
Coordination
docs.text:
The Chief of Staff drafts a Meeting and Staff Liaison Plan at the end of the MPC. Key meetings include:

Meeting Purpose EXCON Planning Meeting Chaired by EXDIR. Plans and coordinates activities for the next 48 hours. Attended by all EXCON cell chiefs. EXCON End of Day Meeting Feedback from cell chiefs on PTA performance and exercise progress. Identifies adjustments needed.

docs.title: Control
docs.text:
Control requires a hands-on approach. Chief Exercise Control and control staff carry out:

  • Managing the Exercise Order/Exercise Plan
  • Overseeing MEL-MIL (MESL)
  • Maintaining the Schedule of Events
  • Managing the Exercise Control Matrix and Exercise Time Line

docs.title: Exercise Control Centre (ECC)
docs.text:
The ECC functions as the hub from where all activities are controlled and managed:

  • Managing and reporting all real-time incidents
  • Coordinating all safety issues
  • Maintaining the war diary
  • Tracking completion of events and receipt of reports
  • Pausing, stopping, and restarting the exercise as instructed
  • Coordinating day-to-day administration

docs.title: Incident Development
docs.text: It is not always possible to develop all incidents and injects required during the exercise in advance. Exercise conditions may change, or the flow may be adapted. The Scenario Cell must be prepared to add additional incidents and supporting injects on an ad hoc basis.

docs.title: Ending the Exercise
docs.text: The code word "ENDEX" (End of Exercise) or "FINEX" is transmitted over all active radio frequencies, signalling the end of the exercise. All exercise/training activities must be brought to an end.

docs.text:
• Detailed Planning Conferences — Stage 3: what the delivery phase executes
  • Exercise Control Structures — EXCON — EXCON during execution
  • Exercise Control Matrix — ECM — The management tool used during delivery
  • Post-Exercise Activities — Stage 5: what follows delivery

docs.title: Inject Control Sheets — ICS
docs.text: "The ICS is the detailed planning document for each individual inject. It provides the controller with all information required to execute the inject correctly." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 7

docs.title: What Is the ICS?
docs.text:
The Inject Control Sheet (ICS) is the detailed planning document for each individual inject. It provides the controller with all information required to execute the inject correctly: timing, delivery method, PTA element, expected response, assessment criteria, safety considerations, and contingency options.

Critical rule: The ICS is an EXCON document. It is never shared with the PTA.

docs.title: ICS Format
docs.text: Field Content Inject Number e.g., 1.1.1-I1 Event / Incident Reference to MEL and MIL entries Date / Time Scheduled date and time Location Grid reference or named location Delivery Method Written, verbal, system input, AV, live PTA Element Specific PTA unit or headquarters receiving inject OPFOR Element OPFOR unit involved (if applicable) Controller Named controller responsible for delivery Inject Text Full text of the inject Expected Response What the PTA should do Assessment Criteria How the response will be evaluated Safety Considerations Safety risks and control measures Contingency What to do if PTA does not respond as expected Status Planned / In Progress / Complete / Cancelled / Modified

docs.title: Quality Criteria
docs.text:
A well-constructed ICS:

  • ✅ Contains all fields in the format above
  • ✅ Has inject text that is clear, concise, and sufficient
  • ✅ Has assessment criteria linked to specific FIOL objectives
  • ✅ Has safety considerations that address real risks
  • ✅ Has contingency options for common PTA failure modes

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text:

  • Inject Design and Construction — How injects are designed
  • Exercise Control Matrix — How the ICS relates to the ECM
  • Exercise Design Templates and Checklists — ICS template

docs.title: Inject Design and Construction
docs.text: "An inject is a pre-determined and pre-planned input directed at a specific element of the PTA, designed to act as a trigger to initiate a specific incident." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 7

docs.title: What Is an Inject?
docs.text:
An inject is the fundamental unit of exercise execution. It is a pre-determined and pre-planned input directed at a specific element of the Primary Training Audience (PTA), designed to act as a trigger to initiate a specific incident. It introduces or confronts the training audience with a situation that requires a response or reaction. The response is measured against a predetermined competency standard.

Key characteristics: - Pre-determined: Injects are planned in advance, not improvised during execution - Pre-planned: Injects are aligned with the MIL and Exercise Concept - Directed: Each inject targets a specific PTA element - Triggering: Each inject initiates or sustains an incident - Measurable: The PTA response is assessed against a standard

docs.title: Inject Entry Points
docs.text:
Injects enter the exercise through different channels depending on the desired effect:

Entry Point Description Ground Level (Bottom-Up) Inject enters at the tactical level, initiated by lower-echelon controllers or simulation systems HQ Level (Top-Down) Inject enters at headquarters level, initiated by higher-echelon controllers Direct / Focused Insertion Inject is delivered directly to a specific PTA element by the controller, bypassing normal command channels

docs.title: Inject Formats
docs.text:
Injects can be delivered in multiple formats, depending on the exercise type and the incident being triggered:

Format Description Example Written Written orders, messages, or intelligence reports delivered to PTA OPORD fragment, INTSUM, situation report System Input Inject delivered through simulation systems (C4I, VBS, JCATS) Digital message in C4I system Verbal Input Verbal message delivered by controller or role-player Radio transmission, face-to-face briefing Audio-Visual Video or audio recording presented to PTA News broadcast, surveillance footage Live Simulation (Enactment) Physical enactment by role-players or OPFOR Civilian protest, ambush, IED discovery

docs.title: Sufficiency
docs.text:
An inject must contain enough information for the PTA to understand the situation and respond meaningfully. Every inject must answer:

  • When is it happening?
  • Where is it happening?
  • What is happening / what will happen / what happened?
  • Who is involved (own forces and OPFOR)?
  • Tasking — what is required, by whom, and by when?

Example inject:

"At 02:35 on 23 February 2022, eight nautical miles east of Richards Bay, the Maltese-registered merchant vessel Pisces Dawn was attacked by three motorboats carrying armed men. The men seized control of the vessel, robbed the crew of personal items, and are holding the captain and crew at ransom. A joint task group consisting of 4 Special Forces Regiment, the Maritime Reaction Squadron, a SA Navy Inshore Patrol Vessel, and two Oryx helicopters has been assembled. C SANDF has tasked the grouping to plan and present a detailed plan for the release of hostages by 250900B Feb 22, addressing both opposed and unopposed boarding options."

docs.title: Escalation
docs.text:
Some incidents require multiple injects to develop fully. The principle of escalation applies when follow-up injects introduce additional detail, changing conditions, or complications that sustain and deepen the incident.

Example escalation:

Inject Content PTA Response 1 IED reported on Route BLUE PTA conducts route clearance 2 Second IED discovered 500m further along route PTA adjusts movement plan 3 Civilian casualty from second IED PTA coordinates CASEVAC and media management

Each inject in the sequence escalates the incident, maintaining cognitive load and testing additional competencies.

docs.title: Inject Numbering
docs.text:
Injects are numbered to maintain traceability to their parent event and incident:

Inject No. Event Incident 1.1.1-I1 1.1 1.1.1 1.1.2-I1 1.1 1.1.2 1.2.1-I1 1.2 1.2.1

This numbering system becomes the reference framework for the Exercise Control Matrix and Inject Control Sheets.

docs.title: Quality Criteria
docs.text:
A well-constructed inject:

  • ✅ Is clear, concise, and sufficient
  • ✅ Contains all required information (when, where, what, who, tasking)
  • ✅ Is linked to a specific incident in the MIL
  • ✅ Is linked to a specific objective in the FIOL
  • ✅ Has assessment criteria linked to specific FIOL objectives
  • ✅ Has safety considerations that address real risks
  • ✅ Has contingency options for common PTA failure modes

docs.text:

  • The Master Incident List — How incidents are defined and numbered
  • Exercise Control Matrix — How injects are managed during execution
  • Inject Control Sheets — How individual injects are planned in detail

docs.title: The Main Events List — MEL
docs.text: "The MEL is the structural skeleton of the exercise. It translates the FIOL's thematic groupings into a sequence of operational events that collectively address every objective." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 7

docs.title: What Is the MEL?
docs.text:
The Main Events List (MEL) is the primary structural document in exercise design. It translates the Final Integrated Objective List (FIOL) into a sequence of operational events that collectively provide the Primary Training Audience (PTA) with opportunities to demonstrate the required competencies.

The MEL is the bridge between objectives and execution — it ensures every objective is addressed by at least one event, and every event traces back to a specific objective.

docs.title: Construction Method
docs.text: The MEL is constructed in four sequential steps:

docs.title: Step 1: Identify Themes
docs.text:
Review the FIOL and identify common operational themes. A theme is a central idea or functional area that groups related objectives.

Standard themes (adapt to your operational context):

Theme Example Objectives Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) Conduct tactical questioning; produce intelligence estimate Operational Planning Produce operations order; conduct staff estimate Conduct of Operations / Decision Making Execute tactical manoeuvre; adjust plan during execution Support and Sustainment Resupply under fire; coordinate casualty evacuation Medical Support Establish Role 1 medical facility; conduct CASEVAC Force Protection Detect and counter IED; implement base defence plan Air Support / Operations Coordinate close air support; conduct aerial resupply Maritime Support / Operations Conduct coastal patrol; board suspicious vessel Civil-Military Cooperation (CIMIC) Coordinate with local authorities; conduct hearts-and-minds operation Logistics Establish distribution system; recover damaged vehicles

Critical rule: Your themes must derive from your FIOL, not from a template. The themes above are illustrative only.

docs.title: Step 2: Sequence Themes
docs.text:
Order themes in the sequence in which they would occur during a realistic operation. This creates a logical operational flow and serves as the backbone of the exercise timeline.

Exception: At the tactical decision-making level (e.g., Staff Exercises, Tactical Training Exercises), theme sequencing may not reflect operational sequence. In such cases, sequence by decision-making priority or functional dependency.

docs.title: Step 3: Decompose Themes into Events
docs.text:
For each theme, identify the specific events that will exercise the associated objectives.

Event definition: A planned activity that consists of one or more incidents and will normally be of a tactical nature. Events are the main building blocks of an exercise and are used during the construction of the exercise concept. (Adapted from NATO AJP-3, Annex C)

docs.title: Step 4: Link Events to Objectives
docs.text: For each event, specify which FIOL objective(s) it addresses. This ensures traceability and prevents design drift.

docs.title: MEL Format
docs.text:
Theme Event Objective(s) / Comments 1. ISR 1.1 Route reconnaissance Obj 2: Conduct tactical reconnaissance 1. ISR 1.2 Intelligence preparation Obj 3: Produce IPB 2. Planning 2.1 Staff estimate Obj 4: Conduct operational estimate 2. Planning 2.2 OPORD production Obj 5: Produce operations order 3. Conduct 3.1 Execute ambush Obj 6: Execute tactical manoeuvre 3. Conduct 3.2 Adjust plan during execution Obj 7: Adapt plan under pressure

Formatting rules: - Themes are numbered sequentially (1, 2, 3...) - Events are numbered within themes (1.1, 1.2, 2.1, 2.2...) - Events are stated crisply: one to five words - Multiple objectives may be linked to a single event

docs.title: Quality Criteria
docs.text:
A well-constructed MEL:

  • ✅ Addresses every objective in the FIOL at least once
  • ✅ Contains no events that cannot be traced to an objective
  • ✅ Is sequenced in a logically coherent operational flow
  • ✅ Is realistic given the available time, space, and forces

Quality check: If you cannot trace every element of your exercise design back to a specific objective in the FIOL, your design is unfocused.

docs.title: Common Pitfalls
docs.text: Pitfall Consequence Solution Events not linked to objectives Design drift; unfocused exercise Every event must reference at least one FIOL objective Too many events Exercise becomes rushed or superficial Prioritise; limit events to what can realistically be executed Themes not derived from FIOL Misalignment with training objectives Always start with the FIOL, not a template Unrealistic sequencing Loss of credibility; poor training value Validate sequence against operational logic

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text:
• Exercise Concept Development — How the MEL fits into the three-phase design process
  • The Master Incident List — How events are decomposed into incidents
  • Exercise Design Templates and Checklists — MEL template and quality checklist

docs.title: Sources
docs.text: [^1]: NATO AJP-3, Allied Joint Doctrine for the Conduct of Operations, Annex C. [^2]: US TC 7-101, Exercise Design, Headquarters, Department of the Army. [^3]: EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 7: Exercise Design and Concept Development.

docs.title: The Master Incident List — MIL
docs.text: "The MIL deconstructs each MEL event into the specific tactical incidents that will require a response from the PTA. If the MEL is the skeleton, the MIL is the nervous system." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 7

docs.title: What Is the MIL?
docs.text:
The Master Incident List (MIL) is the detailed decomposition of the MEL. It takes each MEL event and breaks it down into the specific tactical incidents that will challenge the PTA and force them to demonstrate the required competencies.

The MIL is the link between the structural skeleton (MEL) and the executable products (injects, ECM, ICS). Every inject, every control action, and every assessment traces back to an incident in the MIL.

docs.title: Construction Method
docs.text: The MIL is constructed in three sequential steps:

docs.title: Step 1: Deconstruct Each Event
docs.text:
For each event in the MEL, ask: "What specific occurrences will challenge the PTA and force them to demonstrate the required competency?"

This is a creative, analytical process. The designer must think from the perspective of the PTA and identify the specific moments that will test their ability to achieve the objective.

docs.title: Step 2: Define Each Incident
docs.text:
An incident must contain two elements:

  1. Occurrence: What is happening, has happened, or will happen. This creates the initiating point for PTA action.
  2. Response: The required PTA action to address, solve, prevent, or mitigate the occurrence.

Incident definition: A specific, single-topic occurrence that is pre-determined and pre-planned. It is defined in terms of time and location and directed at a specified training audience. The aim of an incident is to provoke a response from the training audience, this response will then be measured against a pre-determined minimum performance standard to determine whether the objective has been met. (Adapted from NATO AJP-3, Annex C)

docs.title: Step 3: Number Incidents
docs.text: Number incidents to correspond with their parent event (1.1.1, 1.1.2, 1.2.1...). This numbering system becomes the reference framework for injects, the Exercise Control Matrix, and assessment sheets.

docs.title: MIL Format
docs.text:
Event Incident Occurrence Response 1.1 Route reconnaissance 1.1.1 Locals report insurgent infiltration route at Grid ABC123 PTA conducts ambush to neutralise insurgents 1.1 Route reconnaissance 1.1.2 IED discovered on primary route at 0800B PTA conducts route clearance and adjusts movement plan 1.2 Intelligence preparation 1.2.1 UAV imagery shows enemy positions at Grid DEF456 PTA produces updated IPB 2.1 Staff estimate 2.1.1 Higher HQ issues warning order for offensive operation PTA conducts operational estimate

Formatting rules: - Incident descriptions at this stage are broad. Detailed formulation occurs during Exercise Construction (Phase 3). - Each incident must have both occurrence and response. - Incidents are numbered to maintain traceability to MEL events and FIOL objectives.

docs.title: Quality Criteria
docs.text:
A well-constructed MIL:

  • ✅ Deconstructs every MEL event into at least one incident
  • ✅ Contains no incidents that cannot be traced to an event and objective
  • ✅ Provides incidents that collectively stress every objective in the FIOL
  • ✅ Is realistic given the operational context and PTA capabilities

docs.title: Relationship to Other Documents
docs.text:
FIOL → MEL → MIL → Injects → ECM → ICS

The MIL is the critical link in this chain. It translates structural events into actionable incidents that can be executed, controlled, and assessed.

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text:
• Exercise Concept Development — How the MIL fits into the three-phase design process
  • The Main Events List — How events are identified and sequenced
  • Inject Design and Construction — How incidents become injects
  • Exercise Design Templates and Checklists — MIL template and quality checklist

docs.title: Narrative Composition
docs.text: "Drafting the 'Narrative' for a military training exercise — often mistakenly called the 'Scenario' — is as much a science as it is an art." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 5/6

docs.title: What Is the Narrative?
docs.text:
The Narrative (also called the General Idea) describes the geopolitical and socio-economic backdrop of an exercise. It serves as the higher-order framework within which the exercise takes place, describing the strategic and operational-level background and telling the story up to the point where military action is required.

Key distinction: The Narrative sets the stage. The Scenario (Special Idea) puts the Primary Training Audience (PTA) into the tactical situation.

docs.title: The Seven-Part Structure
docs.text:
The Narrative consists of seven interconnected parts, built sequentially from foundational context to tactical mission:

INTRODUCTION → ORIENTATION → HISTORICAL BACKGROUND → ROAD TO WAR/CRISIS → MILITARY PROBLEM

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
The Introduction should be kept short. It introduces the PTA to the narrative and touches on key aspects discussed in detail in the Historical Background and Road to War/Crisis sections.

Best practice: Write the Introduction only after the entire Narrative has been completed. This ensures it accurately reflects the content that follows.

docs.title: 2. Orientation
docs.text: The PTA is introduced to the operational environment. This part is subdivided into:

docs.title: Geographical Orientation
docs.text:
Describes the physical environment — natural features and man-made infrastructure:

Level Description Map Scale Global Position of the country on the world stage 1:100,000,000 Regional Continental position, neighbours, oceans, mountain ranges 1:500,000 Area of Interest Relevant to own force commander; outside direct influence — Area of Influence Direct impact on own force operations — Area of Operations Where physical operations will be executed 1:100,000 / 1:50,000

docs.title: General Orientation
docs.text:
Describes the human environment — structures and government: - Population (size, density, distribution) - Ethnic composition and distribution - Religion - Political system - Military and security forces - Telecommunications and media - Economy and health infrastructure - Geo-political relations - Infrastructure (cities, roads, rail, airports, harbours, electricity, water, sanitation) - Internally displaced persons (IDP) camps where applicable

Tip: Use maps, charts, satellite photos, and other visual aids wherever possible.

docs.title: 3. Historical Background
docs.text:
The Historical Background is the cornerstone of the Narrative. It sets the scene for everything that follows.

Primary aim: Introduce the reader to human dynamics — main role players and underlying conflict triggers.

docs.title: Main Role Players
docs.text: Type Description Protagonists The "good guys" — but avoid creating an innocent party. Add negative characteristics to create moral complexity. Antagonists The "bad guys" or aggressors. Avoid limiting to one entity, but guard against too many parties causing confusion. Sympathisers Supporters of either side. Sub-divide into active supporters and moral supporters. Can include states, NGOs, political parties, ethnic groups, religious factions. Neutrals Parties supporting neither side. Include states, UN, Red Cross, religious groups. Useful for imposing movement restrictions.

docs.title: Conflict Triggers
docs.text:
It is best to use a combination of triggers rather than relying on a single cause:

Category Examples Historical Wars lost, oppression, genocide, tribal feuds Ethnic/Religious Race/ethnic differences, religious friction, xenophobia Geo-Political Border disputes, resource competition, political rivalry, election fraud, constitutional changes, ideology clashes, coup d'état Socio-Economic Urbanisation, overcrowding, unemployment, poverty, income inequality

docs.title: 4. Road to War/Crisis (RTW/C)
docs.text:
The RTW/C is the second major component of the narrative. It sets the scene on the strategic/operational level by chronologically unpacking events that led to the crisis.

Main functions: - Serves as an expansion of the Historical Background - Creates context for the PTA to understand the military problem - Acts as a bridge between Historical Background and Scenario

docs.title: Road to War vs. Road to Crisis
docs.text: Type When to Use Road to War (RTW) Conflict has erupted or has potential to escalate into military conflict. Describes lead-up to war, initial skirmishes, engagements, battles. Road to Crisis (RTC) Military conflict is not central. Used for MOOTWA, conflict resolution, electoral support, law enforcement assistance, or political crisis preceding war. Also covers natural/man-made disasters.

docs.title: The Escalation Curve
docs.text:
The RTW/C maps the escalation of the crisis by listing major events in chronological order that contributed to instability. Selected incidents serve as anchor points for the escalation curve.

Strategic and Operational Escalation indicators: - Countries and organisations affected or involved - Peace initiatives (national, regional, international) - AU and UN efforts - Declarations by regional/international bodies (UN Security Council Resolutions, embargoes, sanctions, punitive actions, travel bans, naval and air blockades, seizure of assets)

Grassroots disruptive actions: - Protests, riots, public unrest - Attacks on government infrastructure and security installations - Rise in criminality and civil disobedience - Declaration of martial law / curfews - Military force concentrations, logistical stockpiling, large exercises

docs.title: 5. Military Problem
docs.text: This is the last component of the narrative — the final step down from strategic/operational to tactical level.

docs.title: Military Problem vs. Mission
docs.text: Term Definition Military Problem A broad, generalised statement indicating that military action or intervention is required to solve a defined situation. Mission A narrowly defined instruction or tasking to be executed within defined parameters (time and space) to achieve a specified end state.

docs.title: Mission Statement Structure
docs.text:
The Military Problem consists of three parts:

Part Description Situation Short, concise summary of the situation Decision The decision that was taken Tasking What must be done; can be stated as a qualified end state

docs.title: Structured vs. Unstructured
docs.text: Type Description Structured Pre-determined mission with detailed end state given by higher HQ Unstructured Commander and staff must analyse the situation and formulate the mission statement

docs.title: Objective-Driven Narrative
docs.text:
The narrative is developed from the stated exercise objectives. The scope, content, and focus are determined by what the exercise must achieve.

Best for: Training-focused exercises with clear, predefined learning outcomes.

docs.title: Situation-Driven Narrative
docs.text:
A fictitious, reality-based, or real-time situation is used without being guided by exercise objectives. The situation drives the narrative.

Best for: Contingency planning and operational rehearsal exercises.

Important: Regardless of approach, success depends on the skill and effort of the narrative writer.

docs.title: When Is the Narrative Written?
docs.text: The type, scope, objectives, available time, and development approach determine when the narrative is drafted. Four options exist:

docs.title: Option 1: Pre-EXSPEC
docs.text:
Narrative is drafted prior to the Exercise Specification Meeting.

When to use: Real-time situations or reality-based narratives for contingency planning.

docs.title: Option 2: Post-EXSPEC, Pre-CDC
docs.text:
Narrative is written immediately after the Exercise Specification Meeting but before the Concept Development Conference.

Advantage: The Narrative and Scenario are available to guide exercise concept development.

docs.title: Option 3: During CDC
docs.text:
Narrative is written during the Concept Development Conference to support the exercise concept.

Challenge: Time is limited; requires extensive consultation and liaison.

Benefit: Ensures the narrative aligns with the exercise concept being developed.

docs.title: Option 4: During Stage 3 (Planning)
docs.text:
Narrative is written during the detailed planning phase.

Advantage: Concept development is complete; MEL/MIL is fixed. The narrative is guaranteed to align with the exercise concept and cover all objectives.

Pressure point: The narrative writer must deliver a complete Narrative by the end of the Final Planning Conference.

Tip: Option 4 is the most common approach, as it ensures alignment with a fixed MEL/MIL framework.

docs.title: The Storyboard: Planning Before Writing
docs.text:
Before the Narrative can be written, the layout and content of the different parts must first be planned using a storyboard — an adapted visual planning tool that allows creative writers to plan and structure a narrative before actually starting to write.

A storyboard ensures: - The narrative is logically structured with events and incidents unpacked in linear, chronological order - The writer can divide the main parts of the narrative into bite-size sections - All required information is contained within the narrative, avoiding unnecessary repetition - Gaps or possible omissions are identified early - Relevant storylines requiring further development are identified early - The step-down from strategic/operational level to tactical level is planned

There is no prescribed format for a storyboard. Some writers prefer graphic displays, while others prefer maps and overlays, mind maps, sketches, or written notes.

docs.title: The Seven-Step Construction Process
docs.text:
To simplify and standardise the process of constructing the Narrative, the following creative process has been developed:

Step Activity Step 1 Geographical placement — Identify the region/country/locality where the conflict or crisis will take place Step 2 Identification and selection of conflict triggers — Create a starting point for the narrative Step 3 Identification and development of the main role players — Define actors, their aims, capabilities, and power bases Step 4 Conflict mapping — Identify and order incidents using timelines, mind maps, or map plotting Step 5 Military mission — Step down from strategic/operational to tactical level Step 6 Identify and draft support documents — UN/AU resolutions, MOUs, SOFAs, country profiles Step 7 Draft the Narrative — Write the full narrative, keeping it concise, accurate, and clear

docs.title: Supporting Documents
docs.text: Supporting documents to the Narrative are divided into two tiers:

docs.title: Higher-Order Documents (Narrative)
docs.text:
• United Nations / African Union Resolutions
  • Memorandum of Understanding (MOU)
  • Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA)
  • Campaign Directive
  • Country Profiles

docs.title: Lower-Order Documents (Scenario)
docs.text:
• Tactical Area Studies
  • Threat Assessments
  • Rules of Engagement and Contact
  • INTREPs and SITREPs
  • Character Profiles

Critical rule: No documents should be included that do not add direct value to the exercise. The temptation to include a host of strategic and operational-level supporting documents that do not directly contribute to the situational understanding of the PTA should be resisted.

docs.title: Opposing Force — OPFOR
docs.text: "The centre of gravity of the Scenario is the introduction and detailed unpacking of the Opposing Force (OPFOR)." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 11, Appendix A

docs.title: What Is OPFOR?
docs.text:
The Opposing Force (OPFOR) refers to all role players in the Narrative that are either actively opposing own forces from achieving their mission or contributing to the destabilisation of the current situation. OPFOR is not limited to conventional forces and may include:

  • Conventional armed forces
  • Non-conventional forces (insurgents, terrorists, organised crime syndicates)
  • Non-human threats (natural disasters, cyber threats, chemical/biological threats)

Note: The term "enemy" becomes ambiguous during Peace Support Operations. Terms such as "belligerents," "spoilers," "undocumented armed groups," or "rebels" may be more appropriate. For training purposes, the term OPFOR is generally preferred.

docs.title: Colour Coding of OPFOR
docs.text:
To assist the scenario writer in developing opposing forces and managing individual story lines, the OPFOR can be colour-coded:

Colour Description Examples Red Formally declared enemy. Actively and aggressively opposes own forces. Conventional armed forces of countries, recognised armed groups declared hostile Orange Does not actively oppose own forces but has a negative influence on stability and security. "Belligerents" or "spoilers" Black/Purple Criminal groups. Organised crime syndicates, smuggling rings (weapons, drugs, humans), street gangs Yellow Forces or role players that have not yet been classified. Identity, aim, intention, and alliances still unknown. Unidentified armed groups

docs.title: Constructing a Conventional Opposing Force
docs.text: The following key aspects should be considered when designing a conventional opposing force:

docs.title: Posture
docs.text: A clear distinction must be made whether the OPFOR is in a defensive or offensive posture, as this impacts all subsequent development.

docs.title: Specification of Size
docs.text:
The size of the opposing force in direct contact or opposition to the PTA must be specified:

Category Examples Single entity Sniper, vessel, aircraft Defined Military Grouping Section, platoon, company, battalion, regiment, brigade, task force

docs.title: Identification
docs.text: OPFOR elements may be identified by unit name and designation, or this detail may be omitted to create a training opportunity (provided later via inject or INTREP).

docs.title: Level of Command
docs.text:
Three levels of command can be identified:

Level Description On the Front Force in direct contact with own forces. Most detail required. One Level Up Next higher level of command. Less technical detail; higher tactical context. Two Levels Up Operational or military strategic level.

docs.title: Aim and Intention
docs.text:
• Aim: What objective is to be achieved (the "What")
  • Intention: The method or approach used to achieve the aim (the "How")

There must be synergy between levels — subordinate commander's aim and intention must fit in with and support the next higher commander's.

docs.title: Composition
docs.text: Composition refers to the make-up of the force in terms of capabilities (e.g., "a brigade-size force consisting of infantry, artillery, armoured cars, anti-tank, reconnaissance, air defence, and engineer capabilities").

docs.title: Force Structure
docs.text: Force structure refers to the broad grouping and organisation of capabilities into units. A bottom-up approach is recommended — begin with the force on the front and work up to the next level(s).

docs.title: Weapons and Equipment List
docs.text:
A list of all major weapons systems, vehicles, aircraft, vessels, and support equipment must be linked to the units depicted on the OPFOR force structure. This information is captured in the OPFOR Weapon and Equipment Booklet (part of the Red Book).

Additional detail may include: - Serviceability levels — percentage serviceable and forecast of additional weapons becoming available - Procurement — certain weapon systems purchased on the international market and becoming operational within a specific period

docs.title: Order of Battle (ORBAT)
docs.text: The ORBAT refers to the manner in which the OPFOR units have been grouped to execute a specific task. Groupings must be both realistic (logic) and balanced.

docs.title: Deployment/Disposition
docs.text: Deployment refers to the tactical placement of the OPFOR in the area of operations. A detailed analysis of both macro and micro terrain must be conducted to ensure deployments are tactically sound.

docs.title: Doctrine and Tactics
docs.text:
• For real-world and reality-based scenarios: Research and obtain copies of real doctrine of the envisaged OPFOR. Refrain from generating fictitious doctrine.
  • For fictional scenarios: More leeway is available, but care must be taken to maintain realism.

Critical rule: The temptation to state that OPFOR will use own doctrine and tactics must be resisted at all costs. It is unrealistic and stifles creativity.

docs.title: Skill
docs.text:
Soldier skill levels can be classified into broad categories:

Category Description Conscript Little or no training; ignorant of basic military skills Trained Received military training but lack combat experience Veteran/Experienced Battle-hardened, well trained, steadfast under fire Fanatical Willing to fight to the last bullet

docs.title: Morale/Motivation
docs.text: Category Description Reluctant/Demotivated Lack motivation; likely to break under pressure Confident Confident in themselves, equipment, and leaders Highly Motivated (Fearless) Very high morale; will fight to the last man

docs.title: Constructing a Non-Conventional Opposing Force
docs.text:
Non-conventional forces or destabilisers are generally structured less rigidly than conventional forces. Key aspects include:

Aspect Description Name and Abbreviation Official name and abbreviation of the group Nickname Alternative name by which the group is known Recognition Markings Visual identifiers used by members Leader Name of primary leader or command structure Approximate Strength Estimated number of fighters/members Objectives Reason for existence; aligned with narrative and scenario Organisation Broad organisation or structure (loosely organised to well-disciplined decentralised cells) Area of Operations Specified area as indicated in the narrative/scenario Command Structure Centralised (single leader/council) or decentralised (small groups under local warlords) Weapons Range of weapons and ordnance at the group's disposal Modus Operandi Broad tactics and techniques used during past actions Support Popular support, regional/international support, financing, military equipment Affiliations/Associations/Alliances Groups sympathetic to the cause or with similar aims

docs.title: Non-State Armed Groups/Militia
docs.text:
Non-state armed groups are volunteer structures formed by local communities to ensure their safety against violent attacks. Members are civilian volunteers acting as self-protection units (SPU) or self-defence units (SDU).

These groups are common in regions where extremist groups are active. Examples include the "Mayi-Mayi" in the eastern DRC, the "Janjaweed" in Sudan, and the "Anti-Balaka" in the Central African Republic.

Typical activities include: - Acting as local neighbourhood watch or community guards - Patrolling and setting up roadblocks and checkpoints - Searching vehicles and people at town entrances - Providing escorts while community members collect wood or work in the fields - Acting as guides, interpreters, and informers to formal security structures

docs.title: Exercise Planning Timeline
docs.text: "The exercise planning process spans from –12 months to +2 months relative to Exercise E (execution month)." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Appendix A

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The exercise planning process spans from –12 months to +2 months relative to Exercise E (execution month). This timeline provides a structured framework for planning and executing a military exercise.

docs.title: Five Stages of Exercise Planning
docs.text: Stage Name Key Activities Milestone 1 Commissioning Identification of requirement, Commissioning Instruction issued –12 months 2 Design and Development Concept Development Conference (CDC) –10 months 3 Planning Initial Planning Conference (IPC), Main Planning Conference (MPC), Final Planning Conference (FPC) –8 to –4 months 4 Execution/Delivery Exercise execution –1 to E 5 Post-Exercise Activities After Action Review (AAR) process +1 to +2 months

docs.title: The Exercise Planning Process
docs.text: "Exercise planning is a continuous process that involves many complex activities that interact, often in indirect ways. The process consists of several integrated planning conferences or sessions, staff liaison, site visits, and back briefs." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 2

docs.title: The Five-Stage Lifecycle
docs.text:
The exercise planning process consists of five integrated stages. Each stage builds on the previous one, and the quality of each stage determines the quality of the exercise that follows.

STAGE 1: COMMISSIONING
    │
    ▼
STAGE 2: DESIGN AND DEVELOPMENT (Initial Planning)
    │
    ▼
STAGE 3: DETAILED PLANNING
    │
    ▼
STAGE 4: EXECUTION
    │
    ▼
STAGE 5: POST-EXERCISE ACTIVITIES

docs.title: Stage 1: Commissioning
docs.text: The exercise is authorised and resourced. The Officer Scheduling the Exercise (OSE) defines the broad requirements, objectives, participating forces, primary training audience, and budget. The Commissioning Instruction (or Exercise Directive for joint/multi-national exercises) is issued, appointing the Exercise Director (EXDIR) and providing the framework within which the exercise will be designed.

docs.title: Stage 2: Design and Development (Initial Planning)
docs.text: The creative and analytical heart of exercise planning. The design team translates objectives into an operational concept. This stage produces the Exercise Concept, which becomes the guiding document for all detailed planning. It culminates in the Concept Development Conference (CDC).

docs.title: Stage 3: Detailed Planning
docs.text: Logistics, force generation, sustainment, and detailed planning products are produced. Work groups develop injects, the Exercise Control Matrix (ECM), Inject Control Sheets (ICS), and the final Exercise Plan. This stage culminates in the Final Planning Conference (FPC).

docs.title: Stage 4: Execution
docs.text: The exercise is conducted. EXCON controls, directs, and monitors events. The PTA is assessed against the exercise objectives.

docs.title: Stage 5: Post-Exercise Activities
docs.text: Hot-wash-ups (intermediate debriefs), After Action Reports (AAR), lessons learned, and knowledge management.

docs.title: Planning Conferences and Meetings
docs.text: A series of conferences and meetings facilitate the planning process, each with a specific purpose and output:

docs.title: Exercise Specification Meeting
docs.text:
Purpose: Initiate the planning process and define broad requirements.

Initiated by: OSE

Attendees: EXDIR and senior EXCON members

Key activities: - Define required end state, aim, and objectives - Identify participating forces and PTA - Establish budget and resource envelope - Provide guidelines for Commissioning Instruction

Output: Commissioning Instruction / Exercise Directive

docs.title: Concept Development Conference (CDC)
docs.text:
Purpose: Design and develop the Exercise Concept.

Initiated by: EXDIR

Attendees: Core EXCON members

Duration: Days to weeks (8–12 months before execution)

Key activities: - Review Commissioning Instruction and objectives - Review lessons learned from previous exercises - Analyse training audience and supporting elements - Design and construct the Exercise Concept

Deliverables: - Planning timeline - Exercise timeline - Schedule of events - Exercise Concept document - Preliminary EXCON structure - Identification of work groups - Training package (narrative, MEL, MIL, injects, assessment concept)

Critical principle: The CDC must be completed before detailed planning begins. Premature transition to Stage 3 risks disjointed planning.

docs.title: Initial Planning Conference (IPC)
docs.text:
Purpose: Present the Exercise Concept and initiate detailed planning.

Initiated by: EXDIR

Attendees: All EXCON members and selected PTA representatives

Key activities: - Present Exercise Specification and Exercise Concept - Establish decentralised work groups - Assign detailed planning tasks

Output: Approved Exercise Concept; work group assignments

docs.title: Main Planning Conference (MPC)
docs.text:
Purpose: Integrate work group outputs into the Exercise Plan.

Initiated by: EXDIR

Attendees: All EXCON members

Key activities: - Review and integrate support plans from work groups - Finalise the Exercise Plan - Convert the Exercise Plan into the Exercise Order

Output: Final Exercise Plan; Exercise Order (draft)

docs.title: Final Planning Conference (FPC)
docs.text:
Purpose: Confirm all planning goals have been achieved.

Initiated by: EXDIR

Attendees: All EXCON members

Key activities: - Review and update the Exercise Plan - Address any unforeseen incidents or changes - Sign and issue the Exercise Order

Output: Signed Exercise Order issued to all role players

docs.title: Detailed Planning Phase
docs.text:
Once the Exercise Concept is approved, detailed planning proceeds through decentralised work groups, each focusing on key areas:

Work Group Focus Scenario / Narrative Narrative development, MEL, MIL Injects Inject design and list development Assessment / Evaluation Training and Evaluation Plan Exercise Control ECM, ICS development Real-Life Support Logistics, accommodation, sustainment Simulation Simulation systems and technical support Medical Medical support and evacuation planning Signal / Comms Communications infrastructure

docs.title: Planning Timeline
docs.text:
A backward planning (reverse engineering) approach is used:

  1. Start from the exercise execution date (D-Day)
  2. Mark key milestones backward: FPC, MPC, IPC, CDC
  3. Include mobilisation periods for participating forces
  4. Ensure the Exercise Concept is completed before the IPC

Critical principle: Initial planning should be done as early as possible and in as much detail as possible. The complexity of physical planning should not be underestimated.

docs.title: The Exercise Warning Order
docs.text: Once the CDC is completed, the EXDIR issues an Exercise Warning Order to all stakeholders involved in detailed planning. The Warning Order indicates: - Date, time, and place of the IPC - Who is to attend - Preliminary planning guidance

docs.title: Integration with the Larger Process
docs.text: The planning process is not purely sequential. Depending on the size and complexity of the exercise, phases and steps may overlap. The key is to ensure the Exercise Concept is completed before detailed planning begins — this is the critical gateway between initial planning and detailed planning.

docs.title: Post-Exercise Activities and Reporting
docs.text: "Post-exercise activities complete the training cycle and serve as the starting point for the next training exercise." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 15

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Post-exercise activities are divided into two categories: administrative tasks and demobilisation. Administrative tasks focus on the writing and handing in of key reports, debriefs, and observations. Demobilisation focuses on the physical process of closing down the exercise and preparing forces to withdraw and return to their home units.

docs.title: In-Exercise Activities
docs.text: These activities take place continuously during the exercise, directly after the completion of a specific event or activity.

docs.title: Hot Wash-Up/Debrief
docs.text:
A post-activity debriefing designed to identify and discuss performance as observed and experienced by participants and controlling staff.

Key questions: - What was the objective aim of the activity/exercise? - What did we (PTA) do? - What did we (PTA) do right? - What did we (PTA) do wrong? - How can we (PTA) improve?

The hot wash-up is facilitated by a member of EXCON (senior controller/evaluator/observer present) and should take place as soon as possible after the completion of the training activity.

docs.title: Evaluation/Assessment Reports
docs.text: Reports compiled by appointed evaluation staff reflecting the outcome of formal evaluation or assessment of the PTA. Based on the Evaluation Plan developed during the Main Planning Conference.

docs.title: Observation Reports
docs.text: Compiled by controlling staff and observers within 24 hours of the completion of an event or activity. Forwarded to Chief EXCON via the Exercise Control Centre. Provides the EXDIR with accurate feedback to allow mid-exercise adjustments.

docs.title: Post Exercise Reports (PXR)
docs.text: PXR are normally required only for larger exercises involving personnel and resources outside of the EXDIR's normal span of command.

docs.title: First Impressions Report (FIR)
docs.text:
Compiled by all elements that participated in the planning, development, and delivery of the exercise. Completed and handed in within 48 hours of completion.

Layout: - Identification of elements or units providing feedback - Identification of the item or topic to be discussed - Observations made (brief description/discussion of the issue) - Recommendations

All elements must draft a FIR to allow for a 360° reflection. No element may withdraw if their FIR has not been presented or submitted.

docs.title: After Action Review (AAR)
docs.text:
A specific date is identified for the AAR, normally 14 to 28 days after completion. The AAR reviews the FIR to identify valid points for inclusion in the final Exercise Debrief Report.

Focus areas: - Shortcomings in training to improve curriculum and method - Shortcomings in doctrine and TTPs - Personnel using incorrect doctrine or procedures - Observations meriting further attention

docs.title: Exercise Debrief Report
docs.text:
The final report for the exercise, submitted by the EXDIR to the Officer Scheduling the Exercise (OSE). Compiled from various "in exercise" report and inputs extrapolated from the FIR.

Contents: - Sequence of all activities that took place during the exercise - Exercise objectives - Lessons learned - Recommendations to improve the standard of the next exercise - Reflection of participant performance

docs.title: Lessons Identified/Learned
docs.text:
Term Definition Lessons Identified Recommendations based on observations relating to the discrepancy between required and actual performance. Not yet formally accepted or captured as doctrine/TTPs. Lessons Learned A Lesson Identified that has been validated and integrated into doctrine and TTPs, resulting in a verifiable improvement in military effectiveness.

Critical distinction: Lessons identified only become lessons learned once they have been integrated into doctrine and applied.

docs.title: Rectification Plan (Follow-Up)
docs.text:
Based on the findings and recommendations in the Final Debrief Report, the OSE identifies and drafts a Rectification Plan. The plan indicates:

  • The area of under-performance, non-performance, or concern
  • The required output or performance
  • The person or entity responsible for the rectification
  • The date by which the rectification should be completed
  • Method of reporting and to whom the report should be addressed

docs.title: Demobilisation
docs.text: Demobilisation is an "operation" on its own requiring detailed planning. EXCON is responsible to centrally plan, coordinate, and control the process.

docs.title: Closing Ceremony
docs.text: An official closing ceremony is held to thank and greet all exercise participants. Exercise trophies and certificates for outstanding performances and conduct may be awarded.

docs.title: Movement
docs.text: On completion of the demobilisation process and closing ceremony, movement back to home units is controlled and coordinated by MOVECON, which remains in place until all units have arrived at their home units.

docs.title: Purpose of Military Exercises
docs.text: "A military exercise is a training activity, manoeuvre, or simulated wartime operation conducted under simulated operational conditions involving planning, preparation, and execution." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Appendix

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A military exercise can be defined as:

"A training activity, manoeuvre, or simulated wartime operation conducted under simulated operational conditions involving planning, preparation, and execution. It is carried out for the purpose of training and evaluation of military personnel and capabilities."

docs.title: The Five Purposes of Military Exercises
1. Training
docs.text:
Exercises provide training opportunities for forces, units, and military personnel to:

  • Practise and hone competencies and skills
  • Train elements in new doctrine, tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs)
  • Train soldiers and commanders in problem-solving and military decision-making
  • Enhance interoperability and foster good relations between different functional environments, Services, Divisions, and allied forces

docs.title: 2. Evaluation
docs.text:
Exercises evaluate and validate:

Evaluation Target Description Fighting ability Skills and proficiency of soldiers and units Doctrine Relevance and effectiveness of doctrine Staff competencies Planning and decision-making capability Structures and procedures Organisational efficiency Equipment and weapon systems Performance and reliability Gaps Identification of existing and future training/doctrine gaps

docs.title: 3. Force Preparation (Combat Readiness and Mission Readiness Training)
docs.text:
• Prepare and rehearse forces for operations or specific missions
  • Ensure forces are ready for deployment

docs.title: 4. Development
docs.text:
• Serve as an experimental test bed
  • Develop and test new TTPs, doctrine, and equipment
  • Provide real-world feedback for capability development

docs.title: 5. Deterrence
docs.text:
• Serve as a show of force
  • Demonstrate preparedness and capabilities
  • Deter potential adversaries

docs.title: 6. Tool of Government
docs.text:
• Used by governments to gain influence
  • Political signaling through military capability demonstration

docs.title: Checklist: Exercise Purpose Alignment
docs.text:
• Primary purpose identified and documented
  • Training objectives linked to exercise purpose
  • Evaluation criteria aligned with purpose
  • Force preparation requirements addressed
  • Development/test objectives stated (if applicable)
  • Deterrence messaging considered (if applicable)
  • Government tool implications assessed

docs.title: Role Players and Script Writing
docs.text: "Script writing is a specialised area of scenario writing, which is used to define a specific role and behaviour that will be required of a character(s)." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 11, Appendix C

docs.title: What Are Role Players?
docs.text:
Role players are individuals appointed to interact with the Primary Training Audience (PTA) in a specific role to enhance the training experience. They are members of EXCON or the Response Cell who portray characters within the exercise narrative.

Role players are essential when personal interaction forms part of an event — for example, negotiations with a rebel leader, media briefings, or civilian-on-the-battlefield scenarios.

docs.title: Role Player Classification
docs.text:
Role players can be classified into the following categories:

Category Description Examples OPFOR Portray opposing force personnel Enemy commanders, insurgents, armed group leaders Civilians Portray local population Local officials, community leaders, displaced persons Media Portray journalists and media personnel News correspondents, reporters, camera operators Dignitaries Portray visiting officials Government representatives, military attaches, UN officials Hostage Takers Portray individuals holding hostages Terrorists, criminals, insurgents Prisoners Portray captured personnel Detainees, POWs, suspects Casualties Portray wounded or killed personnel Simulated casualties for medical training

docs.title: Script Writing
docs.text:
A script is a document that defines the specific role and behaviour required of a character. It guides role players in terms of:

  • Portrayal style: How the character should act (hostile, disruptive, combative, friendly, evasive)
  • Key messages: What the character should communicate
  • Boundaries: What the character should and should not say or do
  • Triggers: How the character should respond to specific PTA actions

docs.title: Script Components
docs.text: Component Description Character Profile Name, background, personality traits, motivations Situation Brief Current situation from the character's perspective Key Messages Core information the character must convey Do's and Don'ts Permitted and prohibited actions/responses Contingency Triggers How to respond to specific PTA actions or questions Safety Considerations Safety boundaries and emergency procedures

docs.title: Constructing a Role Player
docs.text: When constructing a role player, the following aspects must be considered:

docs.title: Character Development
docs.text:
• Name and identity: A distinct name and background for the character
  • Personal details: Age, background, personality traits (limited to what is necessary)
  • Military/past experience: Relevant background that informs the character's behaviour
  • Motivation: Why the character is acting as they are
  • Approach to the situation: The character's attitude and likely responses

docs.title: Interaction Guidelines
docs.text:
• Questions to expect: What the PTA is likely to ask
  • Answers to provide: What information the character should reveal
  • Answers to withhold: What information the character should not reveal
  • Escalation triggers: What PTA actions should provoke a response
  • De-escalation triggers: What PTA actions should calm the situation

docs.title: Safety Considerations
docs.text:
All role players must be briefed on:

  • Safety boundaries: Physical and behavioural limits
  • Emergency signals: Code words or signals to stop the interaction
  • Prohibited actions: What role players must never do (use real violence, reveal classified information, etc.)
  • Welfare arrangements: Rest periods, hydration, medical support

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text:

docs.title: Scenario Development — The Special Idea
docs.text: "The Scenario or 'Special Idea' provides the tactical backdrop for the exercise — figuratively speaking, the scenario can be seen as the 'sandbox' within which the exercise will take place." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 11

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Scenario (also called the Special Idea) provides the tactical backdrop for the exercise. It serves as the point of entry to the tactical level and provides the Primary Training Audience (PTA) with the necessary details to orient themselves with the situation and plan and execute specific actions within the set exercise framework.

"Detailed information on circumstances and events that led to a specific hypothetical crisis situation."

docs.title: Types of Scenarios
docs.text: Type Description Simplistic Scenarios Used to set the scene for a simple problem. Limited background detail; focuses on a specific topic, incident, or action. Complex Scenarios Used for advanced training requiring simultaneous actions on more than one level or area. Elaborate, with high volumes of facts and technical data. Often serves as the foundation for several independent or consecutive problems.

docs.title: Scenario Classification
docs.text: Classification Description Real-world Scenarios Based on actual operations or conflict situations. May be politically and operationally sensitive. Reality-based Scenarios Based on real-world geography, infrastructure, and role players but with fictional or hypothetical events. Simulates possible situations a force may face. Fictional Scenarios Based entirely on fictional situations, role players, and countries. Can be modelled to suit specific training objectives. Care must be taken to maintain realism.

docs.title: Setting
docs.text:
The depth and realism of the training scenario is influenced by the aim and objective of the exercise. Scenarios can be drafted from three distinctive settings in time:

Setting Focus Example Pre-conflict/Crisis Build-up to conflict or crisis. Intelligence gathering, operational planning, deployment, logistical support. Tensions rising between neighbouring countries over a disputed border; PTA tasked to plan deployment. Mid-conflict/Crisis Active phase of conflict. Real-time decision making, military problem solving, tactical manoeuvre, execution of operations. Enemy formations have crossed the border and are advancing; PTA must delay the advance. Post-conflict/Crisis Main crisis has passed. Peacekeeping, reform, disaster management. Hurricane has devastated a town; PTA must manage humanitarian crisis.

docs.title: Development Framework
docs.text: A well-structured scenario follows a developmental framework to ensure logical sequencing, sufficient detail, and grouped information. The framework includes:

docs.title: Part 1: Introduction
docs.text: Serves as the stepping-down mechanism from the operational level (Narrative) to the tactical level. Indicates: - Time now — current time and date - Current location of own forces — deployment areas to orient the PTA

docs.title: Part 2: Current Situation
docs.text: Provides detailed information on the current tactical situation, focusing on current events, incidents, flare-ups, hot spots, and attacks. Must be annotated on maps covering the Joint Area of Operations (JAO) and the Area of Operations (AO).

docs.title: Part 3: Opposing Force (OPFOR)
docs.text: The centre of gravity of the scenario. Includes detailed descriptions of: - Conventional forces - Non-conventional forces (insurgents, terrorists, organised crime) - Destabilisers - Personality Profiles of key OPFOR commanders

docs.title: Part 4: Own Forces
docs.text: Real-time force structure and organisation of own forces (blue forces). May be included in the scenario or attached as a supplementary annex (the "Blue Book"). Also includes allied/host country forces (neutral/green forces).

docs.title: Part 5: Tactical Mission
docs.text: The task the PTA is to execute. The mission must clearly indicate: - Who must do what, where, by when, in order to achieve what, and do what thereafter

docs.title: Part 6: Supporting Documents
docs.text: Supplementary materials to add value to the scenario: - Intelligence Reports (INTREPs) - Intelligence Summaries (INTSUMs) - Media articles - Other open source material

docs.title: Reference Material — Colour-Coded Annexes
docs.text:
For larger, more complex exercises, several independent annexes may be created:

Annex Colour Content Red Book Red OPFOR detail — too much to include in the main scenario Blue Book Blue Own forces and allied/host country forces Green Book Green Host nation and allied forces within the Joint Operational Area White Book White Neutrals — local population, media, NGOs, local and regional role players

docs.title: Script Writing
docs.text:
Script writing is a specialised area of scenario writing used to define a specific role and behaviour required of a character when personal interaction forms part of an event through role-playing.

Scripts guide role players in terms of questions to be asked or answers to be provided. Examples include role-playing as: - A rebel leader with whom negotiations must be conducted - A hostage-taker during hostage negotiations - A visiting dignitary - A news correspondent asking questions during a media briefing - A captured OPFOR commander to be questioned

docs.title: Site Reconnaissance
docs.text: "Once the concept is drafted, a physical site reconnaissance confirms that the training area can support the planned events." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 7

docs.title: Why Conduct a Site Reconnaissance?
docs.text:
A physical site reconnaissance is essential to confirm that the training area can support the planned events. The Exercise Concept may look sound on paper, but only a physical visit can reveal whether the terrain, infrastructure, and local conditions will actually allow the exercise to be executed as designed.

The reconnaissance serves several purposes: - Confirm terrain suitability for planned incidents - Identify infrastructure requirements and constraints - Assess safety risks and environmental sensitivities - Establish liaison with local authorities - Identify required adjustments to the concept

docs.title: Reconnaissance Team Composition
docs.text:
The reconnaissance team should include representatives from all key EXCON functions:

Role Purpose Chief Real-Life Support / Exercise Warrant Officer Accommodation, facilities, sustainment Chief Scenario Development Terrain suitability for planned incidents Chief Exercise Control Control positions, communications, observation Battlefield Preparation / Simulation Representative Live-fire areas, simulation infrastructure Signal Officer Communications footprint, cell coverage Medical Officer Medical facility access, evacuation routes Additional members as required Liaison, safety, environmental

docs.title: Terrain
docs.text:
• Suitability for the type of exercise (size, geography, vegetation, hydrography)
  • Time and distance between key locations
  • Natural and man-made obstacles
  • Potential incident sites
  • Control and observation positions

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
• Office space, mess facilities, ablutions, accommodation
  • Power supply, water, sewerage
  • Road networks and access routes
  • Communications infrastructure

docs.title: Restrictions
docs.text:
• Declared grave sites, heritage sites, environmentally sensitive areas
  • Legislation regarding noise, open fires, flying hours
  • Protected areas and wildlife
  • Land ownership and access rights

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• Live-fire areas and minimum safe distances
  • Risk of veldfires, civilian presence, and livestock
  • Evacuation routes and medical facility access
  • Potential hazard areas (cliffs, water bodies, contaminated ground)

docs.title: Liaison
docs.text:
• Military controlling authority for the training area
  • Local and municipal structures (Mayor, Executive Councils, tribal chiefs)
  • Security structures (Police, Traffic Department, local security forums)
  • Emergency response institutions
  • Landowners and local communities

docs.title: Back Brief
docs.text:
On completion, the reconnaissance team presents a back brief to the Exercise Director (EXDIR) and planning team covering:

  • Site suitability assessment — Does the terrain support the planned incidents?
  • Real-life support implications — What facilities and infrastructure are available? What must be brought in?
  • Required adjustments to the concept — What must change based on what was found?

If the site is unsuitable, the team recommends: - Selection of an alternative venue - Adjustment of the exercise concept (with EXDIR approval) - Postponement or cancellation
