docs.title: Exercise Design Templates and Checklists
docs.text: "A properly planned framework gives the narrative writer great freedom for artistic expression." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This page provides standardised templates and checklists for exercise design. These tools ensure consistency, completeness, and quality across the exercise design process.

docs.title: Exercise Design Checklist
docs.text: A sequential checklist of key design tasks:

docs.title: Stage 1: Commissioning
docs.text:
• Exercise Specification Meeting held
  • Commissioning Instruction / Exercise Directive issued
  • Exercise Director appointed
  • Budget and resources allocated
  • Key appointments identified

docs.title: Stage 2: Design and Development
docs.text:
• Concept Development Conference (CDC) scheduled
  • Final Integrated Objective List (FIOL) compiled
  • FIOL validated and SMART-I compliant
  • Main Events List (MEL) drafted
  • Master Incident List (MIL) drafted
  • Exercise Concept drafted
  • Site reconnaissance conducted
  • Exercise Concept approved by EXDIR

docs.title: Stage 3: Detailed Planning
docs.text:
• Initial Planning Conference (IPC) held
  • Work groups established
  • Injects drafted and validated
  • Exercise Control Matrix (ECM) compiled
  • Inject Control Sheets (ICS) completed
  • Training and Evaluation Plan drafted
  • Main Planning Conference (MPC) held
  • Exercise Plan finalised
  • Final Planning Conference (FPC) held
  • Exercise Order signed and issued

docs.title: Stage 4: Execution
docs.text:
• Exercise Control Centre (ECC) established
  • EXCON briefed and in position
  • Safety briefing conducted
  • Exercise commenced
  • Interim AARs conducted
  • Exercise concluded

docs.title: Stage 5: Post-Exercise
docs.text:
• Hot wash conducted
  • Formal AAR conducted
  • After Action Report submitted
  • Lessons learned captured and integrated
  • Exercise records archived

docs.title: Main Events List (MEL) Template
docs.text:
Theme Event Objective(s) / Comments 1. 1.1 1.2 2. 2.1 2.2 3. 3.1

Formatting rules: - Themes numbered sequentially (1, 2, 3...) - Events numbered within themes (1.1, 1.2, 2.1...) - Events stated crisply: one to five words - Multiple objectives may be linked to a single event

docs.title: Master Incident List (MIL) Template
docs.text:
Event Incident Occurrence Response 1.1 1.1.1 1.1 1.1.2 1.2 1.2.1 2.1 2.1.1

Formatting rules: - Incidents numbered to correspond with parent event - Each incident must have both occurrence and response - Descriptions at this stage are broad

docs.title: Activity List Template
docs.text: Event / Incident Date (D-Day) Time Location Target Audience Expected Outcome Comments 1.1.1 D+1 0600–0700 1.1.2 D+1 0800–0900

docs.title: Exercise Control Matrix (ECM) Template
docs.text:
Inject No. Event Incident Date Time Location PTA Element OPFOR Element Controller Status 1.1.1-I1 1.1 1.1.1 D+1 0600 Planned 1.1.2-I1 1.1 1.1.2 D+1 0800 Planned

Status codes: Planned / In Progress / Complete / Cancelled / Modified

docs.title: Inject Control Sheet (ICS) Template
docs.text: Field Content Inject Number e.g., 1.1.1-I1 Event / Incident Reference to MEL and MIL entries Date / Time Scheduled date and time Location Grid reference or named location Delivery Method Written, verbal, system input, AV, live PTA Element Specific PTA unit or headquarters receiving inject OPFOR Element OPFOR unit involved (if applicable) Controller Named controller responsible for delivery Inject Text Full text of the inject Expected Response What the PTA should do Assessment Criteria How the response will be evaluated Safety Considerations Safety risks and control measures Contingency What to do if PTA does not respond as expected Status Planned / In Progress / Complete / Cancelled / Modified

docs.title: After Action Report (AAR) Template
docs.text: Section Content Executive Summary Significant lessons learned, readiness discussion, recommendations Exercise Objective Restated from the Commissioning Instruction General Discussion Significant events, lessons learned, support requirements Findings and Conclusions Associated with each lesson learned and deficiency Recommendations Specific recommendations for future training

docs.title: MEL Quality Criteria
docs.text:
• Addresses every objective in the FIOL at least once
  • Contains no events that cannot be traced to an objective
  • Is sequenced in a logically coherent operational flow
  • Is realistic given available time, space, and forces

docs.title: MIL Quality Criteria
docs.text:
• Deconstructs every MEL event into at least one incident
  • Contains no incidents that cannot be traced to an event and objective
  • Provides incidents that collectively stress every objective in the FIOL
  • Is realistic given the operational context and PTA capabilities

docs.title: Inject Quality Criteria
docs.text:
• Contains all fields in the ICS format
  • Inject text is clear, concise, and sufficient
  • Assessment criteria linked to specific FIOL objectives
  • Safety considerations address real risks
  • Contingency options for common PTA failure modes

docs.title: Exercise Concept Quality Criteria
docs.text:
• Integrates MEL and MIL into a coherent operational narrative
  • Includes timelines, locations, safety considerations, and control arrangements
  • Has been presented to and approved by the EXDIR
  • Is realistic given available resources and constraints

docs.title: Typology of Military Exercises
docs.text: "War is expensive in terms of funds, material, and human lives. Its destructive nature means that real-world experience is usually limited. The only way for soldiers, sailors, and airmen to prepare for battle is by conducting and participating in realistic military exercises." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 1

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A military exercise is a training activity, manoeuvre, or simulated wartime operation conducted under simulated operational conditions involving planning, preparation, and execution. It is carried out for the purpose of training and evaluation of military personnel and capabilities.[^1]

Military exercises are the bridge between theory and practice. They allow commanders and staffs to test procedures, validate plans, rehearse decision-making, and identify capability gaps — without the cost and risk of actual combat.

docs.title: Purpose of Military Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises serve multiple purposes, often simultaneously:

Purpose Description Training Provide opportunities to practise competencies, train in new doctrine or TTPs, enhance interoperability, and develop problem-solving skills Evaluation Assess fighting ability, staff competencies, doctrine, structures, procedures, and equipment Force Preparation Prepare and rehearse forces for operations or specific missions (combat readiness and mission readiness training) Development Serve as experimental testbeds for new TTPs, doctrine, and equipment Deterrence Demonstrate preparedness and capabilities as a show of force Tool of Government Provide governments with a mechanism for influence and foreign policy

docs.title: Classification by Participation Structure
docs.text: Military exercises can be classified by the participating force structure:

docs.title: Service-Unique Exercise
docs.text: An exercise consisting of one or more force structure elements from a single service or division. Example: An army-only field training exercise.

docs.title: Joint Exercise
docs.text: An exercise in which two or more force structure elements of two or more services participate jointly. Example: A combined army-navy-air force command post exercise.

docs.title: Multinational Exercise (Combined Exercise)
docs.text: An exercise involving the armed forces of two or more countries. Example: NATO's Steadfast Defender series.

docs.title: Joint Inter-Departmental, Inter-Agency, Multi-National Exercise (JI²M)
docs.text: An exercise involving two or more services, one or more government departments or agencies, and military or government departments from a foreign country. This is the most complex classification, typical of whole-of-government crisis response exercises.

docs.title: Classification by Level
docs.text:
Exercises are conducted at different levels of warfare, which determines the type of exercise appropriate:

Level Typical Echelon Exercise Focus Strategic National command authority, combatant command Strategic decision-making, policy, campaign design Operational Joint task force, division and larger Operational planning, sustainment, coordination Tactical Brigade and below Tactical execution, combined arms, decision-making Technical Units and individuals Procedures, systems, communications

The tactical level is further sub-divided into individual, section/crew, platoon, company, battalion, and brigade levels.

docs.title: Training Audience
docs.text: Every exercise is directed at a specific training audience:

docs.title: Primary Training Audience (PTA)
docs.text: The main participants who physically participate in the exercise. The aim and objectives are directed at this group. Their performance is measured, assessed, and evaluated by exercise control (EXCON). The PTA does not form part of the design team.

docs.title: Secondary Training Audience (STA)
docs.text: Elements that assist EXCON in directing and executing events. STAs may exploit ad hoc training opportunities but are not formally assessed. Examples include directing staff at training institutions and logistical support units.

docs.title: Elements in Support
docs.text: Supporting elements not directly involved in the exercise but providing overall support (e.g., base support, medical, transport).

docs.title: Polarity
docs.text:
Polarity refers to the number of opposing sides in an exercise:

  • One-sided: Only the PTA is represented. The opposing side is simulated or virtual. Most command post exercises are one-sided.
  • Two-sided: Two sides oppose each other. Common in tactical exercises with a live OPFOR.
  • Multi-sided: More than two sides are involved, often including non-military actors. Typical of complex stability operations or multi-agency exercises.

docs.title: Types of Military Exercises
docs.text: The selection of the correct exercise type is crucial to achieving exercise objectives. The following types are recognised across international doctrine:

docs.title: Discussion-Based Exercises
docs.text: Type Description Typical Use Study Period / Group Case study analysis, critical discussion, staff papers Develop critical thinking, broaden understanding Staff Ride Visit to historical battle sites for terrain analysis Terrain analysis, decision-making in context Model Exercise (Sand Model) Tactical problems examined using models on terrain representation Teach theory and tactics in modified space/time Map Exercise (MAPEX) Conducted on a map; staff planning, coordination, decision-making Staff training at battalion level and above Table Top Exercise (TTX) Discussion-based; scenarios analysed to confirm roles, evaluate procedures Identify gaps, confirm responsibilities, enhance understanding War Gaming Simulated military training event using real or imaginary problems Force-on-force simulation, optimisation, tactical decision-making

docs.title: Operations-Based Exercises
docs.text: Type Description Typical Use Command Post Exercise (CPX) HQ-focused; simulated forces; commanders and staff Staff procedures, C2 systems, decision-making Field Training Exercise (FTX) Live execution with troops and equipment under simulated conditions Tactical proficiency, combined arms integration Live-Fire Exercise (LFX) Live ammunition and ordnance; manoeuvre and combat drills Combat skills, combined arms live-fire integration Situational Training Exercise (STX) Focuses on specific events, tasks, or techniques Standalone or part of larger FTX Command Field Exercise (CFX) Hybrid CPX + reduced live execution C2 under semi-realistic conditions Computer-Assisted Exercise (CAX) Computer simulation of operations between opposing forces Large-scale operations, joint/combined training Tactical Exercise Without Troops (TEWT) No troops; commanders and staff apply theory to procedures Planning and decision-making training

docs.title: Force Preparation Exercises
docs.text: Type Description Typical Use Combat Readiness Exercise (CRT) Prepare and evaluate combat readiness of a unit or force Service-unique readiness validation Mission Readiness Exercise (MRT) Prepare a unit for deployment to a specific mission Pre-deployment rehearsal Mission Rehearsal Exercise (MRX) Rehearse a specific named operation as part of pre-deployment training Final preparation before deployment

docs.title: Exercise Integration
docs.text:
Exercise integration combines multiple smaller exercises of different types into a single larger, more complex exercise. This allows:

  • Integration of different exercise types
  • Accommodation of different levels of military operations
  • A larger mix of forces exercising together
  • Geographical dispersal of exercise events
  • Full operational flow with different phases conducted simultaneously

docs.title: Progressive Training Approach
docs.text:
A practical approach begins with simple exercises and progressively increases scope, duration, and complexity. Each exercise should build on the previous one:

  1. TTX → Discuss roles and solutions (low resources)
  2. MAPEX / Model Exercise → Apply to enhanced scenario
  3. CPX + CAX → Commander and full HQ staff participate
  4. FTX / CFX → Evaluate under field conditions

This progression ensures foundations are solid before complexity increases.

docs.title: Selecting the Correct Type
docs.text:
The selection of exercise type depends on:

  • Training audience — Who must be trained?
  • Objectives — What must be achieved?
  • Level — Strategic, operational, or tactical?
  • Resources — Budget, time, forces, equipment available?
  • Polarity — One-sided, two-sided, or multi-sided?
  • Complexity — How much complexity is needed to achieve the objectives?

Critical principle: The exercise type must match the objectives. A poorly chosen exercise type will not achieve the objectives, regardless of how well it is executed.

docs.title: Military Training Vignettes
docs.text: "A vignette is a concise description of a realistic hypothetical tactical situation — a snapshot in time that does not require a start, middle, or end." — Adapted from EXDESIGN Textbook, Chapter 10

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A vignette (pronounced vin-yet) is a stand-alone training sketch derived from the French word meaning "little vine." It is defined as:

"A concise description of a realistic hypothetical tactical situation."

Vignettes are often referred to as a "snapshot in time" because they do not require an elaborate back story, narrative arc, or scenario to support them. They are self-contained tactical problems that can be presented and resolved in a short period.

docs.title: Utilisation
docs.text:
Vignettes serve as a versatile training tool to introduce the training audience to a wide range of hypothetical tactical situations covering a broad spectrum of topics without the need for elaborate back story. Their versatility allows use from the tactical to strategic level.

Vignettes can be used to:

  • Prepare and train forces for specific tactical situations
  • Develop and refine tactical decision-making and problem-solving skills
  • Assess and evaluate tactical competency of soldiers, commanders, and units
  • Evaluate and assess force structures, doctrine, and TTPs (interoperability of systems)
  • Provide a central reference point to compare different participants' approaches and solutions to a standard problem

docs.title: Considerations
docs.text:
Before constructing a vignette, the designer must have a clear understanding of:

  • Type of exercise that will be conducted
  • Objective that is to be achieved

Vignettes are best suited to support discussion-based exercises such as table-top exercises, tactical decision-making exercises, and situational training exercises. They are not suitable for exercises that require the planning audience to conduct elaborate and detailed operational planning, as the nature of a vignette normally allows only for minimum detail.

docs.title: Perspective
docs.text:
Vignettes can be written from three perspectives:

Perspective Description Example Second person Uses "You" to address the training audience directly "You have been appointed to..." Third person Uses "he, she, it, they" "The Army has realised that..." Neutral Object is given a name or identity "Cyclone Juliet has..." / "451 Battalion is..."

docs.title: Vantage Point
docs.text:
This refers to the position from which the vignette is drafted:

  • Own Forces vantage point: "Platoon 3 of C-Coy, 1 South African Infantry Battalion has been tasked to..."
  • Enemy vantage point: "The enemy has deployed a large force in..."

docs.title: Time Frame
docs.text:
Three time frames can be used, independently or jointly:

Time Frame Description Future dated The incident is still to take place; focus on prevention or mitigation Present time The incident is taking place right now Past/Completed The incident has occurred; consequence management required

Recommendation: Stay within a single time frame per vignette. Should a different time frame be required, draft a new vignette.

docs.title: Construction
docs.text: The success of a vignette lies in proper construction, composed of two parts:

docs.title: Part 1: Situation Sketch
docs.text:
Sets the scene and describes the when, where, who, and what:

Element Description Example When Time and date "At 07:30 on 15 May..." / "On 29 June at 03:30..." Where Location or position "On the corner of Radebe and Collins Road" / "At grid Ref 987 563" Who Role players involved "39 Bn Group, strengthened with a squadron of armoured cars and a battery of 120mm mortars..." What Action(s) the OPFOR is conducting Detailed description of activities, aim, and intention

docs.title: Part 2: Expected Outcome
docs.text: Stipulates the mission and expected outcome. The expected outcome must clearly indicate the required task, condition, and standard to be achieved.

docs.title: Restrictions and Limitations
docs.text:
Restrictions and limitations may be included as part of the problem statement:

  • Restrictions: Inhibitors over which you have no control (legal prescripts, Law of Armed Conflict, Status of Forces Agreement)
  • Limitations: Inhibitors that are self-imposed (Rules of Engagement, force strength, weapon types allocated)

docs.title: Training Aids
docs.text:
To enhance the training experience when using vignettes, the use of training aids is encouraged:

  • Field training under simulated operational conditions
  • Role players in the form of OPFOR (Real-life Simulation)
  • Computer simulation (Constructive or Virtual)
  • Sand models
  • Maps and aerial photos

docs.title: Daisy-Chaining Technique
docs.text:
Vignettes can be used as individual building blocks to construct a larger exercise by "daisy-chaining" a number of vignettes together to create a series of sequential operational events or incidents.

Technique Description Three-Phased Vignette Past incident → current events → future planning requirement Linear Phased Timeline Vignettes follow one another sequentially on a linear timeline Exploration of Random Possibilities Vignettes scattered across locations within an AO; exposes PTA to diverse challenges and prevents exercise fatigue Phased Escalation/De-escalation Complexity increases or decreases as the exercise progresses

docs.title: Exercise Design
docs.text: "Exercise design is the bridge between learning objectives and realistic decision-making. A well-designed exercise creates the conditions for commanders and staff to practice the art of command under controlled stress."

docs.title: Library Contents
docs.text:
• Exercise Types — from study periods to live field exercises
  • Commissioning and Initiation — tasking, directives, and planning authority
  • Planning and Development — concept development, conferences, and detailed planning
  • Control and Documentation — control structures, MEL/MIL, and exercise orders

This section is part of the Strategos Telos wargaming library. It is intended to be generalizable to military exercise design practice worldwide.

docs.title: Commissioning and Initiation
docs.text: The exercise design process begins when the authority responsible for training identifies a need and issues a commissioning instruction or exercise directive. This document defines: - Exercise name and classification - Purpose and type - Aim and focus - Training and exercise objectives - Participating and supporting forces - Timeframe and locations - Key appointments - Resource allocation and constraints

docs.title: Commissioning Instruction
docs.text: The commissioning instruction serves as the tasking document that: - Mandates the exercise - Appoints an Exercise Director - Demarcates the objectives of the exercise - Provides the framework within which the exercise is to be designed - Stipulates the timeline for development and execution

docs.title: Exercise Specification Meeting
docs.text: Before an exercise is commissioned, the Officer Scheduling the Exercise conveys intent, guidelines, and objectives in a formal conference to the core planning group. This meeting: - Identifies key requirements and objectives - Serves as the framework for drafting the commissioning instruction or exercise directive - Defines the authority for all subsequent planning sessions

docs.title: Initial Planning Conference
docs.text: Once the concept has been developed, the Exercise Director issues an exercise warning order and convenes the Initial Planning Conference. The IPC: - Presents the approved concept to the full planning group - Creates decentralized work groups for detailed planning - Begins the translation of concept into executable plans

docs.title: Exercise Control Structure
docs.text:
A balanced control structure is essential. Too large a control element strains the budget; too small a structure creates safety and control risks.

Typical core elements: - Exercise Director — overall authority and final decisions - Exercise Control — scenario management, timing, and injects - Scenario Development Cell — narrative and scenario maintenance - Evaluation Cell — observation, assessment, and after-action review production - Simulation Control — simulation integration where applicable - Specialist Staff — safety, logistics, communications, medical - Real-Life Support — force protection, emergency response, administration

docs.title: Exercise Documentation
docs.text: Standard exercise documentation typically includes: - Commissioning instruction or exercise directive - Exercise concept paper - Exercise plan and exercise order - Narrative and scenario documents - MEL/MIL list and control matrix - Evaluation plan and after-action review guidance - Safety plan and real-life support annexes

docs.title: Exercise Types
docs.text:
Military exercises exist on a spectrum from study to live field execution.

Type Description Typical Use Study period / staff ride Paper-based or terrain walk-through; low resource Concept familiarization, doctrine review Map exercise / table-top exercise (TTX) Map or model-based decision-making; no troops Command-post training, staff coordination Tactical decision exercise / TDG Short timed decision vignettes; individual or small group Leader judgment drills, PME blocks Command post exercise (CPX) Headquarters-focused; simulated or real staff Staff procedures, C2 systems, decision-making Field training exercise (FTX) Live execution with troops and equipment Tactical proficiency, combined arms integration Computer-assisted exercise (CAX) Virtual, constructive, or live simulation integration Large-scale operations, joint/combined training Command field exercise (CFX) Hybrid CPX + limited live execution Command and control under semi-realistic conditions

docs.title: Planning and Development
docs.text: Concept development and detailed planning turn the commissioning instruction into an executable exercise plan.

docs.title: Concept Development Conference
docs.text:
The core planning team, usually led by the Exercise Director, develops the exercise concept. For complex exercises, this phase should begin 8 to 12 months before execution.

Key outputs: - Exercise concept paper - Preliminary control structure - Planning timeline - Initial exercise objectives and training objectives

The conference should function as a collective think tank. Small break-away groups may be permitted, but centralized planning should be encouraged to keep all planners aligned.

docs.title: Planning Conferences
docs.text: Conference Purpose Timing Initial Planning Conference (IPC) Present concept; create work groups; begin detailed planning 4–6 months before execution Main Planning Conference (MPC) Integrate work group outputs; finalize exercise plan and order 2–3 months before execution Final Planning Conference (FPC) Confirm readiness; review and update plan; issue final exercise order 2–4 weeks before execution

docs.title: Backward Planning
docs.text: All exercise planning should use backward planning from the execution date. Mark milestones for: - Concept development completion - Initial, main, and final planning conferences - Mobilization and force deployment - Rehearsals and validation events

docs.title: Objective Alignment
docs.text: Every element of the exercise — from narrative to injects to evaluation — should map directly to stated training objectives. Avoid adding activities that do not serve the exercise aim.

docs.title: Scenario Writing
docs.text: "A compelling scenario is paramount to the success of a wargame. If the scenario fails to engage the players, the wargame is likely to falter."

docs.title: Library Contents
docs.text:
• Background and Context — actors, objectives, relationships, and resources
  • Narrative Design — constructing the strategic and operational backdrop
  • Design Process — from purpose to validation
  • Inject Design — dynamic events and fog of war
  • Checklist — quality checks and the wargame cycle

This section is part of the Strategos Telos wargaming library. It is intended to be generalizable to military wargaming and exercise design practice worldwide.

docs.title: What Is a Scenario?
docs.text: A scenario provides the context for decision-making and sets the stage for the wargame. It should include a compelling background, clear player objectives, defined relationships, available resources, and mechanisms for information updates.

docs.title: Scenario Background
docs.text: A well-crafted background increases scenario credibility and deters challenges. It should: - Establish the key actors in the wargame - Identify their general attitudes, intentions, and goals - Provide the political, economic, and social context - Explain the historical and strategic background that led to the situation

docs.title: Player Objectives
docs.text: Clearly defining what each player is attempting to achieve creates tension or conflict between key players. Objectives should be: - Specific and measurable - Potentially conflicting between sides - Aligned with the wargame's overall purpose

docs.title: Defined Relationships and Command Affiliations
docs.text: Establish the organizational structure or command relationship of all players: - Hierarchy of command within teams - Diplomatic relations between teams - Chain of command for orders and reporting

docs.title: Available Resources
docs.text: Resources at each player's disposal during the wargame: - Order of Battle (OOB) for military units - Equipment and weapons systems - Intelligence resources - Logistical capabilities - Financial and political capital

docs.title: Information Update Mechanisms
docs.text: How the scenario evolves and how information is shared: - Regular situation reports (SITREPs) - Intelligence updates - Unexpected developments or injects - Communication protocols and delays

docs.title: Scenario Writing Checklist
docs.text:
• Clear connection to wargame objectives
  • Credible background narrative
  • Defined player objectives with potential conflict
  • Complete order of battle for all sides
  • Terrain and environmental conditions specified
  • Information update mechanisms defined
  • Injects planned for key decision points
  • Cultural context incorporated
  • Scenario validated by subject matter experts

docs.title: The Scenario in the Wargame Cycle
docs.text:
Tasking → Design → Development → Testing → Rehearsal → Execution → Post-Game → Archival
                ↑                                                              |
                └──────────────── Scenario iteration and improvement ──────────┘

docs.title: Scenario Design Process
docs.text:
1. Understand the purpose — What analytical question is the wargame answering?
  2. Define the setting — Where and when does the scenario take place?
  3. Establish the actors — Who are the key players and what are their goals?
  4. Create the narrative — What sequence of events leads to the wargame's starting point?
  5. Set the conditions — What are the initial force dispositions, terrain, and weather?
  6. Design the injects — What events will disrupt and challenge player plans?
  7. Validate realism — Does the scenario reflect plausible real-world conditions?

docs.title: Scenario Robustness
docs.text:
A scenario should be robust enough to offer players latitude to make decisions about issues important to the sponsor, without being overly restrictive or permissive.

  • Overly restrictive: Players feel railroaded; exploration is limited
  • Overly permissive: Players lose focus; the wargame drifts from its objectives

docs.title: Inject Design
docs.text: Injects are unexpected developments that keep the scenario dynamic and realistic. Effective injects: - Are timed to challenge existing plans - Test player adaptability - Reflect real-world uncertainty and fog of war - Are plausible within the scenario's context

docs.title: Narrative Design
docs.text: A compelling scenario requires a narrative that resonates with players and aligns with their real-world experiences. The narrative should be credible and internally consistent, reflect the operational environment accurately, include human elements, and account for cultural context.

docs.title: Core Components
docs.text:
1. Orientation — Introduce the operational environment, including geography, climate, infrastructure, and human terrain.
  2. Historical Background — Describe the strategic and operational background that explains how the situation developed. Identify the main actors, their motivations, and the conflict triggers.
  3. Escalation / Road to Crisis or War — Chronologically unpack recent events that led to the current situation. Show a clear increase in tension and the key incidents that pushed the situation toward conflict.
  4. Mission — State the military problem and the mission that brings the primary training audience into the situation. This may be a structured mission from higher headquarters or an unstructured problem that requires analysis and appreciation.

docs.title: Design Steps
docs.text:
1. Geographical placement — Choose real or fictional terrain. Prepare maps at appropriate scales.
  2. Identify conflict triggers — Select one or more political, social, economic, or military triggers that start the conflict.
  3. Identify main actors — Define each actor's aims, capabilities, power base, and threat potential.
  4. Conflict mapping — Plot incidents on a timeline or map to control tempo and escalation.
  5. Mission statement — Define the military mission that transitions from operational to tactical level.
  6. Supporting documents — Prepare orders, intelligence summaries, ROE, and logistics data.
  7. Draft the narrative — Write the full narrative, keeping it concise, accurate, and clear.

docs.title: Applications Across the Spectrum of Conflict
docs.text: Military simulation and wargaming are applicable throughout the entire spectrum of conflict — from near-perfect peace to total nuclear war, including post-conflict conditions.

docs.title: Levels of War
docs.text:
The concept of "levels of war" guides the organisation and execution of military operations.

Level Focus Technical Understanding and improving technical aspects of equipment operation Low-Tactical Training individual soldiers or small units High-Tactical Training commanders to control larger units (battalions, regiments) Operational Planning and coordination of large-scale military operations Military Strategic High-level military planning and decision-making National Strategic Broader implications of military actions on national security and policy Regional/Global Strategic Impacts on regional stability or global peace

docs.title: Beyond Conflict
docs.text:
Military simulation and wargaming also apply to: - Management — organisational decision-making - Business — competitive strategy - Competition — Fittest Soldier-type events for morale and mental fitness

Source: Wargaming and Military Simulation for the SANDF, TRG COMD/R/103/6, May 2025, Capt P.A.R. Malan.

docs.title: Future Trends
docs.text: Military simulation and wargaming are being reshaped by technology trends, particularly AI, ML, and big data analytics.

docs.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
docs.text:
AI-powered agents can simulate enemy forces, creating dynamic and unpredictable scenarios that mirror real-world combat uncertainties.

Benefits: - Enhanced realism and complexity - Dynamic scenario generation - Real-time adaptation to trainee actions

Risks: - Overreliance on technology - Neglect of human intuition - Vulnerability to cyber threats - Limited by training data quality and biases

docs.title: Big Data Analytics
docs.text:
Integration of sensor data, social media, and other sources to create comprehensive battlefield representations.

Benefits: - More nuanced operational environment understanding - Dynamic scenario updating

Risks: - Data security and privacy concerns - Challenge of managing vast information volumes

docs.title: Cloud Computing
docs.text:
Seamless integration of systems and platforms; facilitates data sharing across command levels.

Benefits: - Increased flexibility and accessibility - Cross-level coordination

Risks: - Internet connectivity dependence - Cloud service disruption vulnerability

docs.title: Virtual and Augmented Reality
docs.text:
Immersion in complex operational environments or emergency scenarios.

Benefits: - Safe yet realistic training - Enhanced spatial understanding

Risks: - Costly implementation - Cannot fully replicate physical and psychological stresses of real operations

docs.title: Cybersecurity
docs.text:
As simulations become more digital, cybersecurity becomes critical.

Requirements: - Robust security protocols for simulation data integrity - Ongoing maintenance and updates - Personnel training in cybersecurity practices

docs.title: Personalized Training
docs.text:
AI-powered simulations tailored to individual soldiers' needs and abilities.

Consideration: AI systems are only as good as their training data. Biased or incomplete data produces flawed recommendations.

docs.title: More Realistic Scenarios
docs.text:
AI creates dynamic scenarios adapting in real-time to trainee actions.

Consideration: No simulation can fully replicate the unpredictability and chaos of real combat. Must complement with live exercises.

docs.title: Increased Focus on Decision-Making
docs.text:
Real-time feedback and analysis to develop decision-making abilities.

Consideration: Human judgement of experienced personnel must always play a central role — not over-reliance on AI feedback.

docs.title: Integration of Human Factors
docs.text:
Incorporating fatigue, stress, and psychological considerations.

Ethical consideration: Simulating high-stress situations may have negative psychological impacts. Appropriate safeguards and support systems are required.

docs.title: Enhanced Decision-Making
docs.text:
• Real-time data and analysis for strategic planning
  • Risk: Overreliance leading to complacency and reduced critical thinking

docs.title: Increased Efficiency
docs.text:
• Reduced time and resources for training
  • Risk: Simulations may not replicate real combat pressures

docs.title: Improved Situational Awareness
docs.text:
• Comprehensive battlefield view from multiple data sources
  • Risk: Data quality directly affects effectiveness

docs.title: Enhanced Collaboration
docs.text:
• Real-time data enabling better communication and coordination
  • Risk: Security concerns with sensitive data sharing; information overload

docs.title: Overreliance on New Technologies
docs.text:
Emerging technologies like AI, VR, and AR offer significant advantages, but overreliance leads to: - Neglect of vital military training aspects - Inability to replicate human intuition critical to battlefield decisions - Substantial upfront investment burden for constrained defence budgets

Technology can be a force multiplier for countries that can afford and sustain it. It becomes a burdensome millstone for everyone else.

docs.title: Neglect of Traditional Methods
docs.text: Conceptual wargaming fosters critical thinking, creativity, and adaptability. Traditional methods remain effective and should not be disregarded.

docs.title: Misplaced Focus
docs.text: The primary purpose is not to win, but to learn. Focus on victory rather than learning undermines the wargame's purpose.

docs.title: Poorly Understood Objectives
docs.text: If objectives are not thoroughly understood by participants, the simulation fails to yield useful results.

docs.title: Ignorance of Military Simulation and Wargaming
docs.text: Lack of understanding by key personnel affects realism and usefulness. Remedy through increased awareness, understanding, and communication of benefits.

docs.title: Cultural Context and the Lie of Reasonable Actors
docs.text:
From a South African perspective, the behaviour of Actor A may seem unreasonable, but it is very rational within that actor's cultural context. This can be mitigated by letting participants become specialized in the relevant culture.

Source: Wargaming and Military Simulation for the SANDF, TRG COMD/R/103/6, May 2025, Capt P.A.R. Malan.

docs.title: Generations of Wargames
docs.text: Wargames are classified into generations based on their complexity, modelling fidelity, and underlying technology.

docs.title: First-Generation Wargames
docs.text:
• Abstract competition where outcomes are determined primarily by player decisions
  • No sophisticated models of reality
  • Turn-based; no dimension of time
  • Examples: Chess, Go, Senet

docs.title: Second-Generation Wargames
docs.text:
• Underlying model representative of actual time and space
  • Depicts combat, movement, attrition, logistics
  • Accurate scaled terrain and distances
  • Time incorporated — simultaneous or real-time decisions
  • Examples: Kriegsspiel, Flames of War, board wargames

docs.title: Third-Generation Wargames
docs.text:
• Highly detailed and realistic models simulating system-vs-system interaction
  • Incorporates computer systems and software
  • Can simulate large-scale operations with real-world data
  • Models complex interactions among various factors

Current limitation: No software exists that can be considered a full-fledged third-generation wargame. It is physically impossible to incorporate all possible systems and elements of power. Current "third-generation" products are second-generation wargames with additional features.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
• Represents entire military systems
  • Examines almost all dimensions of conflict
  • Focus on effects, effects-based outcomes, and synergy of systems
  • Forces go beyond military to include NGOs, civilians, journalists, police

docs.title: Fourth-Generation Wargames
docs.text:
• Move beyond war and conflict to include peace as a plausible path to victory
  • Blend politics, culture, religion, mass media, and global information flows with combat
  • Designed for the complexities of modern warfare and fourth-generation warfare

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
• Integration of AI, ML, and advanced technology
  • Dynamic and adaptive scenarios
  • Advanced analytics and feedback
  • Interdisciplinary approach (politics, religion, culture, media)
  • Focus on peaceful outcomes — peace as a desirable and plausible outcome
  • Dependent on current technical trends

docs.title: The Generational Progression
docs.text:
First Gen          Second Gen           Third Gen            Fourth Gen
Abstract          Scaled Model          System-vs-System      Peace + War
Turn-based        Time + Space          Computer-assisted     AI/ML-driven
Chess             Kriegsspiel           COA wargames          Multi-domain
No fidelity       Scaled terrain        High complexity       Adaptive scenarios
Elite pursuit     Mass access           Commercial market     Global information

Source: Wargaming and Military Simulation for the SANDF, TRG COMD/R/103/6, May 2025, Capt P.A.R. Malan.

docs.title: History of Wargaming
docs.text: Wargaming, a manifestation of conflict in abstract form, has been an integral part of military strategy since the dawn of civilization.

docs.title: First-Generation Wargames
docs.text:
The earliest evidence of wargaming can be traced back to toys — miniature versions of adult tools. Young ones used these to learn how to operate in human society.

As societies evolved, games shifted towards abstraction. A miniature spear could aid in training the chieftain's son in combat, but teaching him how to strategize required a different kind of game — one that could teach leadership, decision-making, and conceptual thinking.

docs.title: Early Examples
docs.text: Game Origin Era Significance Senet / T'au Egypt ~2000 BC Abstract strategic games Wei-chi / Go China ~2300 BC Strategic depth, elite pursuit Chaturang India ~600 AD Precursor to chess; spread to Persia, Middle East, Europe Morabaraba Africa Ancient Strategic exercise, tactical thinking for young warriors Mancala Egypt Ancient Strategic depth, African contribution to wargaming history

docs.title: Characteristics of First-Generation Wargames
docs.text:
• Extreme abstraction — often impossible to determine the level of war represented
  • Symmetric forces — game pieces are simplistic, both players have identical pieces
  • Mind-versus-mind — focus on mental performance and decision-making
  • No underlying model — very simplified or absent representation of reality
  • Turn-based — participants take turns; time is ignored or abstracted
  • Elite pursuit — wargames were primarily played by ruling or warrior elites

docs.title: Second-Generation Wargames
docs.text: Second-generation wargaming was almost entirely developed in Prussia during the 18th and 19th centuries. The defining feature is an underlying model representative of actual time and space.

docs.title: The von Reisswitz Innovation
docs.text:
• 1811: Baron Leopold von Reisswitz developed a wargame using a 3D sand table terrain model. Participants prepared orders simultaneously and provided them to an umpire for adjudication.
  • Lt Georg von Reisswitz (the Baron's son) transformed the game by replacing the sand table with a topographic map — equally accurate, easier to prepare and transport. This made the game cheaper, widely accessible, and flexible across levels of command.

General Karl von Müffling, upon seeing the game, exclaimed: "It's not a game at all, it's training for war. I shall recommend it enthusiastically to the whole army."

docs.title: Moltke's System
docs.text:
General von Moltke institutionalised wargaming:

  1. Staff rides — personally took war college students to invasion corridor terrain
  2. Map-based wargames — conducted after staff ride discussions
  3. Live simulations / field exercises — garrisons provided soldiers and equipment to test plans

Results were collated and often became official military plans.

docs.title: German Innovations
docs.text:
1. Level-specific optimisation — games tailored to strategic, operational, and tactical levels from the 1870s
  2. Break points — Capt Naumann (1877) introduced rules for when units cease to function based on casualties
  3. Free Kriegsspiel — Verdy du Vernois proposed replacing cumbersome rules with military judgment of experienced officers, enabling faster outcomes and larger-scale simulation

docs.title: Characteristics of Second-Generation Wargames
docs.text:
• Depicts combat, movement, attrition, and logistics
  • Accurate scaled terrain and distances — break from grid-based layout
  • Time incorporated — simultaneous or real-time decisions
  • Qualifies as a military simulation due to model + time combination
  • Focused on a single level of warfare
  • Knowledge of terrain, units, own and enemy doctrine is crucial
  • Intended to adjudicate the military dimension of conflict

docs.title: The Spread Beyond Prussia
docs.text:
Development was not restricted to the military. As literacy rates increased and elite monopoly loosened, civilian interest grew:

  • 1813: The Peninsula — civilian wargame with abstracted map of Portugal
  • Civilian-commercial market became a major driver of innovation

Source: Wargaming and Military Simulation for the SANDF, TRG COMD/R/103/6, May 2025, Capt P.A.R. Malan.

docs.title: Aim
docs.text: To provide a single reference document for the SANDF. Different countries, departments, and people have differing definitions of words and concepts. This document aims to provide a single understanding for the organisation.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
• Origins and history
  • Modelling, simulation and wargaming overview
  • Types and examples
  • The wargaming process
  • Applications across the spectrum of conflict
  • SANDF-specific context
  • Future trends

docs.title: Working Definition of Wargaming
docs.text:
Wargaming is a tool for exploring decision-making possibilities in an environment with incomplete and imperfect information (Herman, Frost, & Kurz, 2009).

At its core, wargaming is a meticulous model or simulation of warfare that does not require the involvement of actual military forces. Instead, it operates independently, with the sequence of events being influenced by decisions made by players representing opposing sides. This highlights the human aspect of warfare, placing importance on the interplay between human decisions and their simulated outcomes. Consequently, each wargame is unique, making it impossible for two games to be identical.

docs.title: The demarcation: Simulation vs Wargame
docs.text:
The demarcation between simulation and wargaming is found in a thinking adversary. If there is no thinking (human) adversary or opponent that the participant must contend with, then it is a simulation. Once participants play against each other, it is termed a wargame.

In cases where both terms are appropriate, they are used interchangeably.

Note: The term "wargaming" often carries negative connotations due to its association with warfare and conflict. Some perceive it as glorifying or trivializing war. However, in a military context, wargaming is a valuable tool used for strategic planning and decision-making and is not intended to lighten the realities of war.

docs.title: Critical Elements of a Wargame
docs.text:
A professional wargame must address five critical components:

  1. Objective — well-defined, specific objectives that guide all game design
  2. Players — human participants cast in operational roles reflecting their actual positions
  3. Scenario — a compelling narrative providing context for decision-making
  4. Game Engine — models, database, ruleset, and adjudication method
  5. Analysis / After Action Review — structured capture of information defined by the objectives

Source: Wargaming and Military Simulation for the SANDF, TRG COMD/R/103/6, May 2025, Capt P.A.R. Malan.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
A model is a scaled representation of the real world. A topographic map is a model; an abstract sculpture is not. Models are static — they represent a situation at a specific point in time, like a photograph.

The process of distilling the real world into a model is called modelling. A model that serves as the underlying foundation for a simulation or wargame is also called the game engine.

Fidelity is the hallmark of a model. A map or scale model is only useful to the extent that it accurately represents reality.

docs.title: Simulation
docs.text:
Transitioning a model into the realm of time creates a simulation. An aircraft model in a wind tunnel observed over different airspeeds over time becomes a simulation.

A simulation represents a potential real-world process or system by imitating its operations. It relies on models that are iterated over time. When participants compete against each other, it becomes a simulation game. When armed factions are involved, it is a wargame.

docs.title: Wargame
docs.text:
A wargame is a process that imitates aspects of warfare at the tactical, operational, or strategic level. It is used to: - Examine warfighting concepts - Train and educate commanders and analysts - Explore scenarios - Assess how force planning and posture choices affect campaign outcomes

Wargames are adversarial and often focus on specific strategic questions.

docs.title: The Demarcation
docs.text:
Feature Simulation Wargame Adversary No thinking human opponent Thinking human opponent required Competition Against environment/system Against another player Example Flight simulator, CPX Kriegsspiel, board wargame

In cases where both terms are appropriate, they are used interchangeably.

docs.title: Mathematical Foundations
docs.text: Mathematics equations form the foundation for a model. These models then serve as the foundation for a simulation or wargame.

docs.title: Lanchester's Laws
docs.text:
Lanchester's laws are differential equations describing the time-dependent strengths of two opposing armies. Developed independently by Frederick Lanchester and M. Osipov during World War I.

  • Linear Law — for ancient hand-to-hand combat
  • Square Law — for modern combat with long-range weapons

The square law shows that the side with more soldiers or greater firepower at the beginning will win, given equal conditions. Applied to: - Pickett's Charge (Gettysburg, 1863) - Battle of Britain (1940) - Battle of Kursk - Guerrilla warfare modelling

docs.title: Simulation Fidelity
docs.text:
Fidelity Description Low Minimum simulation required to respond to inputs and provide outputs Medium Responds automatically to stimuli with limited accuracy High Nearly indistinguishable from the real system

Source: Wargaming and Military Simulation for the SANDF, TRG COMD/R/103/6, May 2025, Capt P.A.R. Malan.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The preparation, execution, and archival of a wargame broadly takes place over eight phases:

  1. Tasking
  2. Design
  3. Development
  4. Testing
  5. Rehearsal
  6. Execution
  7. Post-Game Analysis
  8. Archival

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
Well-defined, specific objectives are foundational. Objectives should be as specific as possible and drive the entire structure of the wargame.

  • Single objective recommended — multiple objectives complicate design, execution, and analysis
  • Purpose types:
  • Experiential — improving commanders' decision-making skills
  • Analytical — gathering information on decision-making processes and outcomes

docs.title: 2. Players
docs.text:
The human element distinguishes a wargame from a mere simulation. Players bring knowledge, experience, and decision-making abilities.

  • Players should be cast in operational roles reflecting their actual positions
  • Roles should match real-world responsibilities
  • Role substitutions require additional information support (e.g., detailed OOB)

docs.title: 3. Scenario
docs.text:
Provides context for decision-making. A compelling scenario significantly affects the decisions players can make.

Key elements: - Scenario Background — establishes key actors, attitudes, intentions, and goals - Player Objectives — creates tension or conflict between players - Defined Relationships — organizational structure and command relationships - Available Resources — OOB, equipment, intelligence, logistics - Information Update Mechanisms — situation reports, intelligence updates, injects - Compelling Narrative — must engage players or the wargame will falter

docs.title: 4. Game Engine
docs.text: Consists of models, database, ruleset, and adjudication method.

docs.title: Models
docs.text: Translate game data and player decisions into game events. Often a combination of look-up tables and mathematical expressions.

docs.title: Database
docs.text: Repository of information for player decisions: - Available forces and capabilities - Environmental conditions - Technical details

docs.title: Ruleset
docs.text:
Governs how and when to apply models. Sequences game events, ensures players receive the right quantity and quality of information.

Effective rulesets incorporate fog of war elements: - Errors in player information - Delays in order execution

docs.title: Adjudication Methods
docs.text: Method Description Example Free Outcome determined by facilitator/SME professional opinion Free Kriegsspiel, matrix games Rigid Outcome through mathematical model or ruleset (MMT) Rigid Kriegsspiel Semi-rigid Initial MMT result, modifiable by facilitator Common in analytical wargames Consensual Outcome agreed by group discussion Matrix games, seminar wargames

docs.title: 5. Analysis / After Action Review
docs.text: Ensures capture of information defined by the objectives: - Training game: instructor observation and critique - Research game: understanding why decisions were made - Data collected during gameplay is the raw material for synthesis of insights

docs.title: Phase 1 – Tasking
docs.text: Initial contact, problem statements, purpose, objectives, research questions, requirements, schedule, proposal, plan of action, funding, player recruitment, game report, executive brief, authorisation.

docs.title: Phase 2 – Design

docs.title: Types and Examples of Military Simulation and Wargames
Live, Virtual, and Constructive (LVC)
docs.text: The LVC taxonomy classifies modelling, simulation, and wargames by the degree of human and system involvement.

docs.title: Live Simulation and Wargaming
docs.text:
Real people operate real systems. Involves actual forces and equipment in a controlled setting.

Examples: - Field Training Exercises (FTX) - Joint and combined-arms exercises - Medieval jousts → modern military exercises

docs.title: Virtual Simulation and Wargaming
docs.text:
Real people operate simulated systems. Enabled by electronic simulators and computer networks. Central to these is the Human-in-the-Loop, which exercises: - Motor control skills (flying a jet, tank simulator) - Decision-making skills (committing fire control resources) - Communication skills (C4I team member)

Examples: - ARMA / Virtual Battlespace (VBS) - Flight simulators - Maritime simulators

docs.title: Constructive Simulation and Wargaming
docs.text:
Simulated people operate simulated systems. Real people provide inputs but do not determine outcomes. This allows examination of complex systems without actual forces or equipment.

Examples: - Chess to latest campaign-planning wargames - Command Post Exercises (CPX)

docs.title: SANDF Command Post Exercise (CPX)
docs.text: The CPX is regularly used by the SANDF. Mission Readiness and Battle Readiness training are often provided through a CPX. A CPX is essentially a computer-assisted simulation of the processes and procedures that occur at or through particular levels of command and control.

docs.title: Manual / Table-Top Wargames
docs.text: Executed without computers or electronic devices. Can use pen and paper.

docs.title: Formats
docs.text: Format Description Miniature Wargaming Units represented by miniature models on model terrain Board Wargames Printed board symbolizing battlespace; forces represented by counters, miniatures, or tokens Matrix Wargames Players make structured logical arguments to advance the game

docs.title: Matrix Wargame Example
docs.text:
In a scenario involving the SANDF in the DRC, a commander might argue:

"I shall fortify our base, and I am able to do this because: - We have a well-trained force ready to implement defensive measures. - We have an experienced engineer in the team. - The South African Government has allocated the necessary funds."

docs.title: Advantages and Limitations of Manual Wargames
docs.text: # Advantage Limitation 1 Accessibility — minimal resources Time-consuming setup 2 Flexibility — easily adapted Limited complexity 3 Tangibility — physical immersion Human error / bias 4 No technological barrier Oversimplification 5 Cost-effective Lack of visual realism 6 Collaborative learning Limited replayability 7 Develops strategic thinking Scalability limits

docs.title: Computer-Assisted Wargames
docs.text:
Record-keeping and calculations handled by a computer; the "meat" of the wargame still takes place in the physical world.

Example: Virtual Advanced Squad Leader (VASL) - Digital rendition of Advanced Squad Leader (ASL) - Free software; functions as a digital record-keeper - Does not enforce rules — players control rules enforcement and decisions - Second- to third-generation digitally-assisted wargame

docs.title: Digital Wargames
docs.text:
Entire wargame run digitally on a computer. The computer depicts the state of the wargame on a display, from very abstract to extremely detailed.

Example: Hearts of Iron IV - Grand strategy computer simulation by Paradox Development Studio - Player controls any country from 1936 or 1939 - Simulates ground, naval, and aerial forces - Uses database and simplified models for interactions - Considered a simulation (no human opponent) rather than a wargame

docs.title: Advantages and Limitations of Computer-Assisted and Digital Wargames
docs.text:
• Can hold much more information than human participants
  • Enable large and complex wargames
  • Slightly blur the lines between wargames and simulation
  • Technology-dependent; require skilled operators

docs.title: Hybrid Simulation and Wargaming
docs.text:
Characterised by using a mixture of Constructive, Live, and/or Virtual paradigms.

Source: Wargaming and Military Simulation for the SANDF, TRG COMD/R/103/6, May 2025, Capt P.A.R. Malan.

docs.title: Tactical Decision Games (TDGs)
docs.text:
"A tactical decision game is a short, focused exercise in which a commander or leader must make a decision under time pressure, based on a sparse situation and a sketch map — then explain the reasoning."

— adapted from USMC schoolhouse practice, transposed to SANDF command-post training

docs.title: What is a TDG?
docs.text:
A Tactical Decision Game is a decision-forcing vignette. It is not a planning exercise, not a battle simulation, and not a free Kriegspiel. Its purpose is singular: compress the observe-orient-decide-act loop into a two-to-five-minute decision box, then expose the reasoning to peer or umpire critique.

Dimension TDG Command Post EX (CPX) Field EX (FTX) Time per decision 2–5 min 30–120 min Hours to days Fidelity Sketch + narrative Semi-structured Full terrain Audience Section to Company HQ to Bde Battalion+ Purpose Judgment drill Staff coordination Live validation Replayability High — rerun with variants Medium Low — terrain-specific

docs.title: SANDF TDG Format
docs.text: Every TDG in this library follows the same minimal envelope so it can be run in a classroom, on a mapsheet, or over a sand table in 15 minutes flat.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
1. Situation — 3–8 sentences. Who, what, where, when, why. No solution embedded.
  2. Map Sketch — North arrow, scale bar, key terrain labels, unit positions at H-hour. One-page maximum.
  3. Forces — Friendly and enemy ORBAT in SANDF shorthand (unit type, weapons, key attachments).
  4. Constraints / Higher Guidance — Mission, commander’s intent, ROE, logistical limits.
  5. Decision Required — Single verb: deploy, attack, delay, withdraw, report, request. Timed.
  6. Decision Box — Trainee writes: (a) decision, (b) rationale in two sentences, (c) branches.
  7. Umpire / Facilitator Notes — Minimum acceptable standard, likely errors, inject variants.

docs.title: ORBAT Notation (SANDF Shorthand)
docs.text:
Use this throughout the library so every page is readable across units.

Code Meaning Inf Sec Infantry section (~12–15) Inf Plt Infantry platoon (~30–40) Mech Plt Mechanised platoon (Ratel-20/-25) Mot Plt Motorised platoon (Samil 50/100) Arty Bty Artillery battery (GV4/L22) Tk Sqn Tank squadron (Olifant/Rooikat) Engr Sqn Engineer squadron Sig Sqn Signals squadron ADA Tp Air Defence troop Med Coy Medical company

docs.title: Adjudication Rubric
docs.text:
Criterion Pass (2) Marginal (1) Fail (0) Decision aligns with mission/ intent Directly supports higher intent Partially supports Contradicts Terrain used Key terrain seized/denied Terrain mentioned Terrain ignored Force protection Survivability considered Partial Reckless Tempo / surprise Timing creates advantage No consideration Inverted Branch awareness Next 2–3 moves named One branch named None ROE / legal Compliant Borderline Breach noted

Score ≥ 8/12 = ACCEPT. 5–7 = REDO with facilitator. ≤4 = FAIL — retrain before independent command.

docs.title: TDG Library
docs.text:
• TDG-01 — Dry Riverbed Ambush
  • TDG-02 — Checkpoint Alpha
  • TDG-03 — Bridging Team Under Fire
  • TDG-04 — Medevac in the Contact Zone
  • TDG-05 — Silent Net

docs.title: How to Use This Library
docs.text:
1. Select the echelon matching your training event.
  2. Print the TDG + map sketch; distribute one copy per trainee.
  3. State the decision box aloud, start the timer.
  4. Collect at time; read anonymously or call on trainees.
  5. Run the Umpire Notes; score against the rubric.
  6. Re-run with inject variant (see page footer) to test flexibility.

Library curated by Archon Telos for Strategos Telos. Sources: USMC Tactical Decision Games archive (themaneuverist.org), Wargaming and Military Simulation for the SANDF (TRG COMD/R/103/6, May 2025, Capt P.A.R. Malan).

docs.title: Classification
docs.text: Echelon: Section commander Type: Immediate action drill / ambush reaction Decision time: 3 minutes Source: Original design — SANDF context

docs.title: Situation
docs.text:
It is 06:45, 15°C, clear skies, good visibility. Your section is moving along a dry riverbed (wadi) on foot as part of a larger company movement to contact. The riverbed runs east–west; 3-metre banks on both sides with sparse thornveld. You have no communications with platoon HQ since entering the bed.

At the bend 200 m ahead, two trucks and a light troop-carrying vehicle are parked nose-to-tail, engine-off, on the north bank. Three figures are visible near the trucks; no weapons are obvious. Your section is currently in column, moving single file along the wadi floor.

Your section consists of:

Group Composition Forward point (2 men) 50 m ahead of you, entering the bend Section HQ You + 2IC, R4, VHF radio, 2× 60 mm mortar rounds Rifle group 1 (4 men) R4, 2× R1 grenades, 1× 90 mm rocket Rifle group 2 (4 men) R4, 2× 60 mm mortar rounds Machine gun group (2 men) Vektor SS-77, 800 rounds

Platoon order of march placed you in security reserve for this leg.

docs.title: Map Sketch
docs.text:
NORTH ↑

North bank
  [Truck][Truck][LCV] ← enemy suspected
       ∧  ∧  ∧
      3m 3m 3m
  ───────────────────  ← wadi floor (your position)
       ∨  ∨  ∨
      3m 3m 3m
South bank
  thornveld / open

Forward point: → (50 m ahead, entering bend)
Your position: ■ (section HQ, middle of column)

Key terrain: - Bend creates a dead zone 80 m long; no LOS from your position to the trucks until the forward point clears it. - Wadi narrows to 15 m at the bend; widens to 40 m east of the trucks. - North bank has partial vehicle cover at ±20 m from trucks.

docs.title: Commander's Intent (Platoon)
docs.text: "Move through. Locate and fix any enemy. Avoid decisive engagement. Link up with platoon HQ at RV EMERALD by 08:00."

docs.title: Higher Constraints
docs.text:
• You have no indirect fire on call until RV EMERALD.
  • ROE: Positive identification required before engaging — suspected insurgent cache, not confirmed hostile force.
  • Casualty evacuation not available closer than 5 km.
  • Your forward point has not reported.

docs.title: Decision Required
docs.text:
What do you do in the next 3 minutes?

Write: (a) your decision, (b) two-sentence rationale, (c) next three branches.

docs.title: Minimum Acceptable Standard
docs.text:
1. Halt the section immediately. No further movement into the dead zone without reconnaissance.
  2. Deploy forward point to overwatch the bend from the south bank (gain LOS without exposing column).
  3. Send one rifle group to high ground on south bank for flank observation.
  4. Place machine gun group in covering position at 100 m back from bend, oriented north.
  5. Attempt to establish radio contact with platoon HQ to report and request guidance.

docs.title: Likely Errors and How to Adjudicate Them
docs.text: Error Severity Reasoning Move forward to "assess" FAIL Exposes column to dead zone; violates security reserve role Open fire immediately FAIL ROE requires PID; civilians or peaceable persons may be present Withdraw entirely MARGINAL Safe but loses initiative; platoon intent is movement Send whole section to clear bend MARGINAL Overcommits; no reserve; no contact with platoon Halt + deploy as above PASS Standard textbook reaction; matches intent

docs.title: Recommended Inject Variants
docs.text:
1. The forward point reports: "Three armed males, AK-47, moving toward trucks." — Decision box restarts with PID achieved.
  2. The trucks explode: IED detonation on north bank at 06:52. — Reaction drill becomes casualty evacuation + security.
  3. Platoon HQ calls: "Enemy RPG team reported 1 km east. Accelerate movement." — Pressure test on tempo vs. security.

docs.title: Scoring Rubric
docs.text:
See Tactical Decision Games Index for rubric criteria.

Criterion Your Score Notes Mission/Intent alignment Terrain use Force protection Tempo/surprise Branch awareness ROE/legal Total /12

docs.title: After-Action
docs.text:
• What was your decision?
  • What did you learn?
  • If you ran this with an inject, how did your plan change?

docs.title: Classification
docs.text: Echelon: Platoon commander Type: Movement to contact / ambiguous situation Decision time: 4 minutes Source: Original design — SANDF context

docs.title: Situation
docs.text:
It is 08:20, 22°C, light haze. Your mechanised platoon is conducting a road march along Route B1 from Fort iKopan to staging area VICTOR. You are moving in Ratel-20 section pairs with a Samil 100 ammo resupply vehicle at the tail of the column.

You are the advance guard for the company. At Checkpoint Alpha (a crossroads with a small filling station and a police roadblock post), you receive a radio message from the station commander:

"Unknown convoy, five vehicles, northbound on B1. No markings. Approaching your position now. Estimated 10 minutes."

Two minutes later, your point section reports:

"Five vehicles. Two looks like unmarked Toyota Hilux, one covered truck, one white ambulance no Red Cross markings, one Matatu with civilian passengers. No visible weapons. Windows up. Speed 40 km/h. Not slowing."

The crossroads has a t-junction with Route C2 heading east toward the border. Your platoon is currently spread over 800 m along B1. The company main is 4 km behind you.

docs.title: Forces
docs.text:
Friendly — Your Platoon | Group | Composition | |---|---| | Advance guard (2 sections) | Ratel-20 x4, 90 mm + .50 cal | | Platoon HQ | Ratel-25, commander, 2IC, VHF/UHF, 2× 60 mm mortars | | Company main | Rest of company, 4 km south | | Resupply | Samil 100, 800 m behind you |

Unknown — Reported Convoy | Vehicle | Assessment | |---|---| | 2× Toyota Hilux | Possible technical basis; unmarked | | 1× Covered truck | Unknown cargo | | 1× White ambulance | No markings — suspicious | | 1× Matatu | Civilian; women and children visible |

docs.title: Map Sketch
docs.text:
NORTH ↑
Border (20 km)
       ↑
       |
  C2 ←—+—→ B1 (your axis)
       A   ← Checkpoint Alpha (t-junction)
           [Filling station]
           [Police post — unoccupied]

  → Convoy approaching from north on B1
  → Your platoon strung south on B1
  → No terrain defilade within 500 m

Key terrain: - Checkpoint Alpha is open — no cover for vehicles on the north approach. - Fuel station has above-ground tanks; potential hazard. - Police post is unoccupied — no local security force present. - C2 eastbound offers cover and concealment in wooded terrain 800 m east.

docs.title: Commander's Intent (Company)
docs.text: "Move to VICTOR without delay. Avoid contact unless decisive. Report all suspicious activity. Coordinate with SAPS if possible."

docs.title: Higher Constraints
docs.text:
• ROE: Stop and search authorised for suspected smuggling/cross-border crime; positive identification before engaging.
  • You have no authority to block the road without company CO approval.
  • Civilian presence in Matatu means collateral risk is high.
  • Your mortars are not yet registered; no indirect fire without 5-minute setup.
  • Intelligence: small arms smuggling reported on this route in the last 48 hours.

docs.title: Decision Required
docs.text:
What do you do in the next 4 minutes?

Write: (a) your decision, (b) two-sentence rationale, (c) next three branches.

docs.title: Minimum Acceptable Standard
docs.text:
1. Halt advance guard and establish overwatch positions off the road (south side, defilade).
  2. Attempt to hail convoy via siren/loudhailer — demand stop for inspection.
  3. Deploy one section to secure the filling station and police post as a temporary blocking position.
  4. Radio company HQ with situation report; request authority to detain/search.
  5. Identify ambulance as priority — unmarked medical vehicle in smuggling convoy is a war crime indicator under international law.

docs.title: Likely Errors and How to Adjudicate Them
docs.text: Error Severity Reasoning Let convoy pass without action FAIL Violates company intent; smuggling proceeds Block road with vehicles MARGINAL Aggressive; risks civilian casualties in Matatu Open fire on Hiluxes FAIL No PID; civilian vehicle mixed in Halt + hail + secure police post PASS Proportional; preserves options Deploy ambush on C2 MARGINAL Premature; no authority; ambiguous threat

docs.title: Recommended Inject Variants
docs.text:
1. The ambulance stops first: Driver exits, shows weapon, opens fire. — Contact drill initiated.
  2. Convoy accelerates past checkpoint: They are heading for the border. — Pursuit vs. report dilemma.
  3. SAPS arrives: Two police vehicles from the south. — Joint operation / handover protocol.

docs.text:
See Tactical Decision Games Index for rubric criteria.

Criterion Your Score Notes Mission/Intent alignment Terrain use Force protection Tempo/surprise Branch awareness ROE/legal Total /12

docs.text:
• What was your decision?
  • What did you learn?
  • If you ran this with an inject, how did your plan change?

docs.title: Classification
docs.text: Echelon: Engineer troop / section commander Type: Route clearance / hasty bridge / direct fire threat Decision time: 4 minutes Source: Original design — SANDF context

docs.title: Situation
docs.text:
It is 14:30, 28°C, high humidity. Your engineer section (12 personnel, 2× Samil 100 trucks, 1× Meerkat mine detector, bridging equipment) is tasked to reopen Route D5 for a mechanised company advance. The route crosses the Matshakatini River at a single-lane concrete bridge that was demolished by the enemy 18 hours ago with a satchel charge; the east abutment is intact, the west abutment is collapsed 4 m into the river.

The river is 30 m wide, 1.5 m deep at the crossing point, moderate current. The surrounding terrain is dense mopane woodland with limited observation.

Your section has:

Asset Quantity / Status Medium Girder Bridge (MGB) 1 set, 2 spans, requires 4×Samil for transport Meerkat 1, operational R4 / grenades All personnel 60 mm mortar 1, 12 rounds, forward observer trained VHF radio 1, contact with company HQ

The company is waiting at start line HARTS, 3 km west. The enemy is assessed as a light infantry battalion with anti-tank capability, last seen 8 km north — but reconnaissance has not been confirmed for 4 hours.

docs.title: Map Sketch
docs.text:
NORTH ↑
[Woodland]  [Woodland]
    ↑           ↑
    |           |
  River ———————— 30 m
    |           |
    ↓           ↓
[Collapsed    [East abutment
 west abutment] (intact)]
    |
  Route D5
    |
    ↓
  Your position (start line HARTS)
    |
    ↓
  Company waiting (3 km)

Key terrain: - River bend 1 km upstream offers cover for enemy observation. - Single-track approach road on west side; no alternate crossing within 10 km. - Mopane woodland on both banks within 200 m of river — classic ambush terrain. - East bank is open for 400 m; good tank killing ground.

docs.title: Commander's Intent (Company)
docs.text: "Reopen route D5 not later than 16:00. Company advances to phase line HAWK at 17:00. Engineer priority: establish crossing, clear mines, mark route."

docs.title: Higher Constraints
docs.text:
• No organic armour attached to your section.
  • Mortar support available on 10-minute call from company mortar platoon.
  • Close air support not available until 17:00.
  • ROE: engage if threatened; positive identification preferred.
  • Bridge demolition charges may be re-laid by enemy as booby traps.

docs.title: Decision Required
docs.text:
What do you do in the next 4 minutes?

Write: (a) your decision, (b) two-sentence rationale, (c) next three branches.

docs.title: Minimum Acceptable Standard
docs.text:
1. Do not begin emplacement until both banks are reconnoitred and secured.
  2. Deploy Meerkat on west bank approach road to check for mines.
  3. Send 2-person recce team across river (swim/boat if available) to check east bank for booby traps.
  4. Request company security: one infantry section to secure west bank woodline; one section to secure east bank crossing site.
  5. Establish mortar observation post on high ground 300 m south to overwatch crossing site.

docs.title: Likely Errors and How to Adjudicate Them
docs.text: Error Severity Reasoning Begin bridging immediately FAIL Exposes section to ambush; bridge may be booby-trapped Send one truck across first MARGINAL Tests depth but commits asset without recon Call company and wait MARGINAL Safe but loses time; intent requires 16:00 crossing Recon + request security + start prep PASS Textbook engineer procedure Build bridge at night only FAIL Intent requires daylight crossing for company advance

docs.title: Recommended Inject Variants
docs.text:
1. Recce reports: "Booby trap found on west abutment. Wire run to tree line 200 m north." — EOD drill required.
  2. Enemy mortar rounds: 81 mm impacts on approach road at 14:45. — Casualty drill + route alternate.
  3. Company cancels advance: Orders change; your section now has 6 hours. — Bridge construction vs. expedient ford.
